guidance_config.mergeProcess:
Create a github PR for the user to review.

The ship gate means merging that pull request through the github MCP, always with the squash merge method. If the github MCP is not available, stop and say so rather than merging another way.
guidance_config.testingTool:
Use `uv run pytest --testmon` to initialize the red/green test cache, then run it again every time to verify tests with changes made.

Trust `--testmon` to have correctly determined which tests the change affects. A `--testmon` run that reports the affected tests passing IS equivalent to running the full suite - the deselected tests are deselected because testmon has established they cannot be reached by the change, not because they were skipped. Do not re-run the suite without `--testmon` to "make sure", and do not treat a deselected count as an unverified gap: that re-run costs the whole point of the cache and tells you nothing the testmon run did not already.
guidance_config.groundingTool:
Use graphify to locate code and find references, instead of grepping or loading whole files.

The graph is already built at `graphify-out/graph.json`, so query it directly rather than rebuilding: `graphify query "<what you are looking for>"`. It returns the symbol with its file and line, the community it clusters into, and the surrounding call flow - which is what tells you the blast radius. Widen a truncated answer with `--budget`, and use `graphify path "<A>" "<B>"` or `graphify explain "<symbol>"` when you need the connection between two things or a plain-language read of one.

summary.body: A structured-wiki server that exposes one typed core through two front doors: an MCP tool surface (FastMCP) for agents and a read-only browser web UI for humans. Every page is a typed page-type instance governed by a status finite-state machine, authored only through validated commands and persisted to plain files.

purpose.body: Give agents a structured wiki over MCP where knowledge is typed and state-aware. A page cannot drift into free-form text (its shape is fixed by its page type), and status changes are governed by a per-type state machine rather than by convention.

usage.body: The MCP surface runs over HTTP (mounted at /pasta/mcp) or over stdio (--stdio, for a client that spawns the server); its tools divide into reads that change nothing, and writes that go through validated commands. A read still takes the shared half of its workspace's readers-writer lock while it reads the file off disk, so it never observes a write in progress; readers do not exclude one another. The same content is browsable read-only as HTML at / (workspace index → page tree → rendered page). The authoring loop is the same on either transport: describe a page type, then issue commands whose legality depends on the page's current status — the concrete tools and their arguments are discovered from the server, not fixed here.

dataModel.body:
One JSON document per workspace under PASTA_DATA_DIR (default ./.pasta-data). The workspace id ws:<token> maps to the filename ws_<token>.json - ':' is not a legal Windows filename character, so the true id lives inside the file - and listWorkspaces enumerates workspaces by globbing *.json under the data dir. That glob is NON-recursive, which is why pre-prune backups live in a backups/<ws_token>/ subdirectory: a backup written beside the live file would be listed as a duplicate workspace.

A workspace holds every page keyed by id; a page holds sections[sectionKey][fieldKey] = value, where a field is a scalar, a prose string, a list of id'd elements (optionally each with its own status), or an ordered list of typed blocks. A page's section and field shape comes from its page type in the registry, not from disk. Beside its sections a page carries four flat persisted fields: `archived`, `links`, `expires_at` (nullable UTC ISO-8601, written and cleared only by the cleanup sweep), and `status_revision_token` (written only by the store).

Keeping the whole workspace in a single document is what makes the write story simple: the entire workspace is serialized and swapped as one file. The swap is a temp-file write - named with the writing process's pid and thread id - followed by os.replace (src/store.py::_write_file), retried once after a short sleep because a Windows permission error moving the temp file is transient. The replace is atomic, so the destination is never observed partially written. A per-workspace readers-writer lock (src/rwlock.py) orders readers against it: the replace holds the lock exclusively and every read of a workspace file holds it shared, so a reader sees the pre- or post-write file. The lock is in-process only - a second OS process writing the same data directory is still unguarded.

A workspace document can now SHRINK as well as grow: the hourly cleanup sweep permanently deletes expired pages, having written a full timestamped backup first.

Beside each workspace file sits its lifecycle log, ws_<token>.events.jsonl: an append-only JSON-lines record of every page creation, status transition and archive-flag change, which the store appends after each save that made one (see Authoring & mutation) and the timeline view replays (see Timeline replay). Its .jsonl suffix is not matched by the *.json glob, so the log is never taken for a workspace, and backups copy only the workspace document.

inlines.text: The two locks, and which job each does

inlines: - the mechanism behind the invariant that each workspace carries two locks. The transaction lock (a
) is held across a whole load to mutate to save, so concurrent writers cannot lose each other's updates. The readers-writer lock (

) is held for one file operation - exclusively by the replace that swaps a workspace file, shared by every read of one - so a reader never parses a file mid-write. Both are in-process and keyed by workspace id, so one lock covers every file a workspace is stored in, its backups included.

inlines.text: The layering is the seam features slot into

inlines: - why the one-directional layering is worth defending rather than merely true. It is the seam every later feature slots into without reshaping the core: a new field kind is a
plus a serialize case, a new page type is a
entry, and a new tool is a server function.

inlines.text: How the split shows up in the tests

inlines: - the pure-core / stateful-shell split is exactly what the two test tiers key off. The pure core (pagetypes, fsm, commands, serialize, render) is unit-tested in isolation with no I/O, while the stateful shell's transaction helpers (create_workspace, load_workspace, create_page, mutate_page_batch, list_workspaces) get integration tests that drive load to pure-core to atomic-save end to end.

inlines.text: The backup is what makes deletion safe

inlines: - a workspace document is no longer append-mostly. The scheduled cleanup sweep is the one path that removes pages, and it never does so without first writing a full copy of the workspace to backups/ under a UTC-stamped filename. If the backup write fails the whole pass for that workspace is abandoned unchanged, so a deletion without a recoverable snapshot cannot occur.

inlines.text: Corrections at a35b133

inlines: - two mechanism claims on this page had gone stale. First, the file swap:
serializes to a pid-and-thread-unique temp file and then calls
under the exclusive half of the readers-writer lock, retrying once after a short sleep because a Windows permission error moving the temp file is transient. It is not a

followed by an unlink, and there is no window in which the destination is briefly incomplete - so the readers-writer lock is what orders readers against the swap rather than what compensates for a non-atomic copy. Second, the tool shape: all 24 MCP tools are
, not sync functions on worker threads; what serializes conflicting read-modify-write cycles is the per-workspace transaction lock, not the threading model.

inlines.text: Error translation at the boundary

inlines: - each MCP tool resolves its inputs, runs a store transaction and returns a JSON-able dict, translating a
raised by the pure core or the store into a FastMCP
carrying an actionable message. An
additionally carries the currently-legal command set, so a caller that has been refused is told what it can do instead.

items.statement: The pure core (model, pagetypes, fsm, commands, serialize) does no I/O and never mutates its inputs; it copies, edits, and returns a new page. Violated, the domain rules can no longer be exercised without a filesystem, and a rejected write leaves edits on the caller's in-memory page.

Each workspace carries two locks with distinct jobs and neither substitutes for the other: a transaction lock held across a whole write, and a readers-writer lock held for one file operation. Drop the first and updates are silently lost; drop the second and a reader can fail with a corrupt-workspace error.

The layering is strictly one-directional: server to store to pure core (commands / fsm / serialize) to model / pagetypes / errors. The core imports neither store nor server, and only the stateful shell does I/O, creates ids, or serves MCP. Violated, the domain layer can no longer be exercised with no filesystem, and the import graph admits a cycle.

Every expected (non-bug) failure is a PastaError subclass - NotFoundError, ValidationError, IllegalCommandError, ConflictError - and an IllegalCommandError additionally carries the currently-legal command set. Violated, a domain failure reaches the client as an unhandled server crash instead of an actionable message, and a caller has no way to recover.
No page is ever deleted without a full workspace backup written first, in the same locked pass. Violated, an incorrect classification by the cleanup sweep becomes unrecoverable data loss.

summary.body: The typed page-type layer and its finite-state-machine engine. Page types are declared as data (sections, fields, commands, and an FSM spec) in a registry; status transitions are evaluated by building one python-statemachine class per FSM spec.

purpose.body: Make pages typed and state-aware instead of free-form. A page's shape and its legal edits come from its page type, not from prose, and status changes are governed by a per-type finite state machine rather than by convention. All domain rules for a type live in one declarative place: the registry.

usage.body: createPage initializes a page from its PageType. apply_command looks the command up by name, copies the page and backfills any section the type has since gained (re-seeding every fixed field from its declaration), then hands the copy to _apply, which validates the arguments against the command's ArgSpecs, checks legality and applies the edit; the edited copy is returned. A compound runs each of its steps back through _apply - the same validation, legality check and dispatch - before firing its own transition. legal_commands (surfaced by describeMutations) reports what is allowed right now. The FSM decides transition legality, and required-content preconditions additionally gate a transition until named fields are filled. describePageType reports a type's sections, fields, commands, and FSM.

dataModel.body: A PageType composes ordered sections (each a set of typed fields), its commands, a status-FSM spec that carries its status set, its terminal statuses, and an optional per-status guidance text (the transition table is derived, not authored — see the invariants), and optionally pinned auto-children, each declared as an AutoChildSpec (a page-type tag) on the PARENT type and created in the same commit as the page. A field is a scalar (optionally an enum), a prose body (optionally fixed: FieldSpec.fixed declares its whole value, which initial_sections seeds on create and re-seeds on every backfill and which no command may write - the epic's Controller notice is one), a list of id'd elements — which may declare its own element FSM (an ElementFSMSpec) so each element carries a status, and may declare that some of its element fields hold BLOCKS rather than a scalar value (an ElementBlocksSpec naming the field and the vocabulary it accepts) — or a blocks field of structured rich text. A blocks field declares the KINDS it accepts as a tuple of BlockKindSpec: each names a kind and the body args that kind takes in THIS field, which is how one kind name can mean inline runs in one field and a plain text arg in another (paragraph_runs versus paragraph_text), and how a field defines a kind outside the standard set (feature-spec's question-linked decision). The kinds are built by helper factories in core/args.py; a field that accepts every standard kind passes standard_blocks() explicitly, and there is no implicit default. A blocks field is not free markdown: every block (headings, code, lists, tables, quotes, dividers, and question-linked decisions among them) holds its text as an ordered array of inline runs — plain, marked, linked, code, or page-reference — checked against a run grammar before any write, and a block-bearing element field stores exactly the same block shapes one level deeper. A command is one frozen dataclass per kind, carrying exactly the fields its kind uses, and CommandSpec is the union of the fourteen, built in two layers: AuthoringCommand (the twelve non-transition kinds) | TransitionCommand | CompoundCommand. Every command has a name, a description, its argument specs (a block-carrying arg additionally holds the vocabulary it accepts, resolved onto it from the field it targets rather than declared at the command), a uniform legal_in gate (a content command's 'ready' lock, or a transition's source status(es)) and an agency; its kind is a class constant, not a constructor argument. A field command adds the section and field it writes; an element add its element_map and an optional cross-page ref_check; an element write its element_map and constant flags; an element transition the element-FSM event; a block command an optional element_field naming the element field it addresses. A status transition carries its FSM event, its destination status (dest), required-content preconditions and the cross-page child and parent guards the store evaluates; a compound is a status transition that also holds steps - authoring commands applied in order before it fires. A ref check may also sit on a BLOCK KIND rather than the command, because the referencing argument then lives inside a block. The REGISTRY maps each tag to its PageType; the concrete types — the feature-lifecycle family, a general-purpose document, the self-describing architecture type — are each declared in their own module under src/pagetypes/ and imported into the registry there, and are what describePageType reports.

inlines.text: Construction order, and what post-init does not do

does setup only, in a fixed order: it resolves each block argument's vocabulary from the field it targets, derives the FSM transition table from the commands, then builds the machines those declarations describe - its own status machine, and every element machine hanging off its list fields.
walks

and skips a spec that already carries a machine or an error, which is what makes one ElementFSMSpec shared by two page types build exactly once instead of the second declarer overwriting the first's class. It does not validate: constructing a malformed page type does not raise, and a machine that cannot be built is captured on the spec rather than thrown out of the declaration. Resolution is best-effort - it fills a block argument's kinds in when the target field resolves and leaves block_kinds None when it cannot, so a partly-resolvable type still constructs. Validation is a separate recursive pass in core/validation.py:

composes the per-spec validators, validate_page_machine, the two page-type setter validators, validate_pagetype_fixed_fields and validate_pagetype_block_args, each returning a list of messages rather than raising, and
collects every message across the registry and raises a single ValueError listing all of them.

runs that pass at src/server.py module load, which is what stops a cold start on an invalid declaration and fails a hot reload on one: a reload is all or nothing, so it rolls back to the last good build and both surfaces refuse until a reload succeeds. Each surface also asks
- the same pass asked as a question rather than a raise - per request (see
). FSMSpec and FieldSpec keep only their text normalization in post-init, and BlockKindSpec and ElementBlocksSpec have no hook at all.
One machine per spec, built by its declarer

inlines: - every machine is built by the declaration that describes it, so there is one rule rather than two. A page type builds its own status FSM and every element FSM on its list fields in post-init, and each machine is stored on the SPEC rather than on the page type, because a spec and its machine are one to one while a spec may be declared by several page types.
is therefore a pure read: it hands back spec.machine and raises LookupError for a spec no page type declares, never building on demand. One class per spec is what lets

serve one importable name per page type, and only page-status machines are served there, because only they are diagrammed - an element machine is reached through the field that declares it and needs no importable address. Building is also that spec's own well-formedness check: python-statemachine's connectivity, unreachable-state and trap-state checks have run for every registered type before anything serves, and a machine that cannot be built does not raise out of the module declaring it -

reports the captured error inside the aggregated raise. A failed element machine is reported by the page that declares it, named as the element spec plus the section.field it hangs off, which is why an element spec no page type declares needs no reporting at all: it is unreachable, so there is no ownerless failure to attribute.

rewrites each state attribute name back to the state as its author declared it, so the message reads in the vocabulary the declaration is written in. Nothing re-derives reachability in validation.py: the build is the check, and a second implementation of it would drift from the library's.

inlines.text: Why there is no machine cache, and what that retired
- with page and element machines both owned by the declaration that describes them,

holds no memo: a dev session can no longer retain a dead machine class per distinct declaration, and the reload path carries no hook for the FSM layer - a reload re-imports the page-type modules, which build their machines again, and does not know the FSM layer exists. An element FSM that no page type declares is therefore unreachable rather than lazily built, which surfaces the programming error at the call instead of quietly handing out a fresh class per call. What this retires is the hashability constraint on the spec dataclasses - FSMSpec.status_guidance as a tuple of pairs, the block vocabularies as tuples - which existed to key an lru_cache. Those shapes now stand on value semantics alone, so the next reader finding a tuple there is looking at a frozen value type, not a cache key.
A status edge is declared once, on its command

inlines: - a transition or compound command names the FSM event, its source status(es) via legal_in, and its destination via
. The private

derives the whole page FSM table from these commands - one (event, source, dest, agency) edge per legal_in source of every StatusTransitionCommand, declaration order preserved - and post-init writes it onto the otherwise-unset
before building the machine from it. A compound's steps hold no edge to walk: they are typed as authoring commands, and

rejects a status-transition step, so the compound's own event is the only edge it fires. So an authored FSMSpec carries only the status set, the machine reads the derived table, and no status edge is written in two places; legal_in is thereby the uniform "where is this legal" declaration for every command kind. Element lifecycles are the deliberate exception: an ElementFSMSpec keeps its own transition table, because an element_transition command's legal_in is the page-status lock and not the element source state, so there is nothing to derive. describe suppresses legalIn for transition and compound commands, since their source already appears in the derived FSM transition list.

inlines.text: Terminal statuses freeze a page's authoring surface

inlines: - this is declared once on the FSM rather than repeated per command.
names the statuses in which the work is done, and

allows only status transitions there, so every content command is locked automatically while a remaining transition such as reopen stays legal. feature-spec sealing was converted to this form - statuses (draft, sealed) with terminal_states=(sealed,), replacing a legal_in=("draft",) repeated on every one of its authoring commands. The behaviour is identical but the lock is no longer restated on each command, so a newly added spec command cannot forget it. legal_in stays the right tool for a lock covering only SOME statuses of a still-active page, and an authoring command can opt back in inside a terminal status by naming it in legal_in.

inlines.text: Element lifecycles, and how their states render

inlines: - beyond the page-status FSM, a list field may declare an element_fsm so each element carries its own status, fired by an

command: plan steps todo to done or skipped, testing cases pending to passed, failed or skipped, questions open to answered. A step's skip is reversible via reopen back to todo; a case's skip is one-way. An element FSM also carries how its states render as a task checkbox:

names the state shown as a checked box, and the FSM's initial state is then the unchecked box. So the todo/done and pending/passed mapping lives with the element-state definition and is read off field_spec.element_fsm by the renderer rather than matched against hardcoded status strings. A state that is neither the checkmark_done box nor the initial box (a case's failed, a step or case's skipped), an element FSM without checkmark_done (questions), and every page-status FSM render with no box - the state still shows as a trailing status suffix, so a skipped item stays visible.

inlines.text: Blocks: the run grammar, the vocabularies, and element blocks

inlines: - a blocks field declares the KINDS it accepts as a tuple of

: each names a kind and the body args that kind takes in THIS field, which is how one kind name can mean inline runs in one field and a plain text arg in another, and how a field defines a kind outside the standard set. A field that accepts every standard kind passes

explicitly; there is no implicit default. The vocabulary is declared once, on the FIELD, and reaches the commands by resolution rather than by being passed: a command factory names only the section and field it builds for, and PageType fills each block-carrying argument's kinds in from its own sections when it is constructed. This is load-bearing because every consumer reads an ArgSpec's block_kinds as "not a block argument" when it is None - an unresolved argument would otherwise accept any block, describe itself as an untyped array and lose its cross-page ref check silently - so the aggregated validator, which hard-fails before the server serves, is what guarantees no unresolved argument is ever reached. A list element field may hold blocks too, declared as
, a tuple of ElementBlocksSpec naming the element field plus the vocabulary it accepts.

reports element_blocks on a non-list field, a field not in element_fields, or the same field twice, and recurses through validate_element_blocks_spec, which reports an empty vocabulary and a duplicated kind. BlockKindSpec and ElementBlocksSpec have no post-init of their own, so a malformed one surfaces only when a validator runs over it in the primary flows - a typo fails the load rather than producing a field nothing can ever author. Both are tuples, never mappings, because the spec dataclasses are frozen values that compare by content.

is the single accessor every consumer uses to skip those fields when treating an element's values as scalar text - the command layer, both renderers, the search projection and describe all read it rather than re-deriving the names.

inlines.text: The command factories

inlines: - page types declare their field-op commands through a family of pure factories in core/commands.py - the command analog of the field-spec helpers - each building the concrete class of its kind:
(the add/remove/reorder triad, subset-selectable, plus an opt-in in-place edit: editable=True appends

, a SET_ELEMENT_FIELD over the add's args made optional that inherits the list's noun, label and legal_in - only the fields sent are written, null counts as not sent, an edit that writes nothing is rejected, and a ref-checked list cannot be editable because references are checked on adds only),
(element-FSM marks, a mark may also write a field),
(the flag-setting shape),
(a blocks field's whole surface - add, remove, reorder; a blocks field has NO in-place set, so replacing a block is remove plus a positioned add) with
for the same three one level deeper,
, and

(a compound whose single step is the list add, declaring the add's own args, followed by the transition - atomically). The first positional arg is the section; command names and the id arg are derived from the section/field, and transition_cmd parses its edge from a "from to" description, with legal_in overriding the source. A field key reaches a factory as an ordinary parameter because it feeds

and so fixes the command's NAME before any page type exists; only the vocabulary is deferred to resolution. Every factory is annotated to return the CommandSpec union, so a page type's commands stay one homogeneous tuple and consumers narrow by class. No page-type declaration constructs a command class directly. The hand-authored test-* fixtures declare through these same factories and share the field-spec helpers with production, so a fixture reads like a production type and doubles as coverage of both; only the fixtures' element FSMs stay local.

inlines.text: The core layering, and the acyclic package

- the shared machinery is split across src/pagetypes/core/ by what the code IS, in one dependency order each module may only import upward along: specs (the kind constants and the standalone frozen dataclasses, plus the guidance accessor), args (ArgSpec, BlockKindSpec, ElementBlocksSpec, the argument helpers and the block-kind helpers built out of them), fields (FieldSpec, SectionSpec, the field helpers and the FieldSpec accessors), commands (the per-kind command classes with their AuthoringCommand and CommandSpec union aliases, the command factories, the universal add_link_cmd / set_title_cmd, and is_field_setter), pagetype (PageType with its private _status_transitions, plus the free-function accessors and initial_sections), and validation (the inline-run grammar, the block validators, the per-spec validators and the recursive validate_page_type). Validation sits at the TOP of that order:
imports

at runtime - PageType, element_fsm_sites and get_pagetype_field - and there is no TYPE_CHECKING guard anywhere in core/. Nothing in core imports validation back, so the layering is still acyclic; the edge simply runs the opposite way from what this page claimed until a35b133, where it said validation named PageType only under TYPE_CHECKING and therefore sat below it. That older reasoning only bites while pagetype calls a validator, and it no longer does - post-init validates nothing. The read accessors that were once dataclass methods are module-level free functions taking the spec as their first argument. One placement is forced rather than chosen: the command classes sit in commands beside the factories that build them, because add_link_cmd / set_title_cmd construct one while using the arg helpers, so keeping them in args would close an args-commands cycle; the block-kind helpers likewise stay in args beside the arg helpers they are built from. Each module imports cleanly on its own in a fresh process, which is what distinguishes a real layering from one that happens to resolve in the order the package imports it. The package as a whole has no import hub: each page-type module imports its building blocks straight from the concrete core submodules, the registry lives in
, and the package init module is emptied to a docstring - it re-exports nothing and binds no names. The one lazy edge is deliberate:

imports testtypes at call time, because testtypes builds on the same core building blocks and a top-level import would have the two importing each other. Acyclicity is what lets a cold start and a hot reload's full re-import run each page-type module after the core it builds on, in plain import order, rather than against a partially initialised module.
Where a page type lives, and what is deliberately duplicated

inlines: - a page type is declared in its own module under src/pagetypes/, and a parent is declared together with the child types designed against it: feature.py holds feature-brief with its pinned feature-spec, implementation-plan and testing-plan, and epic.py holds epic with agent-plan, whose pages the controller creates under an epic, one per dispatched agent, rather than as a pinned child. The grouping is not a filing preference - a parent's ChildStateGuards read its children's statuses and the children's ParentStateGuards read the parent's, so the wiring only reads as wiring when both ends are on the page, and epic and agent-plan share a ParentStateGuard outright. Nothing a page type owns is left in the package's init module: its enum choice tuples, element FSMs and parent-state guards live in its own file, and the values two types both wanted are DUPLICATED rather than shared - a choice set belongs to the type that offers it, and two types agreeing today is not a reason for a change meant for one to reach the other. Duplicating an element FSM stays cheap but is not identity-free: ElementFSMSpec is a frozen dataclass, so two copies compare and hash equal, but each is built by the page type that declares it and so carries its OWN machine class - equal specs, distinct classes. Sharing one spec OBJECT across two page types is the other case and yields exactly one machine. Stage guidance is the one deliberate exception to the duplication rule, because it is prose rather than declaration: the same working discipline is meant to reach several page types, so the texts live together in

and a text two types can both use is one constant. That module imports nothing at all - not the package, not core, not the standard library - so it stays a leaf every page-type module can import directly, and its leading underscore sorts it above them. A constant is named for its status, and the name is what says whether the text is shared: a bare name is the only text for that status anywhere, while a page-type prefix means several types claim the status name and mean different things by it. One test holds the arrangement: every production guidance text must be one of these constants, so no page type can quietly keep an inline copy.

inlines.text: Sequencing a lifecycle with parent statuses, not by moving pages

inlines: - reparenting a pinned child to reorder a lifecycle is unsafe. ChildStateGuard iterates page.child_ids and matches on child_type, so it only ever sees DIRECT children: moving implementation-plan and testing-plan under feature-spec would let their ParentStateGuard name the spec directly and need no new status, but the brief's ship and submitPlan guards would then find no live child of those types and REFUSE, holding the brief shut until the pages were moved back. Before 9ada650 they passed vacuously instead - a guard that quietly stopped guarding. Ordering between SIBLING pinned children is therefore expressed as a status on the PARENT, because it cannot be expressed any other way: a ParentStateGuard looks up at the parent and a ChildStateGuard looks down at direct children, so there is no sibling guard for one child to name another. feature-brief carries

between grounding and planning - in spec only the feature-spec is unlocked, and beginPlanning is guarded on ChildStateGuard(feature-spec, sealed), so no implementation step or test case can be written until the design is settled. The two plan children's ParentStateGuard is unchanged by this; it still names planning or later, and inserting a status in front of planning is the whole mechanism. It is NOT pinned by a test - production page types are off-limits in tests, so this declaration and this page are the record; a test asserting it was written and then removed as overzealous (35ce056).

inlines.text: The test-registry swap

inlines: - tests are decoupled from the live registry by hand-authored, MINIMAL test-only page types (src.testtypes, tag test-*): six purpose-built capability fixtures - test-fields (every non-block field kind plus the content-mutation patterns), test-blocks (the blocks and inline-run surface), test-element-blocks (blocks one level deeper, on a list element's field), test-flow (a 3-state status FSM with an open state/event name collision plus a compound close), test-lifecycle (required-content gates, agency, a multi-source abandon, a questions element-FSM plus escalate, a pinned auto-child, a guarded ship, and the one wrapped multi-line field description), and test-child (todo/done and pending/passed/failed element-FSMs, a legal_in content lock, and a cross-page ref_check to the parent's questions) - and NOT clones of any production type. The two registries are SWAPPED, not layered, and the swap is total rather than a gate on the accessors: entering test mode EMPTIES REGISTRY into a private stash and leaving refills it, so reaching past

into the map finds nothing and no code can depend on a production type the mode says is off-limits. The map is mutated in place, never rebound, so a reference taken before the switch stays live. Which registry is in play is ASKED rather than inferred:
is the public predicate.

reads the STASH, not REGISTRY, since that is where the production types are while the mode is on; without that the ProductionTypeInTestError guard would silently stop firing. Because the swap is total the suite exercises every consumer through the fixtures, doc generation included: statecharts serves a page-status machine for any production type straight out of the registry through a module

- so there is no bound list that could fall out of step - while testcharts binds one per fixture, and the doc renderer picks between the two modules from is_test_mode(); that fixture import is lazy and reached only from test mode's branch, so production imports neither testcharts nor testtypes. One ordering consequence is load-bearing and easy to reintroduce: tests/test_pagetypes.py must name the production types from their own modules rather than read REGISTRY, because its structural invariants are parametrized at import under test mode, where reading the map would drop production from 132 parametrizations SILENTLY rather than fail - test_production_types_are_exactly_the_registered_ones is what keeps that hand-written list from drifting. A second one is gone and must not be reinstated: tests/conftest.py no longer imports src.statecharts ahead of the flip, because nothing binds a machine out of REGISTRY at import time any more. validate_registry still reads REGISTRY, so load-time validation is production's.

inlines.text: Guidance: per status, and per workspace

inlines: - a STATUS may carry its own stage instruction, the coarse sibling of a field's:

holds (status, text) pairs saying what that status is for and what the work in it consists of. The text is normalized in post-init exactly as a FieldSpec.description is (dedented, then rstripped), but the pairs are not validated there:

reports a pair naming a status absent from states, or naming the same status twice, and that message is collected when the registry is validated - so a typo fails the load instead of producing guidance that can never be looked up. That check is kept beside the machine build rather than folded into it because python-statemachine has no notion of guidance and accepts a spec whose guidance names an undeclared status. Guidance stays optional per status and per type: architecture and decision-record declare it for authoring, the feature-brief for its seven working statuses, simple-change and bug-report for draft, open, review and done, and the epic for decomposition, where

tells the controller to create the epic's feature-briefs and agent-plan pages under the epic itself and to group the agent-plan pages into dispatch waves in the epic's Scheduling section; every other status takes the absent path, where the write response omits its key and the generated doc page keeps its placeholder intro. The
status is the worked example of the naming rule for shared prose: the bare
is what simple-change and bug-report both hand over, while the feature-brief declares its own
- the two gates differ, so the text does, and what each one says is still not due differs with it. Separately, a page type may declare workspace-configurable guidance:

is a tuple of WorkspaceGuidanceSpec (a field name, a set of the type's own statuses the text shows at, and a description), declared as a page-type property beside sections rather than nested in one. Like auto_children it is a tuple of frozen specs, so PageType stays hashable. The descriptions are single-sourced in
, which imports nothing so it can be read early during package setup. Construction does not validate;

, folded into the load-time raise, checks that every guidance_for status is a real status of the declaring type and that a field several types declare carries the same description everywhere. All three of the lifecycle types now declare
for the single status
, which is what makes the workspace's merge process arrive at one point in every flow rather than at a status whose own prose defers merging.

inlines.text: Which cross-page rules the store enforces

inlines: - the concrete cases behind the invariant that cross-page rules live in the store. A feature-spec decision's questionId is integrity-checked against the parent brief's questions, and a dangling id aborts the commit. A feature-brief's building-to-review (submitForReview) and ship gates are both rejected until every child implementation-plan step is done or skipped and every testing-plan case has passed or been skipped. A

matches each child element's status against a SET of accepted statuses rather than a single one, so the review gate does not let unaddressed work through and a deliberately skipped item counts as addressed at both gates. An epic's submitPlan is rejected while any agent-plan child is still in draft, its submitForReview until every agent-plan child is accepted, and its ship until every child feature-brief is shipped; an agent-plan page can be marked ready only once its epic has reached decomposition or later. A ChildStateGuard counts only live children - an archived child is history and is skipped, which is how an agent is dropped - and fails when no live child of its type exists, so an epic cannot pass those gates with no agent-plan pages or no briefs. The guards declared before this rule target pinned children, which always exist, so they behave as they did.

inlines.text: How the revision stamp is maintained

inlines: - mechanism behind the revision-stamp invariant. It is store-owned like expires_at: the pure core (
) moves page.status via fsm.fire but never the token, and

regenerates it whenever a command changed the status - a status change is exactly a TRANSITION or COMPOUND firing fsm.fire, so the store detects it by comparing status before and after apply_command. The per-command optimistic-concurrency check that presents it is documented on the Authoring & mutation page.

inlines.text: Evaluating one transition

inlines: - each evaluation seeds an ephemeral machine instance at the page's current status, and an illegal event raises python-statemachine's
, which
surfaces as
. Resolution itself goes through
, which returns None for an unknown tag but raises ProductionTypeInTestError for a production tag while test mode is on.

inlines.text: The condition that holds the spec ordering

inlines: - feature-brief carries
between grounding and planning, and the condition to hold is that the feature-spec's

minus the two plans' is exactly {spec}. If spec ever joins the plans' tuple the ordering silently collapses and all three children unlock together again. The plans' ParentStateGuard is unchanged by the insertion - it still names planning or later - and only the spec's guard admits spec as well. This is not pinned by a test, because production page types are off-limits in tests, so this declaration and this page are the record.

items.statement: Page types are data, not code: adding or adjusting a type is a REGISTRY entry, enforced uniformly by commands.py rather than by per-type logic.

A transition is legal only when the FSM permits it and every required-content precondition it declares is satisfied. A state with no outgoing transition is inferred final so python-statemachine's trap-state validation accepts terminal statuses like feature-brief's shipped and abandoned.

A state and an event may share a name (bug-report's open state and open event): each state carries its id in State(value=...) under a distinct attribute name, and status is read back from configuration values rather than the attribute name.

A blocks field carries structured inline runs, not raw markdown: text/marked/linked/code/page-ref runs and table/list shapes are validated before anything is written, and markdown emphasis or link tokens inside a plain-text run are rejected — so rich content stays typed and machine-editable instead of turning into opaque prose. Backticks are the one exception: inside a plain-text run they are literal text, stored as sent and never turned into a code run, provided each stands alone and their count is even. Violated, a stray backtick is stored, or a code fence passes on its even total and sits in a run as loose text instead of a code block.

Inline page-reference existence follows the grammar's pure/stateful split: pagetypes.collect_ref_ids purely gathers a command's {ref} ids across every run shape (runs, run-lists, run-grids), and the store checks them against the workspace before applying — just as validate_inline_content purely gates run shape while the store owns cross-page existence.

Auto-created pinned children are declared on the PARENT page type, never on the child: PageType.auto_children is a tuple of AutoChildSpec (each naming a child page-type tag), and a page's 'pinned' status is DERIVED — is_auto_child_type(parent_type, child_type) reports whether a parent type declares a given child type as auto-created. No pinned/auto flag is stored on the Page or its serialization; the fact lives only in the registry, so the store reads it back through the parent at mutation time rather than trusting page data.

Every FSM spec a page type declares carries either a built machine or the error that stopped building it, never both and never neither, and machine_class never builds on demand. Violated, a spec the validator passed raises LookupError at request time, or a rebuild hands out a fresh class per call so class identity stops being stable.

A page-status transition is declared exactly once, on its command, and the FSM's transition table is derived from those commands rather than authored. Violated, a declared edge can disagree with the command that fires it, so the FSM permits a transition no command can perform or the reverse.

PageType construction performs setup only and never validates; every declaration error is reported by one aggregated raise at load. Violated, a malformed type raises from whichever module declared it and the remaining errors are never collected, so fixing a registry becomes a restart-per-error loop.

No request is served out of a registry that does not validate. validate_registry() at module load stops a cold start and fails a hot reload, which then rolls back to the last good build and refuses until a reload succeeds; each surface additionally asks declaration_errors() per request. Violated, an unresolved block argument reaches a consumer, which reads its block_kinds of None as "not a block argument" and silently accepts any block while losing its cross-page ref check.

A blocks field always names its own vocabulary, and a block-carrying command argument gets its kinds by resolution from the field it targets rather than by declaring them. Violated, an argument and its field can drift, and the same kind name stops being able to mean different bodies in different fields.

Freezing a finished page's authoring surface is declared once, as FSMSpec.terminal_states, never repeated per command. Violated, a newly added command can forget the lock, so a sealed page becomes editable again.

An element's checkbox rendering is read off its element FSM (checkmark_done and initial), never matched against hardcoded status strings. Violated, adding or renaming a state silently changes rendering, and a state that is neither box - a failed or skipped item - disappears from view instead of showing its status.

Lifecycle sequencing between sibling pinned children is expressed as a status on the parent, never by reparenting them. Violated, a ChildStateGuard that sees only direct children finds no live child of its type and refuses, so the parent's transition is held shut until the pages are moved back.

Exactly one page-type registry is reachable at a time: entering test mode empties REGISTRY into a private stash, and guard_production_type reads that stash. Violated, a test binds to a production page type, or the off-limits guard silently stops firing because it is reading the wrong map.

The pagetypes package is acyclic - core submodules, then page-type modules, then _registry - with an empty init module that binds no names and one deliberate lazy edge to testtypes. Violated, importing the package - a cold start or a hot reload's full re-import - can run a module against a partially initialised one and fail on a name it has not defined yet.

A spec's built machine takes no part in its identity, and the spec dataclasses stay frozen values that compare by content. Violated, one ElementFSMSpec shared by several page types stops comparing equal after the first build.

Guidance a page type declares must name a status that page type actually has, and a workspace-guidance field shared by several types must carry the same description in each - both checked in the load-time raise. Violated, guidance is stored that can never be looked up, or one field means different things depending on which type surfaced it.

Cross-page rules are enforced in the store, never in the single-page pure core. Violated, a rule that has to see other pages is evaluated where they are invisible, so a dangling reference or an unfinished child slips through the gate meant to catch it.

Page.status_revision_token moves if and only if the page's status moves, and only the store ever writes it. Violated, the token stops being evidence of the status it was read at, so the concurrency check either rejects valid writes or admits stale ones.

A compound's steps are authoring commands only: the steps field is typed as the AuthoringCommand union and CompoundCommand.__post_init__ raises ValueError for a status-transition step, so a compound fires exactly the one edge it declares. Violated, a single command could move a page through a second edge that no command in the derived FSM table owns, and the table would stop describing what commands do.

A fixed field is written by no command and always holds its declared value: initial_sections re-seeds it on create and on every backfill, and validate_pagetype_fixed_fields rejects any field command targeting it at load. Violated, the stored text drifts from its declaration, or a command's write is silently overwritten on the page's next backfill.

An editable list carries no ref_check: list_cmds raises when editable=True meets a ref_check, because the store checks cross-page references on adds only. Violated, an in-place edit rewrites a reference to another page without the integrity check its add received.

The page-type model is also described by hand, in pseudocode, in docs/designing-page-types.md and again inline in .claude/skills/pasta-workflow-creation/SKILL.md - neither is generated from the registry. When a field or field kind, a page type, a command kind or a guard is added or changed, update BOTH files in the same change and keep their brief text identical. Violated, the pasta-workflow-creation skill designs workflows against a model the registry no longer enforces, and the brief the README links and the skill it tells readers to run describe two different systems.

summary.body: The read tools that navigate and render the wiki without changing it: enumerate workspaces, walk the page tree, fetch or render a page, and read its section outline.

purpose.body: Let a client discover structure and read content safely, kept separate from authoring. These operations never change state, and the only lock they take is the shared half of their workspace's readers-writer lock while the file is read off disk, so they never block one another and are always safe to call.

usage.body: listWorkspaces() lists every workspace (id, name, status). tree(workspaceId) returns the ordered page tree; archived pages and their subtrees are always hidden, with no flag to include them - reach an archived page with getPage, which does not filter on archived. getPage(workspaceId, pageId) returns a page's projected state; outline(workspaceId, pageId) returns just its section tree (no body); renderPage(workspaceId, pageId?) returns Markdown for one page, or the whole tree when pageId is omitted. getWorkspaceGuidance(workspaceId) returns the workspace's guidance configuration: every declared guidance field with its description and stored text, plus any text still stored under a field no page type declares.

dataModel.body: tree yields nested nodes {id, title, type, status, children[]}, with archived pages and their subtrees absent. getPage yields the raw serialized page {id, type, title, status, status_revision_token, sections, ...}. outline yields {sections:[{key, name, order, fields}]}. renderPage yields {markdown}, whose page meta line carries the status_revision_token beside the status when the page has one. getWorkspaceGuidance yields {workspaceId, fields:[{field, description, text}], undeclared:{field: text}}: fields are sorted by name, with text null when unset or cleared, and undeclared holds non-empty values only. All are projections of the same on-disk workspace document; getWorkspaceGuidance also reads the registry's declared guidance fields.

inlines.text: What the readers-writer lock buys a reader

inlines: - the mechanism behind the invariant that a read never observes a partial file. A read holds the shared half of its workspace's readers-writer lock (src/rwlock.py) across the read of the bytes, and the write that replaces a workspace file holds the exclusive half, so a reader always sees a whole file - the pre- or post-write version. Readers do not exclude each other, and they never take the transaction lock that serializes writers, so a read stays concurrent with a write in progress.

inlines.text: How an inline ref becomes a titled link

inlines: - mechanism behind the invariant on reference rendering. render builds a pageId to title map over the whole workspace - archived pages included, so an archived target stays linkable - and threads it through rendering as a

rides onto every ref link (as ?archived=true) so following a ref keeps the archived view. A direct render with no workspace context, or a ref id that resolves to no page, falls back to the bare id as plain text.

inlines.text: Rendering a page's shape, not just its content

inlines: - what the shape invariant covers.

emits every declared section and field even when empty (an empty field renders the italic None fallback; scalars keep their key label), then appends a synthetic Child pages section - a render-only list, not a page-type section, never stored, absent from

- linking the page's direct children. Child links follow the same archiving discipline as the tree (archived children hidden unless show_archived, then flagged with a bold (A) marker prefixed before the link; links carry ?archived=true) and are annotated with each child's type and status.

inlines.text: RefContext is the renderer's pure workspace view

inlines: - parallel pageId maps for title, type and status plus the archived-id set, all built once by

, so render resolves inline ref runs and Child-pages links to titled, type-and-status-annotated links with no I/O. The page-header meta and each child link share one form - type in italics, status in inline code - the same styling
uses in the web nav.

inlines.text: Outgoing reference edges render too

inlines: appends a References section (the page.links graph edges) immediately before Child pages, each target rendered as the same titled type-and-status link as a child plus the edge's role. It reuses the Child-pages archiving discipline exactly, and falls back to a bare id without a RefContext, or the None fallback when the page has no visible links. Render-only: it reads Page.links, and the tree() payload is unchanged.

inlines.text: What the two render paths share

inlines: - rationale behind the two-path invariant. The Markdown renderer's bytes are a returned contract - the HTML path was added without changing a single byte of it, which the Markdown renderer's own test file, unedited across that change, is what proves. The two share the model, the page-type registry and RefContext, and they share exactly two pieces of logic:
, which maps an element's status onto done/todo/no-checkbox, and
, which the HTML path calls per blocks field to get a Markdown fragment it then converts. Anything else they each answer for themselves, so a change to one cannot silently move the other.

inlines.text: Why Markdown escaping is per-leaf

inlines: - rationale behind the escaping invariant. That path renders to Markdown and then runs one top-level Markdown-to-HTML pass, which cannot distinguish the renderer's structural Markdown from a plain-text value that contains Markdown-special characters; escaping the whole document, or building HTML per section and merging, would break that generated structure, so
is applied at each emitted plain-text leaf instead. It runs only when
is set - the web routes that still use this path turn it on via render_workspace_links, the store turns it on for the blocks fragments the HTML path converts, and the MCP path leaves it off.

inlines.text: Block-bearing element fields on both paths

inlines: - how the structure invariant is spelled on each side. The Markdown path keeps the bullet line exactly as it was - checkbox, title text, the semicolon-joined remaining scalar fields, the trailing status italic - excludes the block field from that flattening, and emits render_blocks' output below it indented two spaces, after a blank line, so a fenced code block or a nested list parses as part of the list item instead of closing it. The HTML path excludes it from the element's title candidates and from its labelled rows, collecting it into

instead, rendered after the plain rows inside the same field-rows list and routed through render_blocks plus the Markdown-to-HTML pass - which is why an inline page ref inside a step resolves to a titled link there. An element that carries no blocks, or a page stored before the field was declared, renders byte-identically to before on both paths.

inlines.text: Why an element's heading is declared rather than inferred

inlines: - history behind the heading invariant.
names the element field that heads the element - title or name, in that precedence order, and a block-bearing field is never a candidate - and

heads on that field alone, consuming it so it is never also a labelled row. A list field declaring neither is headed by its ordinal. This replaced a rule that promoted the first declared field to a heading whenever its value was non-empty, newline-free and at most 80 characters, under which siblings of one list rendered differently and a value sitting near the bound flipped shape when a word was added. Giving a list headings is therefore a pagetypes change, not a render change.

inlines.text: Corrections at a35b133

inlines: - two claims here had gone stale. The file swap is
after a temp-file write, held under the exclusive half of the readers-writer lock and retried once after a short sleep for a transient Windows permission error - not a
. So the lock orders readers against an atomic swap rather than covering a window in which the destination is incomplete; the reader guarantee is unchanged either way. And
no longer takes an
parameter: it is
alone and archived subtrees are always hidden, so there is no flagged-but-shown mode. Reach an archived page with
, which does not filter on archived, or the web UI's ?archived=true view.

inlines.text: Exactly what the HTML path escapes

inlines: - detail behind the HTML-escaping invariant. Every author-provided leaf it places into the document itself - scalar values, prose, element titles and row values, page and link titles, reference roles, type and status - is HTML-escaped with
, because its structure is HTML rather than generated Markdown. The one exception is a blocks field, which still goes Markdown-to-HTML: there the RefContext carries

so the plain leaves inside it are markdown-escaped first, and wenmode's own escaping covers the HTML specials. So a value can never be reinterpreted as markup on either path, but the mechanism differs by path - which means adding a leaf to the HTML renderer involves choosing its escape rather than inheriting one.

inlines.text: What is and is not escaped on the Markdown path

inlines: - detail behind the per-leaf escaping invariant. The renderer's own structural Markdown - heading and list markers, task checkboxes, table pipes, code fences, and the bold, italic, link and code decoration wrapped around run text - plus literal content (inline code spans, fenced code source, and href URLs) are emitted by the renderer and never escaped. Only author-provided text is escaped: scalar and prose values, list element text and scalar sub-fields, inline-run text, block plain-text fallbacks, page titles, and reference roles. The exact escape set is specific to the Wenmode github preset and is pinned by tests that assert the rendered HTML.

inlines.text: Where the two paths resolve a page id

inlines: - the asymmetry behind the id-resolution invariant. Markdown resolves an id in three places: an inline ref run, the Child pages list, and the References list - so a list element field holding an id, such as an architecture dependency's target, renders there as the bare id. The HTML path resolves on the VALUE instead: any element value that names a page in the RefContext becomes that page's titled type-and-status link, and an archived target carries a bold (A) marker before it. A value naming nothing stays text, and without a RefContext every path falls back to the bare id. The HTML page's top links strip is one more place that path resolves ids, with no Markdown equivalent:

links the page's parent first and its pinned children last, and leaves out a link it cannot resolve rather than showing a bare id. Between them sit the in-page anchors - one per section, then References, Child pages and a Bottom anchor to the shell's
- so every entry that scrolls this page comes before the ones that open another. The two paths therefore disagree on purpose, and the Markdown side is the one carrying the gap.

inlines.text: How the search projection reaches element blocks

inlines: - mechanism behind the search-projection invariant.

collects every top-level string off a list element as before, and additionally walks each declared block element field, taking each block's own bounded strings and the text carried in its inline runs - the same two lines the page-level blocks branch already applies. This is one level deeper than the projection used to reach.

items.statement: A read never mutates and never observes a partial file: it holds the shared half of its workspace's readers-writer lock across the read of the bytes, while the write that replaces the file holds the exclusive half. Violated, a reader can fail with a corrupt-workspace error on a file that is mid-swap.
A page id must be fully type-prefixed: getPage on a partial id returns not-found. Resolve a partial id to its full form with search or tree first.
outline and renderPage derive a page's section shape from its page type in the registry, not from stored data, so a page always renders in its declared section order even if some fields are empty.

A list element's task checkbox comes from its field's element FSM, not from hardcoded status strings: _render_list asks the FSM via _checkbox — the checkmark_done state renders [x], the FSM's initial state renders [ ], and any other state (or a list field with no element FSM, e.g. components or invariants) renders no box. The mapping is thus owned by the element-state definitions in the registry, so adding or renaming a state's checkbox is a pagetypes change, not a render change.

getPage and the render* reads surface a page's status_revision_token, the stamp a mutatePageBatch caller must present. getPage returns the raw serialized page, so it carries the snake_case status_revision_token key directly; render_page and render_page_html append it to the page meta line - rendered only when the page has one, so a page created before this feature (null token) renders the bare type/status meta line unchanged. The search projection (page_text) deliberately omits it, since it is a concurrency stamp rather than content.

Reads honour archiving: tree, search and renderPage hide archived pages and their whole subtrees, always, with no flag to reveal them. Violated, the archived tail reappears inline and buries the active pages.

An inline page-reference run renders as its target page's title, linked to that page's web route, and falls back to the bare id only when no workspace context was supplied or the id resolves to no page. Violated, a reader sees opaque ids where a title was intended.

render_page emits every declared section and field even when empty, plus a synthetic Child pages list that is never stored. Violated, an unfilled page's skeleton becomes invisible and a reader cannot see what remains to be authored.

RefContext is built once per render and resolves ids with no I/O; a render without one still succeeds, falling back to bare ids. Violated, rendering either performs I/O per reference or becomes unusable outside a loaded workspace.

A page renders its outgoing reference edges as a References section immediately before Child pages, reading Page.links and changing no payload. Violated, the typed reference graph is invisible to a reader, or the tree payload starts carrying render-only data.

The Markdown and HTML paths share exactly two pieces of logic - checkbox_state and render_blocks - and answer everything else separately. Violated, a change made for one path silently moves the other, and the Markdown bytes the renderPage tool returns are no longer a stable contract.

On the Markdown path, escaping is applied per plain-text leaf and only when RefContext.escape_plain_text is set - never document-wide. Violated, escaping the whole document destroys the renderer's own structural Markdown, and leaving it off lets an author's value be reinterpreted as formatting.

A block-bearing element field renders as structure on both paths, never as a stringified value, and an element carrying no blocks renders byte-identically to before the field was declared. Violated, either the blocks read as opaque text or every existing page's rendering shifts.

An element's heading is the field its type declares as the heading and no other, so every element of one field renders with the same shape whatever its values are. Violated, siblings of one list render differently and editing prose can change a page's structure.

Every author-provided leaf is escaped before it reaches the document, by the mechanism its path uses - html.escape on the HTML path, per-leaf markdown escaping on the Markdown one. Violated, a value containing markup or Markdown syntax is reinterpreted as formatting.

The HTML path resolves a page id to a titled link on any element value that names a page, while the Markdown path resolves only inline refs, child links and reference edges. The two disagree deliberately and the Markdown side carries the gap; violated unknowingly, a reader assumes an id renders identically on both surfaces.

The flat text projection behind search reaches element blocks, not just an element's top-level strings. Violated, block content stores and renders correctly but is silently unfindable - nothing breaks, the text just stops existing as far as discovery is concerned.

summary.body: Finding content and learning the authoring surface: full-text search over one workspace, plus the type/command introspection a client uses before it writes.

purpose.body: search answers 'where is X'; describePageType and describeMutations answer 'what can I do here'. Together they let a client author correctly by reading the legal surface instead of guessing command names or arguments.

usage.body: search(workspaceId, query, limit?) ranks pages by content match (case-insensitive, word-prefix) with a snippet each; an `id:<token>` query switches to page-id resolution instead, matching the token as a case-insensitive substring of every page id and spanning archived pages. describePageType(type) requires a type and reports its sections, fields, commands, and FSM; listPageTypes() reports the tags of every registered page type - the listing describePageType used to return when its type was omitted. describeMutations(workspaceId, pageId) reports every command for a page with its arg schema and whether it is legal right now.

dataModel.body: search yields {hits:[{pageId, title, type, archived, score, snippet}]}, ranked by descending score; an id hit scores 10_000, or 10_001 when the token equals the whole id, so an exact id sorts first. describePageType yields the type schema (sections/fields with each field's instruction, commands with JSON-Schema args, FSM); a BLOCKS field additionally reports `blockKinds`, the kind names it accepts, and a list field reports `elementBlocks`, each block-bearing element field with its own kinds. Every field reports `fixed`, true when its value is declared by the page type and no command writes it. listPageTypes yields {types:[tag, ...]}. describeMutations yields per-command {name, kind, args, available, requires, legalIn}. There is no `blockKind` key: a command no longer declares a kind, so the vocabulary is reported on the FIELD instead. All are derived, not stored.

inlines.text: Why the id: prefix is a prefix

inlines: - the history behind the invariant that
selects id resolution exclusively. Before it, id resolution was a bare substring test on any colon-bearing query, so
read as a literal keyword but only ever matched an id that actually began with
. Making the prefix explicit is what removed that ambiguity: a query carrying it is never also word-prefix matched, and a query without it is ordinary text search even when it contains a colon.

inlines.text: How a blocks vocabulary describes itself

inlines: - the mechanism behind the invariant that a blocks field's vocabulary stays discoverable. There is no command name per block kind to read the kind off, so the field's single add is where the vocabulary is advertised: its
argument reports a oneOf with one branch per accepted kind, each branch built by
from the same

the validator reads, so schema and grammar cannot disagree. The add is the only command carrying a block argument - the field has no set - which is why losing that one schema would take the whole capability with it. A field whose kind carries overridden body args advertises those args, not the standard ones. describePageType reports the accepted kind names beside the field's other declarations (blockKinds for a page-level field, elementBlocks for an element one).

inlines.text: The precondition that self-description depends on

inlines: builds the oneOf only when

is not None, and those kinds are filled in by PageType from the field the command targets rather than by the factory that built it. An argument that never reached a page type would therefore describe itself as a bare untyped array and report nothing wrong - the same silent reading of None every other consumer takes for "not a block argument". So the thing to introspect is a constructed PageType and never a bare factory result.

inlines.text: Corrections at a35b133

inlines: - three details on this page had gone stale. Resolution does not raise:
is best-effort and leaves an unresolvable argument's
as None, and
reports it as one message inside the aggregated

raise. What guarantees no unresolved argument is ever reached is therefore that hard failure at load, not a raise at import. Likewise the setter-description rule is not rejected by "page-type construction":
is called from
, again at load. And
is a field on BlockKindSpec, read as
, not a method call.

inlines.text: One map behind listing and resolution

items.statement: Search is workspace-scoped by design and never crosses workspace boundaries. TEXT search excludes archived pages; an `id:<token>` search deliberately does not, because an id a caller is already holding may since have been archived, and hiding it makes a real id look invalid rather than archived. Every hit carries `archived` so a caller can still tell the two apart.
Search matches by word prefix (concur finds concurrency). It scores against a flat text projection of each page, so it never exposes more content than getPage would.

describeMutations reflects per-page legality (FSM topology + required-content preconditions + the plan ready lock) but not cross-page guards; a command shown available may still be rejected at apply time by a store-enforced guard such as ship.
describePageType needs no page instance: the authoring surface is a property of the type in the registry, so it is identical for every page of that type.

A field's content instruction lives once, on its FieldSpec.description, and describePageType reports it in exactly one place: the sections listing. A field setter carries a short description of its own, and the registry validator rejects one that is empty, multi-line, or equal to its field's instruction. Violated, the instruction is restated per setter and the two copies drift.

The `id:` prefix selects page-id resolution exclusively: a query carrying it is never also word-prefix matched, and a query without it is ordinary text search even when it contains a colon. Violated, any colon-bearing query is ambiguous between a keyword and an id.

A blocks field's accepted vocabulary is reported by introspection - the kind names on the field, and a oneOf branch per kind on the single add command's block argument. Violated, the capability becomes unauthorable rather than merely undocumented, because there is no command name per kind left to read the vocabulary off.

listPageTypes and page-type resolution read the same map (registered_pagetypes()), so what is listed and what resolves are one set. Violated, a type is resolvable but unlisted - a page can be created of a type no client was ever told about, and which load-time validation never saw.

summary.body: The write path: create workspaces and pages, and drive validated commands (single or batched) that are the only way to change a page's content or status.

purpose.body: All change flows through typed, validated commands rather than raw text edits, so a page can never enter an invalid shape or an illegal status. The command surface for a page is fixed by its type.

usage.body: createWorkspace(name) makes a workspace. createPage(workspaceId, type, title, parentId?) makes a page and returns any auto-created pinned children (e.g. a feature-brief's spec and two plans). mutatePageBatch(workspaceId, pageId, commands) runs an ordered batch of commands on one page as a single atomic commit; a single command is a one-command batch, and there is no separate single-command tool. reparentPage(workspaceId, pageId, newParentId?) moves a page under a new parent (null = top level); reorderPage(workspaceId, pageId, toIndex, precedingId?) reorders a page among its siblings; renamePage(workspaceId, pageId, title) changes a page's title (sibling titles are not reserved). renamePage is also exposed as a setTitle page command on every authorable page type (all but the command-less toc), so a title can be fixed through describeMutations / mutatePageBatch alongside other authoring commands.

dataModel.body: createPage yields {id, type, title, status, parentId, statusRevisionToken, children[], next}. mutatePageBatch yields {pageId, status, statusRevisionToken, count, createdIds[], next}. Each command in a mutatePageBatch is {command, args}, and args carries the page's current statusRevisionToken as its first entry: every command must present that statusRevisionToken (read from getPage, a render* meta line, or a prior write / nextActions echo), which the store reads and strips from args before the pure core sees the remaining arguments. A status transition regenerates it, so at most one transition is legal per batch and only as its final command - a command sequenced after a transition carries a now-stale token and aborts the whole commit. createdIds is ONE id per command, positionally - an add-element returns the ELEMENT's id even when the same command also created that element's blocks, and a block add that creates a RUN of blocks returns the FIRST of them, because those extra ids are created inside the command rather than by commands of their own; they are read back off the page. Internally CommandResult also carries created_ids, EVERY id the command created, which mutate_page_batch feeds to the anchored-slot BatchContext so a later positioned insert can skip ids the caller had no way to name; that list is not part of the response. The store returns the batch as a MutatePageResult {page, created_ids, transitioned}; transitioned says whether the batch moved the page to a new status, and it feeds the tool's choice between a full and a trimmed `next` rather than appearing in the response. Guidance is NOT a response key of its own: both the per-status stage instruction and every configured `guidance_<field>` ride INSIDE `next`, because `next` is next_actions(workspaceId, pageId) and that already carries them for the focused page. createPage embeds that payload verbatim. mutatePageBatch embeds it verbatim on a full write, one that moved the page to a new status or landed after the page's last full delivery lapsed. On any other write it requests the payload with omit_populated_instructions, so a `do` field edge whose field already holds content on its page comes without its `instruction`, and with omit_stage_guidance, so that write carries no guidance keys. reparentPage and reorderPage each yield {id, parentId, siblingIds} - the moved page and its resulting sibling order; renamePage yields {id, title}. The engine creates ids; callers do not supply them, which is why a caller can never name an entry the current batch is creating.

inlines.text: Anchored ordering, and the one exception a batch gets

inlines: - mechanism behind the anchored-operations invariant.

This is what lets concurrent edits neither drop an id (the former whole-list reorder's failure) nor land an entry in the wrong slot (the former bare-index insert's failure); a multi-entry reorder is composed as a batch of single reorders. Within a mutatePageBatch the guard makes one exception for the batch's own not-yet-committed ids:

takes an optional BatchContext - a frozenset of the ids created by earlier commands in the batch - and on a precedingId mismatch it walks left past those ids to match the first committed id it reaches. So a run of positioned inserts anchored on the same committed precedingId composes in command order even though the caller cannot name the ids the batch just created. index stays strict, a genuinely wrong precedingId is still rejected, and a single non-batch mutation or page reorder passes no context so the guard stays the strict check there.

Sibling titles are not reserved: a title is a display label, never an identifier, so create, reparent and rename all allow a duplicate sibling title and only a blank one is rejected. That is also why the title is settable both ways - the renamePage tool and the universal setTitle command - while a page's parent and sibling position stay tool-only: a title carries no referential integrity, so there is no cross-page precheck to keep the two paths honest.

Both endpoints must exist; the source must be non-archived (a link mutates it) while the target may be archived (references still resolve); a self-link and an empty role are rejected; a duplicate (to, role) edge is rejected with ConflictError and unlinking an absent edge with NotFoundError. inlines: derives pinned-ness from the parent type's AutoChildSpec via

Archiving or unarchiving a parent cascades the flag onto its pinned children in the same transaction, so a pinned child's archived state always mirrors its parent's, while non-pinned siblings keep their own flag. No page-removal operation exists, so "cannot be removed" holds by construction; _is_pinned_child is the reusable guard for any future removal path.

inlines: - the per-workspace transaction lock is a
kept in a process-global registry, and it is what fully serializes conflicting read-modify-write cycles for a workspace. The atomic

Optimistic write preconditions exist for the lifecycle status - the per-command status_revision_token - so a writer working against a status the page has since left is rejected rather than silently overwriting. Cross-process locking (an OS file lock) and a full content-hash precondition covering every field remain a documented later hardening step, not a correctness gap today.

inlines: - history behind the guidance-placement invariant.
