A write carries those keys only on a full echo, and nextActions always does. The rule has moved in both directions. An early rule showed a top-level guidance beside next only when a page-status transition was found in the batch, while a second copy of the guidance_<field> keys was merged unconditionally. That rule justified the sibling placement with "nextActions deliberately carries no guidance", which had already stopped being true once nextActions gained guidance for a focused page - the two architecture pages disagreed and the response emitted both readings at once. The fix moved guidance inside next and sent it on every write, reasoning that gating on the transition withheld the instruction across exactly the writes it exists to steer. Pull request 47 returned a write to transition-only by decision, because repeating the same text on every content-only write cost more context than it earned, and it kept the single copy inside next from that fix. That left an agent losing its context mid-stage with nothing from its writes, so pull request 49 added a full echo once the last full delivery has lapsed, and made a transition carry every field instruction as well (see

A block's kind is data inside the argument, so one add takes an array of kinded blocks validated against the vocabulary the field declares. A blocks field's add takes an array of kinded blocks, and a list add on a block-bearing field takes that field's blocks as an optional argument, so creating an element and filling it is also one command. This is what keeps mutatePageBatch's arguments literal JSON: there is no reserved key and no positional back-reference to an earlier command's created id. That alternative was considered and rejected - it would force every consumer to learn a reserved key before it could write a step, would silently repoint the moment a batch was reordered, and would invent four new ways to be wrong purely to compensate for having split creation from content.

A field setter instead carries a short description derived in the factory from the same noun its name is derived from, so name and description always agree - "set the summary", "add a constraint".

The layering is still acyclic, because nothing in core imports validation back.

For today's compounds the step-level ref checks repeat over the compound's own args and the guard check cannot fail for a step; both are accepted for one uniform loop. items.statement: Every write is copy -> edit -> atomic overwrite under a per-workspace lock: conflicting writers serialize, no update is lost, and a crash mid-write cannot corrupt the workspace file.

A command is validated - arguments first, then legality - before it is applied, and so is each step of a compound; a rejected call raises with the currently-legal command set attached and leaves the stored page unchanged, because every edit lands on a working copy. Violated, a compound step bypasses the checks a top-level command gets, so a compound can write content that the same edit made directly would be refused.
A batch is all-or-nothing: each command is decided against the state left by the previous one, and any rejection aborts the whole batch (nothing commits), naming the failing index and command.

Cross-page preconditions (a decision's questionId ref, a link's endpoints, the ship guard) are enforced in the store before the pure core applies, on the command and on each step of a compound alike, so they hold identically for every write and for a step as for a top-level command. An archived page rejects all mutation until unarchived.

Inline page-reference integrity joins that family: before the pure core applies a command, the store collects every {ref: pageId} in the inline-run arguments of the command and of each compound step, and aborts the whole commit if any id names no page in the workspace. A page therefore can never store a dangling inline ref; an archived target stays valid because it remains in the workspace's page map.

Order within a list or blocks field is edited by anchored operations, never by absolute coordinates: precedingId must be the id immediately before the destination slot. Violated, a concurrent edit either drops an id or lands an entry in the wrong slot, and neither is reported.

A page's parent and its position among siblings are changed only by the reparentPage and reorderPage store transactions, never by a page command, and a reparent that would create a cycle is rejected. Violated, the page tree can be made to contain a cycle, which hangs or corrupts every walk over it.

A link's endpoints must both exist, the source must be non-archived, and a self-link, an empty role or a duplicate (to, role) edge is rejected - identically whether the edge is added by the link tool or the addLink command, because both call one validator. Violated, the reference graph accrues dangling or duplicate edges, and the two paths drift apart.

A pinned auto-created child cannot be reparented, reordered, or archived on its own, and its archived state always mirrors its parent's. Violated, a lifecycle's pinned children can be resequenced independently of the parent whose guards read them - and a guard that finds no live child of its type refuses, so the parent's transition is held shut.

Concurrency is in-process by design: one per-workspace transaction lock serializes conflicting read-modify-write cycles, and cross-process safety is not provided. Violated, two writers to one workspace lose each other's updates; relied on across processes, a second server on the same data dir is unguarded.

A block command addresses either a section's own blocks field or one element's block field, decided by BlockCommand.element_field alone, and the store needs no addressing knowledge to enforce its cross-page checks. Violated - if the store must reach into a command's arguments to resolve an element-scoped target - the pure/effectful split has drifted.

Creating a run of blocks is one command, so a batch never has to name an id it has not committed and mutatePageBatch's arguments stay literal JSON. Violated, a caller needs a reserved key or a positional back-reference to an earlier command's created id, which silently repoints the moment the batch is reordered.

A field's content instruction lives once on its FieldSpec.description and is never carried by the command that writes it; the registry validator rejects a setter description that is empty, multi-line, or equal to its field's instruction. Violated, the instruction is restated per setter and the copies drift.

status_revision_token is store-owned: the pure command core never reads or writes it, and it moves if and only if the page's status moves. Violated, a page-type command can forge the concurrency stamp, and the token stops being evidence of the status it was read at.

Workspace guidance is settable only for a field some page type declares, and next_actions is the single place any guidance key is assembled. Violated, a workspace accrues guidance no page will ever surface, or two call sites emit differing copies of it.

A write response carries guidance at most once, inside `next`, and only on a full write, one that moved the page to a new status or landed after its last full delivery lapsed. Violated, either the response emits two copies that can disagree, which is what happened when a top-level guidance key sat beside next, or every content-only write repeats the stage text.

Lifecycle events are appended only after the workspace file is saved, inside the same transaction lock, and only for the creations, status moves and archive-flag flips that save committed; a log that cannot be written never fails the write. Violated, the log claims writes that never landed or misses ones that did, or a full disk turns every edit into an error.

summary.body: The FSM-driven 'what next' tools: roll up the legal edges across a page subtree, and surface the items a human must resolve.

purpose.body: The wiki tells the agent what to do rather than the agent deciding freely. Drive `do` and `blocked` to completion; stop only for `humanGates` and `attention`. This keeps multi-page workflows (the feature lifecycle) on rails.

usage.body: nextActions(workspaceId, pageId?) partitions the model-declared edges over a subtree (or the whole workspace) into do (agent edges to drive now), blocked (agent transitions whose unmet precondition is named), humanGates (sign-off transitions — stop), and attention (items awaiting a human). `do` holds TWO kinds of edge: status transitions AND the stage-relevant field setters — the field setters whose field must be authored to advance the current stage, EXCLUDING any whose transition is barred by a failing ParentStateGuard, so a pinned child stays silent until its parent reaches the stage that unlocks it. A field edge names the ONE command that authors that field — an implementation-plan in draft yields one steps.items edge reading addStep, which alone can author a whole step because it carries its detail blocks. attention(workspaceId) is the workspace-wide awaiting-a-human scan on its own.

dataModel.body: nextActions yields {do[], blocked[], humanGates[], attention[]}. All four lists share one shape: a singular `command`. A `do` edge carries that plus a `kind` — a status transition is {pageId, pageType, kind:'transition', command}; a field setter is {pageId, pageType, kind:'field', section, field, instruction, command} — self-instructing, so a `next` consumer needs no describePageType round-trip. The exception is mutatePageBatch's trimmed echo, which leaves `instruction` off a field edge whose field already holds content on that edge's page; the edge is otherwise unchanged, and nextActions, createPage and a full echo always carry the key. blocked and humanGates are {pageId, pageType, command} (a `reason` on blocked, a `blockedReason` on a not-yet-satisfiable gate). attention items are {pageId, pageTitle, sectionKey, field, itemId, status}. `do` briefly carried a `commands` ARRAY instead, because a blocks field then emitted one edge naming its N per-kind add commands; with one add per field every edge names exactly one command, so the array would always hold one item and the singular key returns. When called for a specific page, the result also carries `guidance` (that page's stage prose for its current status) and zero or more `guidance_<field>` keys (the workspace-configured guidance for that status) - beside the four lists, at the top of this payload rather than inside any of them; a whole-workspace roll-up carries neither. Because createPage and mutatePageBatch both embed this payload as their `next`, it is also where a WRITE response's guidance is found - those tools add none of their own. createPage embeds it verbatim. mutatePageBatch embeds it verbatim on a full write, one that moved the page to a new status or landed after the page's last full delivery lapsed; on any other write it omits populated fields' instructions as above and leaves out both guidance keys.

- describeMutations reports them instead. A field is one edge naming one command:

This is what keeps a feature-brief's pinned implementation-plan, testing-plan and feature-spec silent while the brief is still draft or grounding. Previously the subtree rollup emitted addStep, addCase and setOverview from the first moment, so a grounding brief handed the agent the whole feature's authoring surface and invited planning against a base that did not exist yet.

inlines.text: The three instruction channels

inlines: - what the invariant on guidance placement is enumerating. The per-field instruction rides on a

edge (kind='field') and names which field to author next, until the field holds content: from then on a trimmed mutatePageBatch echo leaves it off, while a full echo and nextActions keep it. The per-status stage guidance is next_actions' own

key for the focused page. The per-workspace guidance - a runtime-configured text keyed by field, surfaced as guidance_<field> while a page of a declaring type sits at one of that field's statuses - is computed by the pure

and emitted beside it. Both guidance keys reach a write only on a full echo, while nextActions and createPage always carry them; a status declaring no text simply omits the key, and a whole-workspace roll-up carries neither guidance key.

inlines.text: Why a write's echo drops a filled field's instruction

items.statement: The partition is generic — no page-type knowledge is baked in. It reads agency and preconditions straight off the command specs and the FSM, so a new page type is classified correctly with no changes here.

A human-gate edge is always a stop point: it is listed in humanGates whether or not its preconditions are met (carrying a blockedReason when they are not), so the agent never silently drives past a sign-off.
blocked names the fix: an unmet required-content precondition lists the fields to author; an unmet cross-page guard (ship) names the incomplete child plan and its offending item's status.
attention uses the awaitsHuman predicate — an escalated, still-open question — and, like every read, ignores archived pages. Answering the question (open -> answered) clears it.

A failing parent guard OUTRANKS unmet content in a blocked edge's `reason`. While the parent has not unlocked the stage the content is not the fix and its setters are absent from `do`, so reporting 'requires: steps.items' would name work that is not due yet; the reason gives the parent-state message instead. Unmet content still outranks a failing CHILD guard, which is unchanged.

Each do / blocked / humanGates edge carries the status_revision_token of its page, beside pageId - the token a caller must present to mutate that page. Because `next` and the nextActions tool are both next_actions output, both surface it identically, so a caller can read an edge and satisfy the mutation token check from the one rollup. attention items name an element awaiting a human rather than a command to fire, so they do not carry it.

A field setter enters `do` only when its (section, field) is a required precondition of a transition topologically legal from the current status, that transition is not parent-gated, and the setter is legal now. Violated, `do` becomes every legal command rather than the stage's work, and an always-legal setter adds noise in statuses where its field is not the goal.

A page type declares at most one do-eligible setter per (section, field), checked when the registry is validated at load. Violated, a `do` field edge names one command while a second exists, so the second is silently dropped rather than reported.

A transition barred by a failing ParentStateGuard contributes none of its required content to `do`, because nothing authored on this page can clear it. Violated, a pinned child advertises its whole authoring surface before its parent has unlocked the stage, inviting work against a base that does not exist yet.

Only a PARENT guard suppresses field setters; a CHILD guard never does. Violated, a page stops surfacing its own authoring work whenever any child is unfinished - so a brief in planning would fall silent instead of surfacing askQuestion.

All three instruction channels ride inside `next`, and createPage and mutatePageBatch add no guidance key of their own. Violated, a write response carries two copies of the same guidance that can disagree - which is exactly what happened when a top-level `guidance` sat beside `next`.

Only mutatePageBatch's echo omits a field edge's instruction, only on a trimmed write, and only for a field holding content on that edge's own page; nextActions always carries every instruction. Violated, an agent resuming work cannot re-establish what a stage requires from nextActions, or a write hides the instruction of a field still to be authored.

nextActions for a focused page and createPage's echo always carry the page's guidance keys; only mutatePageBatch's echo omits them, and only on a trimmed write, one that neither moved the written page to a new status nor found its last full delivery lapsed. Violated, an agent resuming work cannot read a stage's instruction from nextActions, or the write that enters a stage arrives without the instruction for it.

Every path that hands a caller the full payload for a focused page records GUIDANCE_EMITTED: createPage, a focused nextActions and a full mutatePageBatch write. Violated, an unrecorded delivery is repeated inside its window, and if only transitions recorded it, every write after the window would be full.
A disabled event cache stores nothing and answers is_due False before it looks at anything. Violated, an empty cache reads as everything being due, so every write goes full.

Section 2 of the hand-written page-type brief, in docs/designing-page-types.md and again inline in .claude/skills/pasta-workflow-creation/SKILL.md, restates the do / blocked / humanGates / attention partition and the rule that a field setter enters do only when a transition out of the current status requires its field. When that partition or rule changes, or a new or changed field, page type or guard changes how an edge is classified, update BOTH files in the same change and keep their brief text identical. Violated, the pasta-workflow-creation skill designs workflows around a do list the server no longer produces.

summary.body: Hide/restore for pages (and their subtrees) and for whole workspaces, kept separate from a page's lifecycle status. Page archiving is fully reversible and never expires on its own; a page is deleted only once it is also scheduled for deletion, which is a separate, deliberate decision. Workspace archiving is a listing flag only and is never destructive.

purpose.body:
Take a page or workspace out of the default view without touching its FSM status, so stale or superseded content can be tucked away and later restored intact.

Archiving is a visibility decision and nothing more. A page can sit in the archive forever, because plenty of content is worth keeping without being worth showing. Destroying a page is a second decision a person makes explicitly, recorded on the page as `delete_scheduled`; the archive is then the staging area where that page waits out its grace period. Splitting the two is what lets the server reclaim space from content someone has actually condemned, without putting everything a human ever tidied away on a clock.

usage.body:
archivePage(workspaceId, pageId) / unarchivePage(workspaceId, pageId) toggle a page's archived flag. archiveWorkspace(workspaceId) / unarchiveWorkspace(workspaceId) toggle a workspace's status. Archived pages and their subtrees are hidden from tree, search and renderPage - always, with no flag to include them; to read one, use getPage with its id (which does not filter on archived) or the web UI's ?archived=true view.

Archiving alone starts no clock: an archived page is kept until someone asks for it to go. Scheduling that is a web-only action, because it is a decision a person makes in the browser - the Set to delete button on the page view, which POSTs to /ws:{id}/page/{pageId}/schedule-delete, and Cancel delete, which POSTs to /unschedule-delete. There is no MCP tool for it. Scheduling also archives the page, so a page queued for deletion is never left in a live view; cancelling leaves it archived, and unarchiving cancels the schedule outright.

Once a page is scheduled, the next cleanup sweep (hourly, at :05 UTC) stamps it with an expiry five days out at 12:00 UTC, and the sweep after that instant deletes it and its subtree, backing the workspace up first. To find what is genuinely condemned, look for delete_scheduled on a page; a non-null expires_at is the sweep's own bookkeeping and can linger for a sweep after a schedule is called off.

dataModel.body:
A page carries two persisted booleans, `archived` and `delete_scheduled`, and a nullable `expires_at` (persisted, UTC ISO-8601); a workspace carries a `status` of active | archived. archivePage yields {id, archived}; archiveWorkspace yields {id, name, status}. None of them touches sections or FSM status.

Both booleans are written only by Store._set_page_archive_state, which every archive and scheduling entry point goes through, so the pinned-child rules are applied once and the two flags cannot disagree on a pinned child. `expires_at` is written and cleared ONLY by the cleanup sweep (src.cleanup via Store.cleanup_workspace) - no page-type command and no web route can set it, and scheduling does not set it directly; the next sweep does.

The three fields are independent on disk but not in practice: no control produces a page that is scheduled without being archived, and a page hidden underneath an archived ancestor carries archived=False and delete_scheduled=False while still being deleted with that ancestor. A page file written before this feature simply loads with delete_scheduled=False, which is why no migration was needed.

inlines.text: Two decisions, not one

inlines: - archiving hides a page and scheduling condemns it, and the sweep acts only where both are true. The button pair on the page view enforces the useful half of that: scheduling also archives, so nothing is ever queued for deletion while still visible, while cancelling a deletion leaves the page archived, because wanting a page out of sight is the common case and wanting it destroyed is the rare one. Unarchiving clears
as well, so the rule a reader can rely on is that anything findable in the tree is not condemned.

inlines.text: Grace period and the deletion clock

inlines: - the delay between the decision and the destruction. The hourly sweep stamps a scheduled page with an expiry five days out at 12:00 UTC, and once that instant passes the page and its whole subtree are permanently deleted, behind a full workspace backup written first. Cancelling or unarchiving before then drops the stamp on the next sweep and restores the full window, so a mis-click stays undoable for days rather than hours. Nothing deletes a page at the moment a human clicks.

inlines.text: Why a descendant is deleted without ever being scheduled

inlines: - scheduling a page condemns its subtree with it.
flags only the target (cascading to pinned auto-children), and the sweep stamps only the scheduled page itself, not the pages beneath it. When that page's expiry passes,

removes the whole subtree as one unit and unlinks the root. So a descendant carries neither flag and never carries an expiry, yet goes with its ancestor - which is what keeps the flag meaning one person's decision about one page rather than something that spreads downward.

inlines.text: Workspace archiving is deliberately not destructive

inlines: - deleting an archived workspace's contents is out of scope by design: the blast radius of one call would be the whole workspace. The archived flag is otherwise a gate on visibility, not on the reversal itself, which is why
stays runnable while the workspace is archived - it is the way back.

inlines: - the invariants here previously said an archived subtree is hidden "by default" and named tree(includeArchived=true) as the way to reveal it. That parameter no longer exists:
takes

alone, and its own docstring states that archived pages and their subtrees are always hidden, because the archived tail is history and returning it inline buries the active pages. To reach an archived page, use
with its id (which does not filter on archived) or the web UI's ?archived=true view.

inlines.text: Archive changes reach the lifecycle log

inlines: - because every archive and scheduling entry point goes through
, that one transaction logs an
or
event for each page whose flag it actually flipped, the pinned-child cascade included. Scheduling a deletion archives a live page and so logs

; cancelling it leaves the flag as it is and logs nothing. A descendant hidden under an archived ancestor keeps its own flag and gets no event, so the timeline reads hidden-ness from the workspace rather than from the log (see
). The cleanup sweep's deletions are not logged.

items.statement: A page's FSM status is untouched by archive and unarchive, so a page returns from the archive in exactly the status it left. Violated, archiving becomes a lifecycle operation and a page's status stops reporting where its work actually is.

An archived page and its whole subtree are hidden from tree, search and renderPage - always, with no flag to reveal them - and the page cannot be mutated until it is unarchived. Violated, either archived content reappears in the views the archive exists to keep it out of, or a page stays editable while nobody can find it.

Archiving a page is reversible indefinitely: an archived page is never stamped and never deleted unless it also carries delete_scheduled. Violated, the archive becomes a delayed shredder again and content a human meant to keep is destroyed for having been tidied away.

No control leaves a page scheduled for deletion while it is still findable: scheduling also archives, and unarchiving clears the schedule. Violated, a page sits in the tree looking live while carrying a countdown nobody can see.
unarchiveWorkspace is runnable while the workspace is archived. Violated, an archived workspace cannot be restored and the archive becomes a one-way door.

A descendant of a scheduled page is pruned with it although it carries neither flag and is never stamped in its own right. Violated, either a scheduled subtree leaves orphaned pages filed under a parent that no longer exists, or the sweep deletes pages nobody condemned.

archiveWorkspace sets workspace.status only and never touches any page's archived flag, so no page inside becomes a deletion candidate. Violated, a single call puts an entire workspace's contents on a deletion clock.

summary.body: The human-facing browser view of the wiki and the dev-server machinery that keeps both surfaces live. A read-only FastAPI HTML front end renders the same pages agents author over MCP; a browser live-reload socket and an in-process hot-module-reload (HMR) dev server let source and data changes land in open tabs and connected MCP sessions without a restart.

purpose.body: Let humans read the typed wiki that agents write over MCP, and make iterating on the server fast. On a source edit the running server reloads its modules in place — MCP client sessions and browser tabs stay connected and refresh themselves rather than the process respawning. This is a reading and development surface layered over the same core; it is deliberately not a second path for changing state.

usage.body: main.py starts the combined HTTP dev server by default; --stdio instead runs the MCP surface alone, with no hot reload. In the browser, / lists workspaces, /ws:<id> shows a workspace's page tree, /ws:<id>/page/<pageId> renders one page, and /ws:<id>/timeline replays the workspace's lifecycle log (see Timeline replay) - all read-only. The index and tree views, and the page view's nav sidebar, render store data to Markdown and then to HTML; the page BODY instead comes from Store.render_html as structured HTML, built directly rather than converted. Every served page except the timeline opens a WebSocket to /ws/reloader; the server pushes a refresh over it whenever a source file changes (hot reload) or a mutation tool changes data, so open tabs stay current on their own. That refresh fires whether or not the reload took: after a failed reload both surfaces refuse instead of answering - the browser gets a 503 naming the reload error, and a tool call gets the same error back - so a refreshed tab lands on the refusal, and both return to normal on the next reload that succeeds.

dataModel.body: The outer ASGI app is a stable Starlette router, built once: /pasta/mcp is served by a persistent FastMCP proxy, and every other request is forwarded to the src.server.app (FastAPI) of the build serving now. The dev server watches src/ with watchfiles; once the tree has been quiet for 300 ms, a batch carrying any .py change re-imports the whole src package from disk, all or nothing. On success the proxy tears down its old mount, mounts the reloaded MCP server, and notifies every live client connection (tools/list_changed); the FastAPI dispatcher forwards to the new app. On failure the module set loaded before is put back exactly, the last good build keeps serving, and the failure is recorded so both surfaces refuse until a reload succeeds. Long-lived in-process state outlasts a reload by staying out of the re-import. src/hmr_server.py (the reloader) and src/hmr_live_refresh.py (the live browser WebSockets in a single ReloaderConnectionManager, ws_reloader, and the last reload failure) are never re-imported. src/event_cache.py and src/_hmr_debug.py hold state and import nothing from the package, so they are re-imported only when their own file changed. The pure half - which modules a batch drops (modules_to_drop), whether it re-imports at all (needs_reimport), and the failure summary - sits apart from the effectful re-import, swap and watch loop.

items.statement: One process serves both surfaces: a single uvicorn server runs the MCP tool endpoint and the FastAPI HTML front end together, and hot reload happens in-process — a source change never respawns the process.

Live browser connections survive reloads: the WebSocket connection registry lives in hmr_live_refresh, which is never re-imported. Were it re-imported, its in-memory sockets would be dropped and browser auto-refresh would silently stop.

Reloads preserve clients, not just modules: an MCP session is kept alive across a reload — the old mount is torn down, the reloaded server mounted, and every live client connection is sent tools/list_changed — and browser tabs are told to reload over their existing socket. The notification reaches clients on a handshake-era protocol (2025-xx) that hold a standalone stream; a client on the sessionless 2026-07-28 era over HTTP has no channel to receive it and picks up the new tools on its next tools/list. Violated, a handshake-era client keeps calling the tool list it fetched before the reload.

The browser refresh has two independent triggers over one socket — a source-file change (developer hot reload) and a data mutation (any write tool) — so a human watching a page sees an agent's edits land live, and a developer sees code edits land live.

The hot-reload machinery is a dev-only convenience, not part of the served contract: it reaches into two private fastmcp/mcp internals — the proxy's providers list, where each mount appends one provider that unmounting removes, and the constructor of mcp.server.connection.Connection, wrapped for the dev server's lifetime to capture each client connection. tests/test_hmr_server.py pins both, so a framework upgrade that moves them fails in the suite rather than silently in the dev server. The stdio transport has no hot reload at all.

The Model doc overlay is presentation-only and state-aware: clicking Model swaps in a statically-served Sphinx page — the doc for the page's own type AND current status, /sphinx/page-types/<type>-<status>.html — inside an iframe over the rendered body, adding no route, lock, or state. The sole server-side change is passing that page_type_doc stem to the page.html template, so the web UI's read-only contract still holds. It is scoped to page.html via _nav.html, so the index and tree views never carry it.

The inner FastAPI app's lifespan never runs under the HMR dev server, so anything that must start with the dev server has to be started from reloader_lifespan. Violated - i.e. if something is left in server.app_lifespan alone - it is silently dead code in development and never starts.

The web UI is strictly read-only: its routes project store data (a workspace index, a page tree, a page, a timeline replay) into HTML, making no change - whether they get there via Markdown or build the HTML directly. Like every other read they take the shared half of the workspace's readers-writer lock while the workspace file is read, so a page view cannot render a workspace file caught mid-write; they never take the transaction lock. The lifecycle log is read without a lock, because it is only ever appended and a torn last line is skipped. State changes only ever through the MCP command path - which then fires the same browser refresh.

Markdown-escaping still guards every route that renders through Markdown: route_tree and route_index, and the page view's nav sidebar, pass escape_plain_text=True into the renderer (and escape_markdown over the workspace-index names), so a plain-text value cannot be reinterpreted as Markdown by the md2html pass. route_page's BODY no longer takes that path and escapes as HTML instead. Either way it is presentation-only and web-only - the MCP surface returns the same Markdown as before - so the strictly read-only contract is unchanged. Both mechanisms live in the renderers (see Reads & navigation).

There are two renderers over the same page and the caller picks: renderPage returns the Markdown one byte-for-byte, while the web page body is built as structured HTML. Violated, a change made for the human view silently moves the bytes the MCP tool returns.

All structured-render styling is scoped under the pasta-page class and takes every colour from a water.css custom property. Violated, a literal colour reads correctly in only one theme, and an unscoped selector leaks into the nav, index and tree views that share the page shell but are rendered by the other path.

A failed reload is reported at error level through the uvicorn logger, never left as a bare traceback. Violated, the only signal that an edit did not take is a stack trace between INFO lines, followed immediately by an ordinary access-log line for a request answered out of the code that edit was meant to replace.

The quarantine is the hot-reload path only: a cold start still raises out of validate_registry() and never binds a port. Violated, an invalid declaration becomes a server that boots and serves refusals indefinitely, turning a startup error into a running one nobody is watching.

The footer's source link never carries credentials: to_source_link drops the userinfo of every remote form before the link reaches the page shell, and a remote it cannot map gives no link rather than a raw URL. Violated, a token embedded in an HTTPS remote is served to every visitor on every page.

A reload is all or nothing: a failed import puts back exactly the module set loaded before it. Violated, a lazy import inside the last good code picks up a half-imported module and the server answers out of a mix of two builds.

Only src.hmr_server and src.hmr_live_refresh are never re-imported, and src.event_cache and src._hmr_debug are kept only until their own file changes; every other src module is re-imported on any .py change. Violated - a module kept without that reason - an edit to it silently takes nothing until a restart, and a kept module that reads from the package keeps reading a build that has been replaced.
src/event_cache.py imports nothing from its package, which is what makes keeping it across a reload safe. Violated, the kept cache keeps calling into a build that has since been replaced.

A module that owns a live task has it stopped on the old module before a reload swaps it out and started on the new one after. Violated, the old task survives into the new build, still running the old code with nothing left holding a handle to cancel it.

A failed reload is never served silently: both surfaces ask per request whether the last reload failed and whether the live registry validates, and refuse until a reload succeeds. Violated, the last good build answers as if the edit had landed, and an agent keeps working against code the developer believes was replaced.

summary.body: The pure generator that turns the page-type registry into the docsite's per-state reference — one Sphinx page per page-type state — so the page-type docs are a projection of the code and cannot drift.

purpose.body: Make the page-type reference documentation a projection of the registry rather than hand-written prose. Every page type and every one of its FSM states gets a generated page, so the docs always match the sections, commands, and state machine the code actually enforces. It replaces the earlier hand-authored per-type overview pages, whose content could silently fall out of step with the registry.

usage.body: scripts/gen_page_type_docs.py drives the pure src.docsgen over the registry and writes one docsite/page-types/<tag>-<state>.md per reachable state plus a generated states.md toctree index; Sphinx builds them (the statemachine-diagram directive renders each machine with :format: dot), and the web Model overlay serves the built page for a page's current type-and-state. Re-run the script after changing the registry or the doc templates, then rebuild the docsite.

dataModel.body: docsgen is pure: it reads the PageType registry and returns markdown strings, doing no I/O. reachable_states walks FSMSpec.transitions breadth-first from the initial state, giving every reachable state the shortest event path that reaches it — emitted as the diagram's :events: option. For each state it seeds a content-less Page pinned at that status and calls describe_mutations to read the legal command surface, splitting it into the page-status transitions out of the state (kind transition/compound) and the authoring commands legal there. The whole describe_page_type result — the type's sections/fields and its complete command catalog — is rendered on every state page. The scripts/ driver is the only stateful part: it splits the returned {stem: markdown} map into files and writes the toctree index.

It reads a file back only when it is present and skips the rewrite when the content is byte-identical, reporting the written/unchanged split. Because regeneration is idempotent, the steady state is "0 files written, N unchanged", which makes an unexpected write a signal that the registry moved. Tolerating a missing file is what lets the generator run on a clean checkout and after

A state declaring none keeps the placeholder, so pages for undocumented states remain byte-identical and regeneration stays idempotent - which is what let simple-change and bug-report each pick up guidance on three of their states, and a new review page apiece, while every page of every other type stayed byte-for-byte where it was. The guidance is read through the describe projection rather than off the registry directly, so the generated docs and the write-path echo an agent receives are one text that cannot disagree.

items.statement: The page-type reference is generated, never hand-authored: every docsite/page-types/<tag>-<state>.md and the states.md index come from docsgen over the registry, so the only hand-authored docsite pages are the landing (index.md, page-types.md). Regeneration is idempotent, so a docs diff reflects a real registry change.

The FSM is walked on topology alone: because the StateMachine classes built per FSMSpec are guardless, a state's :events: path and its outgoing transitions derive from FSMSpec.transitions, so content preconditions never block the walk or the diagram.

ignore_requirements skips ONLY the required-content preconditions — not FSM topology and not the legal_in status-lock — so a content-gated transition is documented as available at its source state while a status-scoped command lock is still shown truthfully. It is internal to doc generation and is never surfaced by the describeMutations MCP tool.

Each state page is self-contained for its type: it captures the full describePageType result (sections and fields, and the complete command catalog, identical across the type's states) alongside the state-specific diagram, the transitions out of the state linked to the sibling state pages, and the authoring commands legal there.

Pure core, thin shell: all markdown is produced by pure functions over the registry and is unit-tested, while scripts/gen_page_type_docs.py only splits the returned map into files; the web Model overlay that serves the built docs is a consumer, not part of generation.

Each state page renders describe_page_type and describe_mutations verbatim, so a change to the describe projection's command schemas reaches the docs with no docgen edit. Violated, the generator carries its own copy of the schema shape and the docs can describe a command differently from the tool.

A field-line note is derived from the projection and never restated in the generator: if a reader has to open docsgen.py to learn what a field accepts, the projection is missing the key rather than the generator missing a line. Violated, a new field-projection key is silently invisible in the docs.

The generator writes only what actually changed and never assumes an output file exists. Violated in the first respect, a docs diff stops signalling a real registry change; in the second, a from-scratch generation on a clean checkout cannot complete.

A state page opens with that state's own declared guidance when the page type has one, read through the describe projection, and keeps the placeholder line otherwise. Violated, the generated docs and the guidance an agent receives on a write become two texts that can disagree - and pages for undocumented states stop being byte-identical, so regeneration is no longer idempotent.

The diagram's class path is derived from the page type and verified to be served before it is emitted. Violated, a page type whose machine binding was never added goes silently undocumented, or the Sphinx directive fails to import a path that does not resolve.

Doc generation enumerates registered_pagetypes() - the same map that backs resolution and the describePageType listing - so what is documented is exactly what is advertised. Violated, the site can publish a type that does not resolve, or omit one that does.

summary.body: An in-process hourly timer that sweeps every workspace, stamps a uniform expiry on pages a person has condemned and on pages filed nowhere, and permanently deletes the ones whose expiry has passed - writing a full timestamped workspace backup before any deletion.

purpose.body:
Workspaces only ever grew. Nothing removed a page someone had finished with, or one left unreachable by a structural bug, so every workspace document carried its whole history forever and the tail got steadily more expensive to store and to read past.

This is the one path in the system that destroys data, so it acts on an explicit decision and then only after a delay. Being out of sight is not that decision: a page is a candidate once a person schedules it for deletion, and the archive is where it then waits. The one exception is a page filed nowhere at all, which is a candidate on its own because nobody can reach it to condemn it. Delete this component and workspaces resume growing without bound; widen it back to everything hidden and an archive stops being somewhere content can simply live; make it act immediately and a mis-click becomes unrecoverable.

usage.body:
Nothing calls this deliberately - it runs itself. start_scheduler(store) is invoked from BOTH src.server.app_lifespan and src.hmr_server.reloader_lifespan, and is idempotent so the double call creates one task; stop_scheduler() cancels it.

The task wakes every MAX_SLEEP_SECONDS (30) and sweeps when the :05 tick has just gone by - less than one sleep of elapsed time since it, measured as SWEEP_PERIOD_SECONDS - seconds_until_next_run(now). run_once(store) then goes through asyncio.to_thread so its blocking file I/O never stalls the event loop.

run_once is also the manual entry point: call it directly to force a pass without waiting for a tick. Store.cleanup_workspace(workspace_id, now) does one workspace and returns a SweepReport; it accepts an explicit `now`, which is how the tests drive a page across its expiry without waiting five days.

One environment variable. PASTA_CLEANUP=0 disables the timer entirely; any other value, or leaving it unset, enables it - scheduler_enabled() tests nothing else, and in particular does not branch on the transport. Whether the sweep actually runs therefore depends on whether anything calls start_scheduler: the two lifespans that do are the FastAPI app's and the dev server's, and under --stdio neither fires, so a stdio server never sweeps however the variable is set. That is deliberate, because a stdio server is a per-client subprocess and several could race on the same data dir with only in-process locking. That is the whole configuration surface - there is no switch for individual parts of the sweep.

dataModel.body:
Owns exactly one persisted field: Page.expires_at, a nullable UTC ISO-8601 instant. It is written and cleared ONLY by this sweep - no page-type command and no web route can touch it - and is orthogonal to FSM status.

It reads, but does not own, two booleans belonging to archiving: `archived`, through the reachability walk rather than directly, and `delete_scheduled`, which is what a person sets and what decides whether a hidden page is a candidate at all. Both are written only by Store._set_page_archive_state.

Three in-memory shapes, all frozen dataclasses in src/cleanup.py. Reachability{findable, hidden, unfiled: set[str]} is the bucketing of every page. Sweep{stamp: dict[str,str], clear: list[str], prune: list[str]} is the intent for one pass, where prune holds only maximal subtree roots. SweepReport{workspace_id, stamped, cleared, pruned, backup, error} is what a pass actually did; a non-null error means nothing at all was written.

On disk it owns <PASTA_DATA_DIR>/backups/<ws_token>/<YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ>.json - one full workspace document per pruning run, written with the same serializer as the live file, so restoring is a plain file copy. These are never deleted by anything; retention is deliberately out of scope.

inlines: Two arms decide what is a candidate, and they are not symmetrical. The first is a page that is out of sight AND carries
- either archived itself or sitting under an archived ancestor with

, since tree and search hide the whole subtree. Being hidden is not enough on its own: an archived page nobody condemned is left alone forever, which is what makes the archive a place content can live rather than a delayed shredder. The second arm is the classic orphan the offline validator already reports: a page in
that is in neither
nor any page's

, so it is filed nowhere. That one needs no flag, because nothing can reach it to set one - it is unreachable by accident rather than by decision, and leaving it would be an unbounded leak with no control able to drain it.
Reachability is decided by walking DOWN from
through
- the structure the tree renders from.
is ignored entirely, and that is a safety property rather than an omission: a page whose

disagrees with its filing stays exactly what it is today, a repair the validator reports to a human, and can never escalate into a deletion on the strength of a stale pointer. The walk carries a visited set, so a cycle accidentally introduced into
terminates rather than hanging the server inside the workspace lock.

body.source:
One pass over one workspace, entirely inside Store._transaction_lock_for(workspace_id):

  load -> classify -> [backup] -> clear -> stamp -> prune -> save
                         |
                         +-- only when something will be pruned, and if this
                             write raises the whole pass is abandoned: no
                             stamps either, so the workspace is left untouched
                             rather than half-applied.

Holding the lock across the whole sequence is what guarantees the backup is a
snapshot of exactly the state the prune then acts on - no MCP mutation can land
in between.

inlines: The stamp is sticky and the clear is what makes it a real grace period. A sweep writes

only on a page that has none: re-stamping every hour would push the deadline forward forever and nothing would ever expire. Conversely the moment a page stops being a candidate - the schedule cancelled, the page unarchived, its archived ancestor restored, or the page re-filed - the next sweep drops the stamp. So a page condemned, reprieved a day later and condemned again gets a fresh full window instead of inheriting a nearly-elapsed one. The same clear arm is what retired the previous rule without a migration: pages stamped while merely archived stopped being candidates and had their stamps dropped by the first sweep that ran.

The expiry is a uniform wall-clock instant, not a duration: 12:00:00 UTC on the date five days after the sweep. Every page stamped on the same UTC day therefore shares one deadline. The cost, accepted deliberately, is that real grace runs between 4 days 12 hours and 5 days 12 hours depending on the time of day the stamp was written.
Neither framework facility could have provided the timing, which is worth recording because it is the obvious first thing to reach for. FastAPI's

runs a callable once, after a response, on a request that a client made - there is no request here and no repetition. FastMCP's background tasks implement the MCP tasks extension (SEP-1686 / SEP-2663) so a client can poll a long-running tool call; in FastMCP 4 that is a separate

package backed by Docket, and it is still triggered by a tool call rather than a clock. Recurring wall-clock scheduling is out of scope for both, so the mechanism is a plain asyncio task owned by a lifespan - which also costs no new dependency, unlike APScheduler or Celery.

inlines.text: The module is hot-reloadable, both the sweep logic and the timing, and holds nothing of its own for that. A reload re-imports it with the rest of the package, so the dev server owns the handover: once the new build has imported cleanly it awaits
on the old module, swaps the new build in, and calls
on the new module with the new store. A failed reload changes nothing, so the old sweep keeps running on the build that keeps serving. The dev server reaches the module only as the
attribute of the src.server build it is swapping, because the dev server itself is never re-imported and a module it imported directly would stay the first build's for the life of the process.
Corrections at a35b133

no longer exists. It was split into
(a threading.Lock taken only by writers, which is the one the sweep holds across its whole pass) and
(a readers-writer lock held for a single file operation). The guarantee is unchanged - the pass still runs under one per-workspace transaction lock - so only the name moved. Second, the environment:
is just PASTA_CLEANUP not equal to "0", with no transport branch anywhere, and

is reached only from server.app_lifespan and hmr_server.reloader_lifespan. Under --stdio neither lifespan runs, so the sweep is off there because nothing starts it - not because the env default distinguishes transports, and PASTA_CLEANUP=1 cannot force it on.

items.role: depends-on
items.note: Consumes `delete_scheduled` as the signal that a hidden page may be destroyed, and the archived-subtree hiding rule that makes a non-archived descendant count as out of sight. Archiving stays fully reversible: this component acts only where a person has also scheduled the page.

items.role: depends-on
items.note: Is started by reloader_lifespan, because the inner FastAPI app's lifespan never fires under the dev server. It is re-imported with the rest of the package on every reload, and the dev server stops the sweep on the old module and starts it on the new one around the swap, so the task is handed over rather than leaked.

items.role: depends-on
items.note: Shares the per-workspace lock and the copy -> edit -> serialize -> write transaction shape with the authoring path, and is the only writer of Page.expires_at, which no page-type command can reach.

items.statement: A page is never deleted without a durable backup of the workspace it came from. The backup is written before any mutation in the same locked pass, and an OSError there abandons the pass entirely - no stamps, no deletes - so a prune on top of a missing backup cannot happen.

A page is only ever deleted after being continuously a candidate for its whole grace period. Ceasing to be one at any point - the schedule cancelled, the page unarchived or re-filed - clears the stamp, so condemning it again starts a fresh five days and there is no state in which a visible or reprieved page carries a live countdown.

Being out of sight is never sufficient for deletion: a hidden page is stamped only when it also carries delete_scheduled, so an archived page nobody condemned survives indefinitely. Violated, the archive silently destroys content a human meant to keep. The single exception is a page filed nowhere, which is a candidate without a flag because no control can reach it to set one.

Pruning deletes whole subtrees and leaves no dangling reference: every descendant goes with the root, the root is unlinked from its parent's child_ids or from root_page_ids, and links held by surviving pages to deleted ones are stripped in the same commit. Violating this would have the sweep manufacture the orphans and dangling links it exists to remove.

The whole per-workspace pass runs inside one Store._transaction_lock_for(workspace_id), so no MCP write can interleave between the backup and the deletion it protects. Cross-process safety is NOT provided - the store's in-process-only locking is unchanged - and is avoided instead by having only the single long-lived HTTP server sweep.

One bad workspace never ends a pass or kills the timer: each workspace is swept in its own try/except and reported with an error, and the task loop catches everything except CancelledError, which propagates so stop_scheduler shuts down cleanly.

Backups are never deleted by this component, and never appear as workspaces. They live under backups/, which the non-recursive '*.json' glob in list_workspaces cannot see, and their filenames are colon-free so they remain legal on Windows.

The loop sleeps MAX_SLEEP_SECONDS (30) at a time rather than the hour to the next tick, and sweeps when less than one sleep has elapsed since the tick. Consecutive wakes are a whole sleep apart, so exactly one lands inside that window and the sweep runs once per hour.

The sweep task never outlives a reload: the dev server awaits stop_scheduler() on the old module before the new build is swapped in and calls start_scheduler(STORE) on the new one after, reaching each only through the src.server build it belongs to. Violated - the old task left running, or the module imported directly by the never-reloaded dev server - the old task survives into the new build still running the old code, with nothing left holding a handle to cancel it.

feature-brief:mtiml5v4-6c209f.title: Surface stage-entry commands in `do`: a legal_in command highlights only in the statuses where it first becomes legal

summary.body:
Today `do` only surfaces a field setter when its field is required content for a transition out of the current stage. A command that is scoped to a status by `legal_in` but required by no transition - setPullRequestUrl in `review`, recordCommit in `building` - is therefore invisible in `next`, and an agent only finds it by calling describePageType and reading the whole command list. The outcome I want is that arriving in a status also tells the agent which optional-but-status-scoped work opens up there.

The nudge should fire once, when the work first becomes available, not in every status the command stays legal in. Because the page FSM is not a straight line, "first" is defined structurally: of the statuses in a command's legal_in, highlight it in the ones that have no incoming edge, so a status you can only arrive at from another status that already offered the command does not repeat the offer. setPullRequestUrl (legal_in = review only) is the trivial case and must highlight.

Simplicity is the point: this should be a small, generic derivation off the existing FSM and command specs, resolvable per page type without page-type knowledge, and it must not be confused by terminal statuses or statuses that are authoring-locked. If the structural rule turns out to mis-fire on the real page types in this repo, that is a question for the user, not something to patch with special cases.

items.name: src/commands.py :: field_setter_edges
items.text: PURE. The single place a `do` field edge is derived. Today: collect every (section, field) in the `requires` of a transition topologically legal from the current status (minus `blocked_events`), then emit one edge per such field whose setter is legal now, keyed by (section, field) so a field is one edge naming one command. The new stage-entry rule belongs here - it is the same shape of derivation over the same inputs (page, page_type).

items.name: src/commands.py :: legal_commands / _status_ok / _opts_into_terminal_status
items.text: PURE. The legality gate `field_setter_edges` already consults. `_status_ok` is the `legal_in` lock itself (legal_in is None -> always legal, else page.status must be in it). `_opts_into_terminal_status` is what lets a command explicitly named in a terminal status stay writable while every other authoring command is locked. Intersecting the new edges with `legal_commands` is what keeps terminal/authoring-locked statuses from being surfaced - no separate terminal handling is needed.

items.name: src/pagetypes/core/commands.py :: is_field_setter
items.text: PURE. The kind filter that decides what may enter `do` at all: SET_SCALAR, SET_PROSE, ADD_ELEMENT and a PAGE-LEVEL ADD_BLOCK count; element-scoped add-block, remove, reorder, set_element_field (flag setters) and element_transition do not. Reusing it unchanged is what keeps removeFinding / reorderStep / markStepDone out of the new surface.

items.name: src/pagetypes/core/pagetype.py :: _status_transitions + specs.py :: FSMSpec.transitions
items.text: PURE. The status edge table is DERIVED, not declared: each transition/compound command with an event contributes one (event, source, dest, agency) per entry in its own `legal_in` (its source statuses), with `dest` as the target. FSMSpec.transitions is filled in by PageType.__post_init__. This is the only source of "incoming edges" for the new rule: a status's incoming sources are the `source` of every edge whose `dest` is that status.

items.name: src/store.py :: Store.next_actions
items.text: EFFECTS (loads the workspace from disk). The shell: walks the subtree, classifies transition commands into do/blocked/humanGates, collects each page's parent-guard-blocked events, calls commands.field_setter_edges(page, page_type, parent_blocked) and extends `do` with the result, then attaches guidance for a focused page. The new edges arrive through that same one call, so this file changes little or not at all.

items.name: src/server.py :: nextActions / createPage / mutatePageBatch
items.text: EFFECTS. The three MCP tools that expose the payload - the latter two embed store.next_actions output verbatim as `next`. They add nothing to the lists, so a new `do` edge shape reaches every caller through these unchanged. The module also carries the MCP instructions prose that describes what `do` means.

items.name: src/fsm.py :: allowed_events
items.text: PURE (python-statemachine, cached per spec). Gives the events legal from a status. Used to decide which transitions' `requires` count as the current stage. The new rule needs the transition TABLE rather than the allowed events, so it reads page_type.fsm.transitions directly.

items.name: src/testtypes.py
items.text: PURE declarations. The hidden fixture page types the suite asserts against, so production types need not be churned. items.text: PURE tests / store tests. The existing contract for `do`: edges carry instructions, are stage- AND legal_in-scoped, drop legal_in=None noise, drop parent-blocked events, and a terminal state yields no field setters. Any new rule has to leave all of these passing - they are the regression surface.
requires-python = ">=3.14" (pyproject.toml, read verbatim). Dependencies pinned by floor include python-statemachine>=3.2.0, fastmcp>=3.4.4, pytest>=9.1.1, pytest-testmon>=2.2.0.

Tests run with pytest and, for red-green work, with --testmon (CLAUDE.md project hint; justfile `testincr` = `uv run pytest --testmon`, `just test` = full run, `just types` = basedpyright). Type checking must stay clean under basedpyright.
Use the word "create" instead of "mint" in code, comments and prose (CLAUDE.md project hint).

The partition must stay GENERIC - no page-type knowledge baked into next_actions or field_setter_edges. Declared as an invariant on the Self-direction architecture page: agency and preconditions are read off the command specs and the FSM, so a new page type is classified correctly with no changes there. The new rule must be derived the same way, off legal_in and the derived transition table alone.

A FIELD IS ONE EDGE NAMING ONE COMMAND: field_setter_edges keys entries by (section, field) holding a single command name, and pagetypes.core.validation.validate_pagetype_field_setters enforces at declaration time that a type declares at most one do-eligible setter per (section, field). New edges must not break that - a field must not be able to yield two `do` entries.

The pure/effect split in this codebase is explicit: src/commands.py is pure (takes a Page, returns a new Page or a derived value, never does I/O), src/store.py performs the storage effects. The derivation belongs in commands.py; store.py only calls it.

THE LITERAL RULE MATCHES NOTHING. Read as "a status with no incoming edge anywhere in the page FSM", the rule selects ZERO statuses across all 11 registered page types - verified by enumerating REGISTRY and the derived transition tables. Only an FSM's initial status can qualify, and every type that scopes a content command by legal_in also has a `reopen`-style edge back into its initial status (implementation-plan: ready->draft; simple-change/bug-report: closed->open). The only reading that produces the behaviour the summary asks for is the WITHIN-SET one: a status qualifies when no OTHER STATUS IN THAT COMMAND'S OWN legal_in has an edge into it. This has to be settled before anything is specced.

CYCLES INSIDE A legal_in SET SILENCE THE COMMAND ENTIRELY. Under the within-set reading, recordCommit (feature-brief: building/review/shipped) highlights NOWHERE, because building<->review is a cycle (submitForReview and requestChanges) and shipped is entered from review. The same silences markCommitStale, reorderCommit, bug-report/simple-change recordCommit (open<->review), decision-record setSupersededBy (authoring<->accepted) and the implementation-plan element marks (draft<->ready). This is the direct consequence of the "not strictly ordered" FSM the summary names, and it hits the one command whose stage guidance explicitly says "Record each commit as you make it".

OVERLAP WITH THE EXISTING STAGE EDGES. Several stage-entry candidates are already emitted today because their field is required content for the stage's transition (implementation-plan addStep in draft, agent-plan addAgent/addDispatch/setReporting in draft, setReviewVerdict in planReview). The new rule must be a UNION deduplicated by (section, field), not a second list, or `do` would carry the same field twice.

IT CHANGES WHAT A `do` FIELD EDGE MEANS. Today a kind='field' edge in `do` is exactly "author this to advance the stage" - every one of them is named in some blocked transition's `reason`. The new edges are optional-but-available work that no transition requires, so an agent reading `do` can no longer assume a field edge is a precondition. Either the edges are marked as distinct, or the documented meaning of `do` widens to "what is worth doing here".

THE EXCLUSION LIST IS AN EXISTING INVARIANT, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. The Self-direction page states that remove/reorder, set-block, flag setters, element transitions, addLink and setTitle never enter `do` (describeMutations only). Most legal_in-scoped commands in this repo are exactly those kinds - implementation-plan alone has removeStep, reorderStep, removeStepDetail, reorderStepDetail, reorderDataModel, markStepDone/Skipped/Todo all scoped by legal_in. Surfacing "operations that have legal_in that status" literally would flood `do` with them; reusing is_field_setter is what keeps the addition small.

MEASURED DELTA (union rule, is_field_setter filter, deduped against fields the stage already requires, over every registered type and status): bug-report review -> setPullRequestUrl; simple-change review -> setPullRequestUrl; feature-brief review -> setPullRequestUrl and planReview -> addFinding; epic planReview -> addFinding; implementation-plan draft -> addDataModels. Six edges in total, none in a terminal status. Everything else is either already surfaced or silenced by a cycle. Worth checking against intent: addDataModels on an implementation-plan is the one that is a real behaviour change rather than the obvious win.

MISSED IN GROUNDING, FOUND WHILE BUILDING: production page types are off-limits to the WHOLE test suite, not only to page creation. tests/conftest.py flips _registry.set_test_mode on for the session, and guard_production_type is called by get_page_type as well as by create_page - so get_page_type('feature-brief') raises ProductionTypeInTestError inside pytest. Grounding recorded only the creation half. Implementation-plan step 3 and testing-plan case 6, which asserted stage_entry_statuses against the real feature-brief / bug-report / decision-record FSMs, are therefore impossible as written and are marked skipped rather than forced through by reaching into REGISTRY behind the guard. Coverage is not lost: the ad-hoc FSM in the step-1 tests reproduces all three production shapes exactly - a single-status scope, a ('review','done') scope entered from outside, and a cyclic pair - and the literal production tuples are verified by the throwaway script in step 7, which runs outside pytest where the guard is inert.

architecture:mrtqsthj-dfd190 "Self-direction" - the Usage paragraph ("`do` holds TWO kinds of edge ... the field setters whose field must be authored to advance the current stage") and the invariant beginning "do surfaces the STAGE's field setters, not every legal one" both state the current rule as an exclusive one. Both need to state the widened rule and the new (section, field) dedupe. The Data model paragraph needs updating too if the new edges carry any distinguishing key.

architecture:mrtjuul6-5221b2 "Page types & FSM implementation" - describes legal_in as "a uniform legal_in gate (a content command's 'ready' lock, or a transition's source status(es))". It becomes stale in that legal_in on a content command now also drives what is SURFACED, not only what is permitted.

src/server.py - the MCP instructions prose ("Drive `do` edges as needed, following instructions") and the nextActions tool docstring describe `do` as edges legal now. If a new edge kind or flag is introduced, this is the text an agent reads first and it must name it.

"No incoming edges" has to mean WITHIN the command's own legal_in set - confirm? Read globally (a status nothing in the whole FSM transitions into), the rule selects zero statuses on every registered page type, because the only candidate is the FSM's initial status and every type that scopes content by legal_in also has a reopen-style edge back into it. Read within-set (no OTHER status listed in that same command's legal_in has an edge into this one), it gives exactly the behaviour the ask describes, including the setPullRequestUrl trivial case. Is within-set the intended rule?
items.answer: Within-set. A status in a command's legal_in qualifies when NO OTHER status listed in that same legal_in has a transition into it. Edges from statuses outside the set are ignored, which is what lets setPullRequestUrl (legal_in=['review']) highlight in review even though building transitions into review. Settled by the user.

items.text: A cycle inside a legal_in set silences the command everywhere - accept that, or add a fallback? recordCommit is legal_in building/review/shipped, and building<->review is a cycle (submitForReview / requestChanges), so no status in the set is uneentered and recordCommit highlights nowhere. Same for markCommitStale, bug-report/simple-change recordCommit, and decision-record setSupersededBy. Options: (a) accept the silence - the rule stays four lines and only ever speaks when the entry point is unambiguous; (b) fall back, when no status qualifies, to whichever legal_in status is nearest the FSM's initial status by shortest path, which would surface recordCommit in building.
items.answer: Fall back to nearest-to-initial. When the within-set rule leaves no qualifying status - the set is cyclic - highlight the legal_in status(es) at the shortest BFS distance from the FSM's initial status, over the derived transition table. recordCommit therefore highlights in `building` on a feature-brief and in `open` on a bug-report / simple-change. Statuses unreachable from initial are not candidates; if none is reachable the command stays silent. Settled by the user.

items.text: Should a stage-entry edge be distinguishable in `do` from a stage-required one? Today every kind='field' edge in `do` means "author this or the stage cannot advance", and each is named in some blocked transition's reason. A stage-entry edge is optional-but-available work no transition requires. Options: (a) identical shape - simplest, but `do` silently stops meaning "required"; (b) same shape plus one discriminating key (e.g. "required": true/false, or kind='available' beside kind='field') so an agent can tell must-do from may-do.
items.answer: Identical shape - no discriminator. A stage-entry edge is emitted as the same kind='field' edge with section, field, instruction, command and statusRevisionToken, indistinguishable from a stage-required one. The payload gains no key, so no consumer changes. The consequence is accepted deliberately: `do` now means "what is worth doing in this status" rather than strictly "what is required to advance", and the Self-direction page has to say so. Settled by the user.

items.text: Which command kinds are eligible - field setters only, or every legal_in-scoped command? Reusing the existing is_field_setter predicate (set_scalar, set_prose, add_element, page-level add_block) yields six new edges across the whole registry: setPullRequestUrl in review on three types, addFinding in planReview on two, addDataModels in implementation-plan draft. Taking "operations that have legal_in that status" literally instead would add removeStep, reorderStep, reorderStepDetail, reorderDataModel, markStepDone/Skipped/Todo, markCasePassed/Failed/Skipped, markCommitStale and escalateQuestion - which the Self-direction page currently declares are describeMutations-only and never enter `do`.
items.answer: Field setters only - the existing is_field_setter predicate, unchanged (SET_SCALAR, SET_PROSE, ADD_ELEMENT, page-level ADD_BLOCK). Element transitions, remove, reorder, element-scoped block adds, flag setters, addLink and setTitle stay out of `do` exactly as the Self-direction invariant already states. Settled by the user.

items.text: Does a stage-entry edge disappear once its field is populated? setPullRequestUrl targets a scalar, so once the URL is set the edge would keep repeating for as long as the page sits in review. Suppressing it when populated would keep `do` shrinking as work is done; keeping it unconditional matches how stage guidance behaves (present on every write in the status, not only the one that entered it) and avoids a rule that reads page content rather than page type.
items.answer: Unconditional - the edge stays while the page sits in the status, whether or not the field is populated. This keeps the derivation a function of page type and status alone rather than of page content, matches how stage guidance already behaves, and avoids a scalar setter blinking out of `do` mid-stage. Decided during spec, not escalated: it follows from the identical-shape decision, since the existing stage edges are already emitted regardless of whether their field holds content.

items.text: Do stage-entry edges have to respect the parent-state gate, and how? blocked_events withholds stage-REQUIRED content because nothing authored on the page can clear a parent guard, but a stage-entry edge is tied to no transition, so the existing mechanism does not reach it. Left alone it would leak: a pinned test-child in draft would emit addStep, addCheck, addNote and addDecision the moment it is created, which is exactly the parent-gated stage exposure the current invariant exists to prevent, and it would break test_field_setter_edges_drop_blocked_events and test_next_actions_withholds_child_field_setters_until_parent_unlocks.
items.answer: Yes, and by a directly stated condition rather than by routing through blocked_events: stage-entry edges are withheld when the stage is WHOLLY parent-gated, meaning every event legal from the current status is in blocked_events. Rejected: passing legal_in through the blocked_events machinery (a stage-entry edge has no transition to be blocked, so there is nothing to subtract), and dropping the gate entirely (it leaks the pinned child's authoring surface and breaks two existing tests). A partially gated stage keeps its edges - some other transition is still this page's to drive - and a dead-end terminal status keeps them too, since nothing gates it and legal_commands already locks authoring there.

The implementer would have written a test that fails for a reason unrelated to the feature and could easily have concluded the parent gate was leaking. Step 4 told the implementer to 'check the exact scalar helper names in the imports before writing, and follow the shape another fixture uses if they differ' - a soft TBD that hands a decision to the build. Checked: _scalar exists in src/pagetypes/core/fields.py and set_scalar_cmd in src/pagetypes/core/commands.py, and NEITHER is imported by tests/test_commands.py today, so the fixture as written would fail on a NameError. The step now names the two imports to add and states that set_scalar_cmd derives the command name from the field, which is what makes the expected setUrl correct.

Checked and found sound, recorded so it is not re-litigated during the build: the ad-hoc fixture's transitions are declared with transition_cmd, whose source and destination are parsed out of the 'draft -> open' arrow in its description, so the FSM table the new rule reads is derived exactly as it is for a production type. No explicit transitions tuple is needed on the FSMSpec, and the spec's requirement that the derivation stay generic is therefore genuinely exercised rather than bypassed by a hand-written table.

Coverage check of the spec against the steps, and back: every design section has a step that delivers it - stage_entry_statuses with both its rules (steps 1 and 2), the union and the removed early return (steps 4 and 5), the parent gate (steps 4 and 5), the unchanged edge shape (step 4's key-set assertion), the untouched store (step 6), and the ten-edge production surface (steps 3 and 7). No step builds anything the spec did not ask for: there is no caching, no new payload key, no page-type-specific branch, and no documentation step, since reconciling the architecture pages happens at ship rather than here.

Build the FSM specs directly rather than through a page type. FSMSpec is a frozen dataclass whose transitions field is normally filled in by PageType.__post_init__, but it accepts a transitions tuple straight in the constructor, and each entry is (event, source, dest, agency). That keeps these tests to pure input and output with no fixture at all. FSMSpec is imported from src.pagetypes.core.specs.

detail.source:
# --- stage-entry statuses (stage_entry_statuses) -----------------------------
# Ad-hoc FSMs built straight from FSMSpec: the helper reads only `initial` and the
# transition table, so a page type would add nothing but noise here.
_LINE = FSMSpec(name="XLine", initial="draft", states=("draft", "open", "review", "done"),
                transitions=(("begin", "draft", "open", "agent"),
                             ("submit", "open", "review", "agent"),
                             ("bounce", "review", "open", "agent"),
                             ("finish", "review", "done", "agent")))


def test_stage_entry_statuses_single_status_scope_always_qualifies():
    """The trivial case: a scope of one status has no other scoped status to be entered from,
    so it qualifies however many transitions arrive from outside it."""
    assert stage_entry_statuses(_LINE, ("review",)) == {"review"}


def test_stage_entry_statuses_ignore_edges_from_outside_the_scope():
    """Only edges BETWEEN scoped statuses disqualify. `review` is entered from `open`, but with
    `open` outside the scope `review` is still where the scope opens; `done` is entered from
    `review`, which is inside it, so it is not."""
    assert stage_entry_statuses(_LINE, ("review", "done")) == {"review"}


def test_stage_entry_statuses_fall_back_to_nearest_initial_when_the_scope_is_cyclic():
    """`open` and `review` enter each other, so no scoped status is unentered. The fallback picks
    the one the page reaches soonest from the FSM's initial status: draft->open is one edge,
    draft->open->review is two."""
    assert stage_entry_statuses(_LINE, ("open", "review")) == {"open"}


def test_stage_entry_statuses_fallback_keeps_every_status_at_the_shortest_distance():
    """A tie is not broken arbitrarily - both branches are entry points."""
    fork = FSMSpec(name="XFork", initial="draft", states=("draft", "a", "b"),
                   transitions=(("toA", "draft", "a", "agent"), ("toB", "draft", "b", "agent"),
                                ("aToB", "a", "b", "agent"), ("bToA", "b", "a", "agent")))
    assert stage_entry_statuses(fork, ("a", "b")) == {"a", "b"}


def test_stage_entry_statuses_empty_scope_and_unreachable_scope_yield_nothing():
    """Total over any input: an empty scope has nothing to offer, and a cyclic scope no path from
    the initial status reaches has no entry point rather than an arbitrary one."""
    assert stage_entry_statuses(_LINE, ()) == set()
    island = FSMSpec(name="XIsland", initial="draft", states=("draft", "x", "y"),
                     transitions=(("xToY", "x", "y", "agent"), ("yToX", "y", "x", "agent")))
    assert stage_entry_statuses(island, ("x", "y")) == set()


def test_stage_entry_statuses_ignore_a_status_the_fsm_does_not_declare():
    """A scope naming an unknown status cannot match a real page status, so it is simply absent
    from the result rather than an error."""
    assert stage_entry_statuses(_LINE, ("nope",)) == set()
