# Follows the label of a strip entry that opens another page, setting it apart from the
# anchors that only scroll this one.
_PAGE_LINK_MARK = " \N{LINK SYMBOL}"

def _contents_html(page_type: PageType, page: Page, ref_context: RefContext | None) -> str: """A strip of links to every section, each carrying its element count when it has one, so a page of long lists can be navigated without scrolling it. The strip opens with the page's parent and closes with its pinned children, linked by title.""" links: list[str] = [] if ref_context is not None and page.parent_id is not None and page.parent_id in ref_context.titles: links.append(f'Parent{_PAGE_LINK_MARK}') for section in page_type.sections: count = _section_count(section, page) badge = f'{count}' if count else "" links.append(f'' + f"{_escape(section.name)}{badge}") links.append('References') links.append('Child pages') if ref_context is not None: links += [f'' + f"{_escape(ref_context.titles[child_id])}{_PAGE_LINK_MARK}" for child_id in _pinned_child_ids(page_type, page, ref_context)] return f'

'

overview.body: Changes the links strip at the top of a page in the web view (the `nav.page-contents` row built by src/render_html.py `_contents_html`). Every page that has a parent gets a `Parent 🔗` link as the FIRST entry of the strip. After the existing section, References and Child pages anchors, a page whose type auto-creates pinned children (e.g. a feature-brief's Implementation plan, Testing plan and Spec) gets one link per pinned child, labelled with the child's title followed by the same 🔗 mark and pointing at that child's page. The existing anchors are unchanged. The change is confined to the pure HTML renderer. Out of scope: the Markdown renderer and so the renderPage MCP output (byte-for-byte unchanged), the bottom Child pages section, the store, the server routes, toc pages (they have no strip), grandchildren, and any styling change.

body.text: Behaviour

The strip reads, in this order: (1) a `Parent 🔗` link, shown when the page has a parent that resolves in the RefContext; (2) one anchor per declared section with its count badge, unchanged; (3) the References anchor, unchanged; (4) the `Child pages` anchor (href `#section-children`), always shown, unchanged; (5) one link per pinned child, in the page's stored child order. Nothing else in the page changes.

A child is pinned exactly when `is_auto_child_type(page_type, ref_context.types[child_id])` is true, which is the same rule the store's `_is_pinned_child` applies. A child id missing from `ref_context.types` is treated as not pinned. Pinned children are listed whether or not they are archived: the store never archives a pinned child on its own, so it is archived exactly when the page being viewed is.

Examples: a feature-brief under the Features toc shows `Parent 🔗, Summary ... Commits, References, Child pages, Implementation plan 🔗, Testing plan 🔗, Spec 🔗`. Its Spec child shows `Parent 🔗, Overview ... References, Child pages`, the Parent link pointing back at the brief. An epic shows `Parent 🔗 ... References, Child pages, Agent plan 🔗`. A page with no parent and no pinned children shows exactly the strip it shows on main.
Link markup

Every new entry is a bare `<a>` inside the existing nav, like the section anchors: no type/status annotation and no archived flag. The parent link's text is `Parent`; a pinned-child link's text is the child's title from `ref_context.titles`, escaped with `_escape`. Both are followed, inside the anchor, by a non-breaking space and the LINK SYMBOL U+1F517, held in one module constant `_PAGE_LINK_MARK = " \N{LINK SYMBOL}"`. The mark sets an entry that opens another page apart from the anchors that only scroll this one; the non-breaking space keeps the mark on the same line as its label when the strip wraps. Both hrefs come from `_page_href`: the page web route `/{workspace_id}/page/{page_id}` with `?archived=true` appended when `ref_context.show_archived` is set.

{"".join(links)}

body.text: Pure versus effectful

All new logic is pure: it reads only the Page, its PageType and the RefContext the store already builds once per render, and performs no I/O. Store.render_html and server.route_page, the effectful shell, are not touched; they already pass the RefContext through.
Fallbacks and error paths

Without a RefContext (a direct render, as in tests), nothing can be named or linked, so the strip is exactly main's: section anchors, References, Child pages, with no Parent link and no child names. A parent id that does not resolve in the RefContext gets no Parent link, matching how `_page_link` treats an unresolvable id. A toc keeps no strip at all, since render_page_html returns before building one. There are no new error paths: nothing here raises.

Yes: a page with no pinned children keeps today's Child pages anchor unchanged. The ask limits the new listing to auto-pinned children, so pages without them are out of scope. Rejected: listing all child names on every page, which the ask explicitly ruled out, and dropping the anchor on childless pages, which changes pages the feature is not about.

Each link shows the child's current title and they appear in the stored child order (for a feature-brief: Implementation plan, Testing plan, Spec, the auto_children declaration order). Rejected: a fixed order such as Spec first, because it would be a second ordering rule that disagrees with the tree and the Child pages section, and pinned children cannot be reordered to match it. Rejected: showing type labels instead of titles, because the ask says child page names.

Without a RefContext, keep today's strip: section anchors, References, Child pages, and no Parent page link. Rejected: emitting bare ids or a relative parent href, because without a workspace id there is no correct href, and every production render supplies a context anyway.

Decided by the user in review of PR #45: the parent link is the first entry of the strip, labelled Parent followed by the link symbol. This supersedes the earlier decision (a last-position link reading Parent page). Rejected: keeping it last, because the way back to the brief belongs where it is found without scanning past every section anchor; labelling it with the parent's title, because a fixed short label keeps the strip compact whatever the parent is called.

Decided by the user in review of PR #45: the Child pages anchor is always shown, directly before the pinned child-page links. This supersedes the earlier rule that dropped the anchor once every child was pinned. Rejected: that rule, because it made the strip's shape depend on the mix of children and removed the one top-of-page route to the full child list. Consequence: the anchor code stays exactly as on main and the feature only adds entries around it.

Decided by the user in review of PR #45: every pinned child-page link ends with the same link symbol as the Parent link. Both use one constant, a non-breaking space plus U+1F517 placed inside the anchor, so the mark is clickable and never wraps away from its label. Rejected: putting the symbol after the closing tag, where it would be dead text that can wrap onto its own line; separate marks for parent and children, which the review ruled out by asking for the same symbol.

feature-brief:mw0kfj8w-ab4d9b.title: Drop field instructions from mutatePageBatch `next` once a field is populated

summary.body: Every successful mutatePageBatch write echoes a `next` summary whose `do` field edges each carry that field's full authoring `instruction`. After an agent has filled a field, getting the same paragraph back on every later write in the stage is repeated noise that costs context without telling the agent anything new. The outcome: in the `next` echoed by mutatePageBatch only, a `do` field edge for a field that currently holds content on its own page still appears (so the agent can see it may still edit it) but without its `instruction` key; a field not yet populated, or since cleared, keeps its instruction. `nextActions` is deliberately unchanged and keeps emitting every instruction, because it is the call an agent uses to resume work or re-establish what a stage requires; createPage is unaffected because a new page has nothing populated.

items.name: src/commands.py - _field_setter_edge / field_setter_edges / _is_populated
items.text: PURE. `field_setter_edges(page, page_type, blocked_events)` (L195) builds the stage-relevant `do` field edges for one page; each edge is made by `_field_setter_edge` (L180), which always inlines `instruction` = the field's FieldSpec.description. An already-populated field keeps its edge (e.g. addComponent stays in `do` after a component exists) because membership is decided by `requires` + legality, not by whether the field is set. `_is_populated(value)` (L86) is the existing 'counts as set' test used by `unmet_requirements` (non-blank prose, non-empty list, non-null scalar). This is where the decision to omit the instruction belongs.

items.name: src/store.py - Store.next_actions
items.text: EFFECTFUL (loads the workspace from disk), otherwise a thin roll-up. Walks the page's subtree (`_subtree_pages`, so a feature-brief write also reports its pinned children's edges), calls `commands.field_setter_edges(page, page_type, parent_blocked)` per page (L492), and is the single place the focused page's `guidance` and `guidance_<field>` keys are assembled (L499-508). Its only callers are the three server tools nextActions, createPage and mutatePageBatch (graphify explain).

items.name: src/server.py - mutatePageBatch / nextActions / createPage tools
items.text: EFFECTFUL shell. mutatePageBatch (L494) runs STORE.mutate_page_batch then embeds STORE.next_actions(workspaceId, pageId) verbatim as `next` (L507, L515). nextActions (L440) returns STORE.next_actions unchanged and must keep full instructions. createPage (L466) also embeds next_actions verbatim; a fresh page has no populated field, so it is unaffected either way. The tool docstrings say the write 'Echoes ... next actions'.

items.name: src/instructions.py - instructions() text
items.text: PURE text assembled into the `instructions` tool response. L58: the field instruction 'is echoed as `instruction` on a `next` field edge'; L63: 'Every successful write echoes a `next` summary object same as `nextActions`'. Both become inaccurate for mutatePageBatch and are what an agent reads to learn the response shape. Tests in tests/test_instructions.py cover the assembly, not this wording.

items.name: tests/test_commands.py, tests/test_store.py, tests/test_server.py

All use src/testtypes.py fixtures.

items.text: File-based user doc (also mirrored by the pasta page 'GitHub README (user-facing)'). L38: the `do` bucket is 'transitions that are legal, plus the field setters *this stage* needs, each carrying its own authoring instruction' - true for nextActions, no longer for every write echo.
Python `requires-python = ">=3.14"` and the project is run through `uv` (pyproject.toml).

basedpyright is a gate: `[tool.pyright] typeCheckingMode = "recommended"`, include `src/**/*` (pyproject.toml); `just types` = `uv run basedpyright` must pass (made a gate by commit a50cfdc, Pyright stage 4).

Copy rule: use the word "create" instead of "mint" when creating something (CLAUDE.md).

Pure/effectful split: src/commands.py is the pure write path (module docstring: 'Every function here is pure ... never performs I/O'), and `next_actions` is the single place any guidance key is assembled (Authoring & mutation invariant). The populated-field decision must stay on the pure side and must not create a second assembly site.

Architecture 'Authoring & mutation' (Data model; Details 'Why guidance rides inside next') and 'Self-direction' (Data model) state that mutatePageBatch's `next` is VERBATIM `next_actions(workspaceId, pageId)`, identical to the nextActions tool. This feature makes the write echo deliberately differ (instruction omitted on populated fields). What has to give: the 'verbatim' claim. To keep one assembly site, the difference should be a parameter of next_actions / field_setter_edges rather than a post-processing pass in server.py.

Self-direction 'Data model' describes a field edge as self-instructing - 'so a `next` consumer needs no describePageType round-trip'. For populated fields in the write echo that stops holding: the consumer must call nextActions (or describePageType) to re-read the instruction. This is the intended trade-off of the ask, but it is a change to a documented invariant, not just an optimisation.

src/instructions.py L58 ('echoed as `instruction` on a `next` field edge') and L63 ('Every successful write echoes a `next` summary object same as `nextActions`') become inaccurate for mutatePageBatch; the agent-facing text must say the write echo drops the instruction of a populated field and that nextActions carries it in full.

Self-direction (architecture:mrtqsthj-dfd190): Data model - the field-edge shape (instruction always present) and 'Because createPage and mutatePageBatch embed this payload verbatim as their `next`'; Details 'The three instruction channels' - the per-field instruction on a `do` edge is now conditional on the write echo; add an invariant that nextActions always carries every instruction.

Authoring & mutation (architecture:mrtqsspj-0a2ae4): Data model - "`next` is verbatim next_actions(workspaceId, pageId)"; Details 'Why guidance rides inside next' (same claim) and 'Where a field's instruction lives' (the instruction key of a next field edge is now omitted for a populated field in mutatePageBatch's echo).

GitHub README (user-facing) (document:mtiodadq-2fb6a6) and README.md: 'The loop' table row for `do` - 'each carrying its own authoring instruction' needs the qualifier that a write echo omits it for a field already populated.
Does "populated once for the page" mean the field currently holds content (the `_is_populated` test the FSM's `requires` uses), or that it was ever written, even if since cleared?
items.answer: Currently holds content, by the existing `_is_populated` test (non-blank prose, non-empty list or blocks, non-null scalar). A Page records no write history (src/model.py), so 'ever written' would need new persisted state and serialization for no gain; and the ask frames it as fields that 'meet their requirement in the current stage', which is exactly the current-state test. A field later cleared gets its instruction back, which is right because its requirement is unmet again.

items.text: mutatePageBatch's `next` rolls up the written page's whole subtree (a brief's pinned plans/spec). Is the populated test applied per edge, against the page that edge belongs to, or only to edges of the page the batch wrote?
items.answer: Per edge, against the page that edge belongs to. The instruction describes that page's field, and whether it has been filled is a property of that page - so a feature-brief write that also reports its spec child's setOverview drops that instruction once the spec's overview is set, and keeps it while it is not.

items.text: For a populated field, is the `instruction` key omitted from the edge entirely, or kept as an empty string?
items.answer: Omitted entirely. The ask is for the edge to appear 'without' it; an empty string still costs a key and reads as 'this field has no instruction', which is false. The rest of the edge (pageId, pageType, kind, section, field, command, statusRevisionToken) is unchanged.

items.text: Should createPage's echo and the stage `guidance` / `guidance_<field>` keys also be trimmed, or is the change confined to field-edge instructions in mutatePageBatch's echo?
items.answer: Confined to field-edge instructions in mutatePageBatch's echo. createPage keeps calling next_actions unchanged (a new page has nothing populated, so it would not differ anyway). The `guidance` and `guidance_<field>` keys are stage and workspace guidance, not field instructions, and were not part of the ask - they stay as they are.

items.text: Should the mutatePageBatch bullet in src/instructions.py be reworded, as the spec's tool surface section and implementation step 7 planned?

The bullet keeps its 'same as nextActions' wording; the mutatePageBatch tool description and the README carry the qualifier instead. Implementation step 7 is marked skipped and its testing case was replaced by one asserting the file is unchanged. The sealed spec's tool surface section and this brief's third conflict describe the plan as it stood before that review; this answer supersedes them.

Applied: replaced that code block with a quoted heredoc (<<'EOF') script that splits the source on the createPage heading once and asserts the old mutatePageBatch wording is gone, the new wording is present, and the createPage bullet is unchanged.

def test_field_setter_edges_omit_the_instruction_of_a_populated_field_when_asked():

        "pageId", "pageType", "kind", "section", "field", "command", "statusRevisionToken"]
    assert by_field[("overview", "body")]["command"] == "setOverview"

def _field_setter_edge(page: Page, page_type: PageType, section: str, field: str,
                       command_name: str, with_instruction: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """One self-instructing `do` field edge: kind='field' with the (section, field), the field's
    instruction (its FieldSpec.description) and the single `command` that writes it, all inline -
    so a `next` consumer needs no describePageType round-trip to know what to author.
    `with_instruction=False` leaves the instruction out, for a field that is already written."""
    edge: dict[str, Any] = {
        "pageId": page.id, "pageType": page.type, "kind": "field",
        "section": section, "field": field,
    }
    if with_instruction:
        field_spec = get_pagetype_field(page_type, section, field)
        edge["instruction"] = field_spec.description.strip() if field_spec is not None else ""
    edge["command"] = command_name
    edge["statusRevisionToken"] = page.status_revision_token
    return edge


def field_setter_edges(page: Page, page_type: PageType,
                       blocked_events: Collection[str] = (), *,
                       omit_populated_instructions: bool = False) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    ...  # body unchanged down to the return
    return [_field_setter_edge(
                page, page_type, section, field, command_name,
                with_instruction=not (omit_populated_instructions and _is_populated(
                    page.sections.get(section, {}).get(field))))

overview.body: Covers one subsystem, the self-direction roll-up: the `do` field edges that mutatePageBatch echoes in its `next` drop their `instruction` key when the field they author already holds content on that edge's page. nextActions and createPage keep emitting the edges exactly as today. Deliberately left out: any trimming of transition edges, `blocked`, `humanGates`, `attention`, the stage `guidance` key or the `guidance_<field>` keys; any history of past writes on a page; any new tool, argument or response key; and the pasta architecture pages and README, which are reconciled after the implementation lands.

body.text: Behaviour

Which field edges enter `do` is unchanged: membership is still decided by the stage's `requires` and current legality, so a populated field's setter is still listed. What changes is only the edge's content, and only in mutatePageBatch's echo. There, a field edge whose (section, field) value on the edge's own page passes the existing `_is_populated` test carries no `instruction` key. A field that is empty, blank prose, an empty list or blocks field, or a null scalar keeps its instruction, so clearing a field brings its instruction back. The test is per edge: edges for a pinned child in the written page's subtree are judged against the child page. nextActions always returns every edge with its instruction, and createPage's echo is unchanged.
Pure side - src/commands.py

field_setter_edges gains one keyword-only flag, default off, so every existing caller and test keeps today's output. It passes a per-edge decision to _field_setter_edge, which builds the edge without the instruction key when told to. The populated test reuses _is_populated on the same lookup unmet_requirements already performs. No I/O; still a function of (page, page_type, blocked_events, flag).

Error paths and edge cases

A section the page predates (missing from page.sections) reads as None and keeps the instruction, matching how unmet_requirements treats it. A field with no FieldSpec keeps today's empty-string instruction when not populated and has no key when populated. A whitespace-only prose value is unpopulated. No new errors are raised. feature-brief:mw0l93ml-a44e6b.title: A stray backtick in an inline text run no longer fails the write

summary.body: A stray backtick in an inline text run aborts the whole write. Prose is not the problem: prose fields, scalars, list element text and plain-text blocks are unchecked strings that already accept backticks. The rejection lives only in the run grammar (`_MARKDOWN_TOKENS` in the pure core), which reaches exactly three production fields: architecture details, document body, and implementation-plan step detail. The outcome wanted: backticks are allowed in inline fields, and a code span typed with them is stored as a real `{code}` run, so a slip ends up identical to correct usage. Symbols such as `**` inside a `{code}` run or a backtick span pass validation, because they are code. A backtick that forms no span stays literal text, and nothing rejects a backtick any more. `**` and `](` outside a span stay rejected everywhere, with no repair. describe shows the run shapes so correct usage is visible up front, and feature-spec design stops claiming its paragraphs take inline runs.

items.name: src/pagetypes/core/specs.py
items.text: Pure constants. `_MARKDOWN_TOKENS = ("**", "`", "](")` (L64) is the entire rejection list. The run-grammar comment (L44-51) defines the four run shapes: a bare string, `{text, bold?, italic?, href?}`, `{code}`, and `{ref}`. `INLINE_RUNS` / `INLINE_RUN_LISTS` / `INLINE_RUN_GRID` (L52-54) are the three run-bearing arg shapes: a run array, an array of run arrays, and table rows of cells.

items.name: src/pagetypes/core/validation.py
items.text: Pure. `_reject_markdown` (L41) raises on any of the tokens. `_validate_run` (L50) applies it to a bare-string run and to a text run's `text`, and never to `{code}` or `{ref}`. It is reached through `validate_inline_content` -> `validate_arg_value` -> `validate_block`/`validate_blocks`, so every block path shares it: a page-level add, an element `add<X>Detail`, and a list add that creates an element with its blocks. The error text (L45-46) only suggests a bold/href run and never names `{'code': ...}`, even when the offending token is a backtick.

items.name: src/pagetypes/core/args.py (block-kind helpers)

Run-bearing: `_paragraph_runs` and `_heading_runs` (inlines: INLINE_RUNS), `_list_block` (items: INLINE_RUN_LISTS), `_quote_block` (paragraphs: INLINE_RUN_LISTS), `_table_block` (header: INLINE_RUN_LISTS, rows: INLINE_RUN_GRID). Plain-string bodies, never token-checked: `_paragraph_text`, `_heading_text` (text), `_code_block` (language, source), and feature-spec's custom `decision` kind (questionId, text).

Everything else is a plain string the grammar never checks: every prose field (feature-brief/epic/bug-report/simple-change summaries, architecture summary/purpose/usage/dataModel, decision-record context, feature-spec overview, epic reporting), every scalar, every list element text, and the plain-text block fields (feature-spec design + decisions, decision-record decision + consequences).

The run grammar is pure: validation.py does no I/O, and cross-page existence belongs to the store (architecture invariant). Any leniency or normalisation goes in the pure core, inside or before `validate_arg_value`. Every block path then inherits it, and a block legal to create stays legal to set: one grammar, changed once.

Invariant on Page types & FSM implementation (architecture:mrtjuul6-5221b2): 'markdown emphasis or link tokens inside a plain-text run are rejected - so rich content stays typed and machine-editable'. Accepting a stray backtick contradicts it as written, so the invariant has to be restated to say what does hold afterwards rather than be quietly broken.

The strictness is not only where the ask places it. Implementation-plan step `detail` is run-bearing and strict but is neither architecture nor documentation, and it is the field agents write most during planning, so it is the likeliest place for slips to land. Separately, feature-spec `design`'s description (feature.py L357-358) tells authors 'Emphasis and links are structured inline runs' although its paragraphs are plain `_paragraph_text` with no runs, so it misstates its own grammar.

An asymmetry already exists. Every plain-string surface accepts backticks; the MCP render returns them raw, where they read as inline code, while the web render escapes them, where they read as literal backticks. A lenient text run that keeps the backtick as plain text inherits that split: the same slip reads as code to an agent and as a stray character to a human.

`_MARKDOWN_TOKENS` bundles three tokens. The ask names only the backtick, but `**` and `](` fail the same way, and they are what the existing 'Markdown syntax' tests mostly pin (six of seven use `**`). Changing only the backtick leaves the same slip class failing for bold and links.

The ideal usage is under-taught at the two points an author meets it. The rejection for a backtick advises a bold/href run instead of `{'code': ...}`. describe shows run-bearing args as bare arrays (describe.py `_block_schema`), so the `{code}` shape is invisible before the first failed write. Part of the failure rate is the error and the schema not naming the right run.

Normalising makes the write path rewrite an author's value for the first time: `_apply` has only ever validated and stored args as sent. Order matters. Run after validation, a span such as `` `**kwargs` `` would be rejected for the `**` inside it, so normalisation has to run first, on unvalidated input, and pass anything malformed through for the validator to reject, the way `collect_ref_ids` already does.

Found while building, by running a stray backtick through the production types: pairing backticks strictly left to right lets a stray one take the next span's opening backtick. `` see `foo` and a stray ` and `**kwargs` `` paired ` and `, left `**kwargs` outside any span and was rejected for the `**`, and `` `foo and `bar` `` stored `foo and ` as the code. A stray backtick is the slip this feature exists to absorb, so the span rule was tightened: a span opens and closes against its text, never against whitespace.

architecture:mrtqsrk1-6d455c Search & introspection: the statement that the block schema is built from the same source the validator reads 'so schema and grammar cannot disagree'. This needs revisiting if describe gains a run-shape schema; today the run shape is simply absent from the schema.

architecture:mrtjuul6-5221b2 Page types & FSM implementation. Usage: 'hands the copy to _apply, which validates the arguments against the command's ArgSpecs' gains the normalisation step that runs first. Invariants: the 'A blocks field carries structured inline runs, not raw markdown ... markdown emphasis or link tokens inside a plain-text run are rejected' statement gains that a backtick code span becomes a code run and a stray backtick is literal text. Details: the 'core layering' paragraph's description of validation's contents gains normalisation.

Which mechanism should stop a stray backtick in a text run from failing the write? (a) ACCEPT: drop the backtick from `_MARKDOWN_TOKENS`, so it is stored as literal text the way prose already stores it. Simplest, but code refs written that way never become `{code}`. (b) NORMALISE: in the pure core, before validation, split a balanced `` `x` `` inside a bare or text run into a `{code}` run and keep an unmatched backtick as literal text. It never errors, and it stores the ideal shape, so the slip is hidden and the result is identical to correct usage. The cost is that the stored value differs from what was sent. (c) SCOPE: keep the rejection only on architecture details and document body, and make implementation-plan step detail (and any other run field) lenient through a per-field flag. Slips in architecture/document still fail. (d) Both (b) and the teaching fixes in the third question. Recommended: (d).
items.answer: User decided (c) SCOPE, and only (c). Code blocks and codeRefs are very different things, and a codeRef needs additional context the backtick does not provide, so normalising a backtick into a `{code}` run (b, d) would not produce one. The rejection stays on architecture details and document body; implementation-plan step detail becomes lenient through a per-field flag.

items.text: Should `**` (bold) and `](` (link) get the same treatment as the backtick, or does only the backtick change? They fail through the same `_MARKDOWN_TOKENS` check and are the same class of slip. Under NORMALISE, `**x**` maps cleanly onto `{text, bold: true}`, but a `[t](url)` link needs a small parser. Recommended: backtick now (and `**` if NORMALISE is chosen); links stay rejected.
items.answer: User decided: no fix. `**` and `](` keep being rejected in every run-bearing field, including a lenient one. Only the backtick changes.

items.text: Whatever the mechanism, should the ideal usage be made visible where authors meet it? That means three changes: the backtick rejection names `{'code': ...}`; describePageType/describeMutations advertise the run shapes (string | {text, bold?, italic?, href?} | {code} | {ref}) for inlines/items/paragraphs/header/rows instead of a bare array; and feature-spec design's description stops claiming its paragraphs take inline runs. Recommended: yes, all three, as part of this feature.
items.answer: User decided: yes, all three are in scope. The backtick rejection names `{'code': ...}`; describePageType/describeMutations advertise the run shapes instead of a bare array; feature-spec design's description stops claiming its paragraphs take inline runs.

items.text: Revisiting the first question, whose recorded answer (c) was changed by the user during planning: which mechanism stops a backtick in a text run from failing the write, now that code references are confirmed to be a separate place (the architecture `codeReferences` list)?
items.answer: User decided: normalise code backticks only. Code references are a different place (the architecture `codeReferences` list), so a `{code}` run does not pretend to be one, and the objection recorded on the first question no longer holds. This supersedes that answer: option (c) and its per-field flag are dropped. A backtick pair in a run becomes a `{code}` run; nothing else is normalised, so the second question's 'no fix' for `**` and `](` stands. Of the third question's teaching fixes, the run schema and the feature-spec description stand; the improved backtick error falls away because nothing rejects a backtick any more. Assumed by the agent, not stated by the user: this applies to every run-bearing field, and a backtick that forms no pair stays literal text rather than being rejected, matching option (b) as it was offered and the original goal that small slips stop failing the write.

_RUNS_ARG = _array("inlines", content=INLINE_RUNS)
_SPAN, _CODE = ["`x`"], [{"code": "x"}]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("sent, stored", [
    (["call `foo` now"], ["call ", {"code": "foo"}, " now"]),
    ([{"text": "`foo`"}], [{"code": "foo"}]),
    (["`a` and `b`"], [{"code": "a"}, " and ", {"code": "b"}]),
    (["pass `**kwargs` on"], ["pass ", {"code": "**kwargs"}, " on"]),
    # A stray backtick, a doubled pair and a pair across lines are not spans.
    (["a stray ` here"], ["a stray ` here"]),
    (["``doubled``"], ["``doubled``"]),
    (["`across\nlines`"], ["`across\nlines`"]),
    # A code run carries no marks, so a marked run keeps its text.
    ([{"text": "`foo`", "bold": True}], [{"text": "`foo`", "bold": True}]),
    # A run holding no span is stored as sent, its shape included.
    (["plain", {"text": "plain"}, {"code": "`x`"}, {"ref": "page:1"}],
     ["plain", {"text": "plain"}, {"code": "`x`"}, {"ref": "page:1"}]),
])
def test_a_code_span_is_normalised_into_a_code_run(sent, stored):
    assert normalize_arg_value(_RUNS_ARG, sent) == stored
    assert normalize_arg_value(_RUNS_ARG, stored) == stored      # idempotent


def test_normalising_reaches_every_run_shape():
    assert normalize_arg_value(_array("items", content=INLINE_RUN_LISTS), [_SPAN]) == [_CODE]
    assert normalize_arg_value(_array("rows", content=INLINE_RUN_GRID), [[_SPAN]]) == [[_CODE]]
    blocks = _array("blocks", content=BLOCK_ARRAY, block_kinds=standard_blocks())
    assert normalize_arg_value(blocks, [
        {"kind": "paragraph", "inlines": _SPAN},
        {"kind": "table", "header": [_SPAN], "rows": [[_SPAN]], "align": None},
    ]) == [
        {"kind": "paragraph", "inlines": _CODE},
        {"kind": "table", "header": [_CODE], "rows": [[_CODE]], "align": None},
    ]


def test_normalising_leaves_an_arg_holding_no_runs_alone():
    blocks = _array("blocks", content=BLOCK_ARRAY, block_kinds=(_code_block(), _paragraph_text()))
    sent = [{"kind": "code", "language": "md", "source": "`x`"},
            {"kind": "paragraph", "text": "`x`"}]
    assert normalize_arg_value(blocks, sent) == sent
    assert normalize_arg_value(_text(), "`x`") == "`x`"


def test_normalising_returns_a_malformed_value_for_the_grammar_to_reject():
    lists = _array("items", content=INLINE_RUN_LISTS)
    grid = _array("rows", content=INLINE_RUN_GRID)
    blocks = _array("blocks", content=BLOCK_ARRAY, block_kinds=standard_blocks())
    for arg, malformed in ((_RUNS_ARG, "`x`"), (_RUNS_ARG, None), (_RUNS_ARG, [1]),
                           (lists, "`x`"), (lists, ["`x`"]), (grid, ["`x`"]), (grid, [["`x`"]]),

overview.body: This spec covers the inline-run grammar and what it advertises. Inline fields allow backticks: a code span typed with them in a run-bearing field is rewritten into a `{code}` run before validation, so it is stored exactly as correct usage would be, and symbols such as `**` inside it pass as code. A backtick that forms no span is literal text, and nothing rejects a backtick any more. describe shows the run shapes for run-bearing body args, and feature-spec design's description stops claiming inline runs. It deliberately leaves out any repair of `**` or `](` outside a span, which stay rejected; any change to prose, scalar, list-element or plain-text block fields, which are not run-bearing; any change to rendering or stored data; and any per-field configuration.

body.text: The behaviour

It applies to a bare-string run and to a `{text}` run with no marks, in every run-bearing body arg of every field: architecture details, document body, implementation-plan step detail, and any field declared later. There is no per-field setting. A span is a single backtick either side of some text on one line, opening and closing against that text rather than against whitespace, and each becomes its own `{code}` run with the text around it kept. The whitespace rule is what stops a stray backtick pairing with the opening backtick of the span after it. A run containing no span is stored exactly as sent, including a `{text}` run staying an object. A backtick that forms no span stays literal text, and it passes validation because the backtick is no longer a rejected token.

A marked run is left as sent because a `{code}` run carries no marks: splitting it would drop the emphasis or the link to repair a backtick. `{code}` and `{ref}` runs are never touched. Code blocks' `source` and plain `text` body args are not run-bearing and are never touched, so a backtick in a code block survives. `**` and `](` are rejected as they are today, outside a span; inside a span they are code and pass, as `{code}` runs always have.
Pure core: the normaliser (validation.py)

Normalisation sits beside the grammar it feeds. It runs BEFORE validation, because run afterwards the `**` in a span like `**kwargs` would already have been rejected, and so that the grammar checks exactly what will be stored. Running first means it sees unvalidated input, so a value of the wrong shape is returned untouched and left for the grammar to reject, the same stance `collect_ref_ids` takes. It is idempotent, so a compound's args passing through it twice, once at the compound and once at the step, change nothing further.
Pure core: the rejected tokens (specs.py)
The backtick leaves the token list. `_reject_markdown` and its message are otherwise unchanged. With no backtick rejection left, the error needs no wording about code runs.

body.source:
# Markdown emphasis/link tokens rejected inside a plain-text run. Kept deliberately narrow (bold/link
# markers) so ordinary prose containing a lone `*` or `_` or even a file with double '__' is not
# falsely rejected. A backtick is absent on purpose: a code span is normalised into a code run
# before this check, and a backtick that forms no span is literal text.
_MARKDOWN_TOKENS = ("**", "](")

body.text: Pure core: the call site (commands.py)
`_apply` is the one place every write passes through, including each compound step, so normalising there reaches every block path without any of them knowing. The caller's `args` dict is not mutated.
Pure core: the feature-spec description (feature.py)

The feature-spec design field's description loses its final sentence, 'Emphasis and links are structured inline runs, not markdown syntax.' Its paragraphs are `_paragraph_text`, so it holds no runs. The same sentence stays on architecture details and document body, where it is true.
Pure introspection: the run shapes (describe.py)

`_block_schema` reports a run-bearing body arg with its real nesting instead of a bare array: one array level for INLINE_RUNS, two for INLINE_RUN_LISTS, three for INLINE_RUN_GRID, each ending in the run schema. Every other body arg keeps `{"type": arg.type}`, including table `align`. describePageType and describeMutations both read this through `command_arg_schema`, so neither needs its own change. docsgen reads only arg names from the schema and is unaffected.
Effects

There are none to add. Everything above is a pure function of its inputs or a declaration. The store's ref precheck runs on the raw args and only reads `{ref}` runs, which normalisation leaves alone, so it does not change. Rendering does not change: a `{code}` run already renders as inline code on both paths, and a literal backtick renders as a backtick in prose already does, raw on the MCP path and escaped on the web path. No migration is needed: the grammar runs only on write, and stored runs cannot hold a backtick today.
Error paths

A backtick never raises. `**` or `](` outside a span raises the existing "Markdown syntax" ValidationError. Malformed runs raise exactly what they raise today, because normalisation returns them untouched. As today, one rejected run aborts the whole batch and nothing is written.
Superseded by the decision on the revisited mechanism question. The user first chose per-field scope, then changed to normalisation during planning. Nothing of that option was built.

Normalise: a backtick code span in a run becomes a `{code}` run before validation, in every run-bearing field, and a backtick that forms no span is literal text. Chosen by the user. A slip then stores the same shape as correct usage, so the rule is hidden without blurring it. Rejected: per-field scope with a `literal_backticks` flag, which left slips failing on architecture and document and added a declaration knob; accepting backticks as literal text everywhere, which would leave code spans untyped; and normalising after validation, which would reject a span like `**kwargs` for the token inside it. A marked run is deliberately left as sent, because a code run carries no marks and splitting it would lose the emphasis or link. Refined during the build: a span cannot open or close against whitespace. Strict left-to-right pairing, the rejected alternative, let a stray backtick take the next span's opening backtick, which stored the wrong code and could fail the write on a `**` that belonged inside the span. The cost is that a deliberately padded span stays literal text, which loses nothing.
No fix: only backticks change, and `**` and `](` outside a span stay rejected in every run-bearing field. Chosen by the user. Rejected: repairing them into bold and link runs.

The user chose all three teaching fixes before normalisation was chosen. Two stand: `_block_schema` reports the run shapes, and feature-spec design's description drops its inline-run sentence. The third, the backtick rejection naming the code run, falls away because nothing rejects a backtick any more; the `**` and `](` messages are unchanged. Rejected: a describe hint or field description explaining the normalisation, because hiding the rule from authors is the point and the run schema already shows correct usage.
The architecture `codeReferences` list is out of scope and nothing here reads or changes it. Code refs in this feature means the inline `{code}` run.

feature-brief:mw4znaz1-e5165a.title: Send stage guidance in mutatePageBatch `next` only when the page transitioned

summary.body: Every successful mutatePageBatch write echoes the page's full per-status guidance in `next`, even on a content-only write that left the page in the status it was already in, so an agent working through a stage gets the same long text back on every write. The outcome: the `next` echoed by mutatePageBatch carries the `guidance` and `guidance_<field>` keys only when that batch moved the written page to a new status, and omits them otherwise, through an omit flag in the same style as omit_populated_instructions. `nextActions` always includes them, because it is the call an agent uses to resume work or re-establish what a stage requires, and createPage keeps them because a new page has just entered its first stage. This deliberately reverses the earlier decision that stage text rides every write.

items.name: src/store.py - Store.next_actions
items.text: EFFECTFUL (loads the workspace), otherwise a thin roll-up. Lines 503-514 assemble both per-status keys for the focused page: `guidance` (PAGE_STATUS_GUIDANCE + status_guidance(...)) and the `guidance_<field>` keys from the pure workspace_guidance(). Already takes the keyword-only omit_populated_instructions from PR #46, so the new flag has a direct precedent, and this block is the single place any guidance key is assembled. Callers: the nextActions, createPage and mutatePageBatch tools.

items.name: src/store.py - Store.mutate_page_batch and CreatePageResult
items.text: EFFECTFUL. Returns a bare `tuple[Page, list[str | None]]`, so its caller cannot tell whether the status moved. Inside the loop it already compares `working.status != status_before` to regenerate the revision token, and `page` stays the unedited original because apply_command copies, so `working.status != page.status` is available at the return. CreatePageResult (L95) is the existing named result type for the sibling write; its only src caller is the mutatePageBatch tool (src/server.py:507).

items.text: EFFECTFUL shell. L507-508 run STORE.mutate_page_batch then STORE.next_actions(workspaceId, pageId, omit_populated_instructions=True). The docstring is the tool description MCP clients see and already names the field-instruction omission. nextActions (L445) and createPage (L475) call next_actions with no flags and are left as they are.

The omit flag follows the field-instruction precedent the ask names: keyword-only, default False, in the style of omit_populated_instructions, so every existing caller of next_actions keeps its output.

This reverses a deliberate decision. Authoring & mutation, Details 'Why guidance rides inside next': 'The stage text rides every write rather than only a transitioning one ... gating on the transition withheld the instruction across exactly the writes it exists to steer', and the rule it replaced was guidance only on a batch with a transition. Its invariant says 'A write response carries guidance exactly once, inside `next`, on every write'; Self-direction says guidance 'is unconditional'. What has to give: those statements, because the human has explicitly asked for transition-only. What stands from the old decision: guidance stays inside `next` with no second copy, and nextActions carrying it is what now covers the writes it no longer reaches.

Does 'stage instructions' mean only the `guidance` key, or also the `guidance_<field>` workspace guidance keys that are shown per status beside it?
items.answer: Both. `guidance` and the `guidance_<field>` keys are per-status text for the focused page, assembled in one block of next_actions, and they repeat on every write in exactly the same way, so one gate covers both. Keeping the workspace keys would leave guidance_testingTool on every write of a build. nextActions keeps both. This is a judgment call, flagged to the user at hand-back.

items.text: What counts as 'the stage was transitioned': the status of the page the batch wrote changing, or any transition in the page's subtree or an element status change?
items.answer: The status of the page the batch wrote: `working.status != page.status` at the end of the batch. A batch writes one page and guidance is focused-page only, so nothing else could change what is shown. An element status change such as markStepDone is progress inside a stage, not a new stage, so it does not count.

items.text: Should createPage's echo also omit stage guidance, given a create is not a transition?
items.answer: No, createPage keeps its guidance. A new page has just entered its initial status, which is the same moment a transition marks: the agent has not seen this stage's instruction yet. Omitting it would hide the first stage's instruction until someone called nextActions. test_create_page_carries_initial_status_guidance_and_children_do_not already pins this.

items.text: How should the mutatePageBatch tool learn whether the batch transitioned?
items.answer: Store.mutate_page_batch returns a named MutatePageResult with page, created_ids and transitioned, beside the existing CreatePageResult. The store already holds the status before and after, so the fact is reported where it is known. See the spec's decisions for the rejected alternatives.

items.answer: No. Rewording that bullet was undone in review on PR #46 as mostly noise, so src/instructions.py stays unchanged. The mutatePageBatch tool description carries the qualifier instead, as it does for the field instructions.

def _write(store, workspace_id, page_id, commands):
    """Run a batch presenting the page's current status_revision_token on each command - the ordinary
    single-batch caller pattern (read the token, then write against it). A batch that transitions
    mid-sequence is deliberately not expressible this way: the transition regenerates the token, so
    a later command's stamp is stale - such tests present tokens explicitly instead."""
    token = store.get_page(workspace_id, page_id).status_revision_token
    stamped = [{**command, "args": {"statusRevisionToken": token, **(command.get("args") or {})}}
               for command in commands]
    return store.mutate_page_batch(workspace_id, page_id, stamped)


def _mutate(store, workspace_id, page_id, commands):
    """`_write`, reduced to the (page, created ids) pair most tests read."""
    result = _write(store, workspace_id, page_id, commands)
    return result.page, result.created_ids


# after test_next_actions_omits_populated_instructions_against_each_edges_own_page:
def test_mutate_page_batch_reports_whether_the_status_moved(store):
    """Content alone leaves `transitioned` False; a batch ending in a transition or a compound sets it."""
    workspace = store.create_workspace("demo")
    page = store.create_page(workspace.id, "test-flow", "C").page
    assert _write(store, workspace.id, page.id, [
        {"command": "setSummary", "args": {"text": "s"}}]).transitioned is False
    assert _write(store, workspace.id, page.id, [
        {"command": "setSummary", "args": {"text": "t"}}, {"command": "open"}]).transitioned is True
    assert _write(store, workspace.id, page.id, [
        {"command": "close", "args": {"sha": "abc", "message": "done"}}]).transitioned is True


def test_mutate_page_batch_does_not_count_an_element_status_change_as_a_transition(store):
    """A step changing status is progress inside a stage, not a new stage."""
    workspace = store.create_workspace("demo")
    child = _child(store.create_page(workspace.id, "test-lifecycle", "F"), "test-child")
    _, step_created = _mutate(store, workspace.id, child.id, [
        {"command": "addStep", "args": {"text": "build"}}])
    assert _write(store, workspace.id, child.id, [
        {"command": "markStepDone", "args": {"stepId": step_created[0]}}]).transitioned is False

def test_mutate_page_batch_omits_guidance_on_a_content_only_write(mcp):
    """A write carries the stage text only when it moved the page to a new status, and nextActions

    workspace_id, page_id = _flow_page(mcp)

overview.body: Covers one subsystem, the self-direction roll-up as it reaches a write: the `next` that mutatePageBatch echoes carries the focused page's `guidance` and `guidance_<field>` keys only when that batch moved the page to a new status. nextActions and createPage keep emitting them as today. Deliberately left out: any change to `do`, `blocked`, `humanGates` or `attention`, or to the field instructions; any change to what guidance text exists or when a status shows it; src/instructions.py, which review on PR #46 said to leave alone; and the pasta architecture pages and README, which are reconciled after the implementation lands.

body.text: Behaviour

A mutatePageBatch batch that moves the written page to a new status echoes `next` exactly as before, with both kinds of guidance key for the status it entered. A batch that does not, whether it writes content only or fires only element transitions such as markStepDone, echoes `next` with no key starting with guidance. The four lists are identical either way. A batch mixing content and a transition counts as transitioned. nextActions for a page always carries the keys, and createPage's echo always carries them, because a new page has just entered its first stage. A whole-workspace nextActions carries none, as today. A rejected batch returns an error and no `next`, as today.
Store - src/store.py

This logic is thin and stays in the store, the effectful shell, because the guidance block already lives in next_actions and the status comparison already lives in the batch loop. mutate_page_batch returns a new named result beside CreatePageResult. `page` is never edited by the batch, because apply_command works on a copy, so comparing it to the working copy at the end is the status change. next_actions gains one keyword-only flag, default off, which skips the focused-page guidance block and nothing else, so it stays the single place guidance keys are assembled.
Tool surface - src/server.py

The mutatePageBatch tool reads the result and passes the flag. nextActions and createPage are unchanged. The tool response keeps its shape: pageId, status, statusRevisionToken, count, createdIds, next. The last sentence of the tool docstring adds that stage guidance comes only with a transition. src/instructions.py does not change.

next_actions = STORE.next_actions(

body.text: Data shapes
Error paths and edge cases

A transition into a status that declares no guidance omits the key, through the existing absent path. Two transitions in one batch are already rejected, so the comparison sees at most one move. No new errors are raised. The cost is one string comparison per batch, and a content-only write's response gets shorter.
A consequence to accept

An agent that loses its context mid-stage no longer gets the stage text back from its next write, which is the failure the earlier every-write rule was written to prevent. Calling nextActions recovers it, and the MCP instructions already tell an agent to call nextActions when unsure.

Both `guidance` and the `guidance_<field>` keys are omitted, behind one flag named omit_stage_guidance. Rejected: omitting only `guidance`, which leaves per-status workspace text such as guidance_testingTool repeating on every write of a stage, the same noise the ask is about; and two flags, which is configurability nobody asked for.

Transitioned means the written page's status differs at the end of the batch. Rejected: counting subtree or parent changes, because a batch writes one page and guidance is focused-page only; and counting element transitions, because a step or case changing status is progress inside a stage, and treating it as new would re-send the text on every markStepDone.

createPage keeps its guidance and passes no flag. Rejected: applying the omission to creates because a create is not literally a transition. A new page has just entered its initial status, so this is the moment the agent needs that stage's instruction, and omitting it would mean the first stage is never shown on the write path.

mutate_page_batch returns a MutatePageResult with a transitioned field. Rejected: reading the status before the write in the tool, which costs a second workspace load and reads outside the transaction lock; comparing the presented and returned revision tokens in the tool, which works by the token invariant but makes the shell reach into command args and hold a rule; and a third tuple element, which touches the same call sites as a named result while leaving the meaning positional, against the CreatePageResult precedent.
src/instructions.py stays unchanged and the tool docstring carries the qualifier. Rejected: rewording the bullet to be strictly accurate, because review on PR #46 undid exactly that as mostly noise.

feature-brief:mw50p0fw-81f7b2.title: Agent sessionId on MCP tool calls and a session activity cache

summary.body: Give every MCP tool call an optional `sessionId`, the supported way for an agent to say which working session it is acting from, and keep a short-lived in-memory record of when each session last ran a tool. The outcome wanted is that the server can answer "which sessions are active right now, and when did each last act?" without that answer becoming durable data: an entry expires by itself 15 minutes after a session's last call, and losing the record on a restart or reload costs nothing. An agent that sends no id is still counted, under its connection's transport id. No reader is added yet, neither a tool nor a view: that stays a follow-up.

items.name: src/server.py (MCP section)
items.text: Effects: serves MCP. Holds `_RefuseInvalidDeclarations` and its `mcp.add_middleware` registration (the precedent for behaviour hung on the call rather than on each of the 25 `@mcp.tool` functions), the module-level `STORE` that tests repoint per test, and `instructions()`, whose `mcp.list_tools()` runs middleware. The new middleware and the cache instance belong here. This module re-executes on every HMR reload, so state held here resets on a reload.

items.name: src/instructions.py
items.text: Pure: `_PROSE` plus `render_tool_schemas` and `render_instructions`, called only from `instructions()`. `_PROSE` is where agents are told what to do, so the supported way to send a session id is documented here. The schema section projects live tool schemas and needs no change.

items.text: Effects: the stable `pasta-hmr-proxy` that mounts the reloaded `src.server.mcp`. Read, not changed. Probed against fastmcp 3.4.4: middleware on a mounted server runs for calls through the mount over streamable HTTP, and its `on_list_tools` edits reach the client. Its `_active_sessions` WeakSet is unrelated: it holds live `ServerSession` objects so `tools/list_changed` can be pushed on reload.

items.name: tests/test_server.py and tests/test_instructions.py
items.text: Test harness. test_server.py drives tools through an in-memory `fastmcp.Client(mcp)`, with the module-global `STORE` repointed per test by its `mcp` fixture; the middleware's tests belong here. test_instructions.py covers the pure renderer with hand-built tool lists, and no test pins a real tool's input schema, so adding `sessionId` to listed schemas breaks none of them.

Versions, from pyproject.toml: `requires-python = ">=3.14"` and `fastmcp>=3.4.4`. Installed: fastmcp 3.4.4, mcp 1.28.1. No cache library is declared. Inferred, not read: the dependency list should stay unchanged, because a dict with a TTL check is all this needs.

Layering, from the Pasta Project Overview invariant: "The layering is strictly one-directional: server to store to pure core (commands / fsm / serialize) to model / pagetypes / errors. The core imports neither store nor server, and only the stateful shell does I/O, creates ids, or serves MCP."

Errors, from the Pasta Project Overview invariant: "Every expected (non-bug) failure is a PastaError subclass", translated to a FastMCP `ToolError` at the tool boundary. Middleware has no `_guard_tool` around it and raises `ToolError` directly, as `_RefuseInvalidDeclarations` does, with an actionable message.
Persistence: each workspace is one JSON document under `PASTA_DATA_DIR` (default ./.pasta-data). The activity record stays out of those files, per the summary: it must not become durable data.
Copy, from CLAUDE.md: "Use the word "create" instead of "mint" when creating something." This applies to the agent-facing text that tells an agent how to obtain a session id.

Gates: tests with `uv run pytest --testmon` (CLAUDE.md: "Run pytest with --testmon to speed up red-green testing.") and types with `uv run basedpyright` (`typeCheckingMode = "recommended"`, `include = ["src/**/*"]`). Middleware hooks carry `@override`, as `on_call_tool` does today.

Every tool schema is `additionalProperties: false`, and fastmcp refuses an undeclared `sessionId` with `unexpected_keyword_argument` (probed, direct and through a mount). Middleware sees the argument before that validation runs. So a plain extra argument cannot work: it has to be advertised on the listed schemas and removed from the arguments before the call reaches the tool.

Prior art: fastmcp already gives each connection an id through `Context.session_id` (the `mcp-session-id` header over HTTP, a generated id otherwise). It covers part of the ask but cannot be what an agent communicates: probed, two connections from one client get two ids, so it moves on every reconnect, and everything sharing a connection shares it. It gives way as the primary id and can serve as the fallback. The two also read alike: `sessionId` the argument and `session_id` the transport id must stay distinct in the code.

`_meta` looks like the protocol's natural channel but is not usable here: a client's `meta={...}` on `call_tool` arrived as None on `context.message.meta`, both direct and through a mount (probed), and an LLM agent does not control request metadata in any case. It gives way to a tool argument.

`instructions()` in src/server.py lists schemas through `mcp.list_tools()`, which runs middleware (probed), so `sessionId` will appear on every tool under '## Request tool schemas' and lengthen that text. The Search & introspection page promises the schemas an agent reads and the tools served cannot drift, so the growth is accepted and `instructions()` stays as it is.

Vocabulary: in this repo a command is a page-type command run inside `mutatePageBatch` (src/commands.py), while the ask says 'MCP command'. If the repo's sense were meant, read-only tool calls would not count as activity. Raised as a question.

Search & introspection (architecture:mrtqsrk1-6d455c), the paragraph 'How the instructions tool stays in step with the surface': the projected schemas now include a `sessionId` added by middleware rather than declared on the tool function.

Web UI, HMR & live reload (architecture:mrw6s6q6-fb2ff5), Data model: the sentence "The one piece of long-lived in-process state that must outlast a reload is the set of live browser WebSockets" stays true, but the page should name the activity record as in-process state that deliberately does not outlast a reload. 'Why a failed reload refuses both surfaces' describes the fastmcp `on_call_tool` middleware as if it were the only one.

Pasta Project Overview (architecture:mrteq39m-de7a49): Usage needs the optional `sessionId` on the MCP surface, and Data model needs the activity record as the one thing held outside the workspace files. Separately, 'Corrections at a35b133' says "all 24 MCP tools" and src/server.py now has 25 `@mcp.tool` functions.
Who owns the recorded session id: does the agent supply its own `sessionId`, or does pasta use the transport session fastmcp already assigns to the connection?
items.answer: The agent supplies it. The ask says agents communicate which session they work from, and the transport id needs no communicating; it also moves on every reconnect and cannot tell apart agents sharing a connection. The channel is an optional `sessionId` tool argument on every tool, because arguments are the only part of a call an LLM agent controls.

items.text: When an agent omits `sessionId`, is the call still tracked under the connection's transport id, or left out of the record?
items.answer: Still tracked, under the transport id. The ask is to track each session, and a caller should not have to change to be counted. A session mixing both styles shows as two entries, which is harmless in a record that expires.

items.text: Does 'an MCP command' mean every tool call, or only page-type commands run through `mutatePageBatch`?
items.answer: Every tool call, reads included. A session grounding through reads is active, so 'command' is taken in its plain sense of an MCP request rather than the repo's page-type term. A refused call counts too, because the session still acted. `initialize` and `tools/list` do not count: they are handshake, not commands.

items.text: Should this feature add a reader for the activity record (an MCP tool or a web view), or stop at an in-process record that later work reads?
items.answer: Stop at the in-process record: the cache gets a read method and there is no new tool or view. Nothing named so far consumes it, a reader is an additive follow-up, and the brief's own rule counts building past the ask as a defect. This is a judgment call the user may want to reverse, so it is repeated in the hand-back.

items.text: How long should an entry live before it expires?
items.answer: 15 minutes, as one named constant. That spans a long test run between calls and still reads as active right now. It is one line to change if the user prefers another window.

from .session_activity import SessionActivity, with_session_id_argument

# src/server.py - directly under `STORE = Store(DATA_DIR)`
SESSION_ACTIVITY = SessionActivity()

# src/server.py - above `class _RefuseInvalidDeclarations`
class _TrackSessionActivity(Middleware):
    """Give every tool an optional `sessionId`, and record when each session last ran one.

    Hung on the call rather than on each tool, so it covers any tool added later. The argument is
    advertised on the listed schemas, because a client only sends what a schema declares, and taken
    out of the call again, because the tool functions do not declare it.
    """

    @override
    async def on_list_tools(
        self,
        context: MiddlewareContext[mt.ListToolsRequest],
        call_next: CallNext[mt.ListToolsRequest, Sequence[Tool]],
    ) -> Sequence[Tool]:
        return [tool.model_copy(update={"parameters": with_session_id_argument(tool.parameters)})
                for tool in await call_next(context)]


# src/server.py - replacing the single add_middleware line. The first added runs outermost, so a

mcp.add_middleware(_TrackSessionActivity())

items.text: Baseline: `uv run pytest` and `uv run basedpyright` are clean before any change, so a later failure belongs to this feature. Carried by plan step 1.

A recorded session is active with its time, and two sessions are tracked apart. Direct calls with a fixed `now`. Tests: test_a_recorded_session_is_active_with_its_time, test_sessions_are_tracked_apart.
A later call moves the session's time and keeps one entry. Test: test_a_later_call_moves_the_time_and_keeps_one_entry.

The TTL boundary: an entry one second under 15 minutes old stays, and an entry exactly 15 minutes old is gone, with no sleeping. Tests: test_the_ttl_is_fifteen_minutes, test_an_entry_just_under_the_ttl_stays, test_an_entry_exactly_one_ttl_old_is_gone.
A session refreshed before its TTL outlives the first TTL, measured from the refresh. Test: test_a_refreshed_session_outlives_its_first_ttl.
Recording one session evicts other expired sessions, so the map cannot grow with sessions that have gone quiet, even if nothing ever reads it. Test: test_recording_evicts_other_expired_entries.
`active` hands back a copy: clearing the result leaves the cache intact. Test: test_active_returns_a_copy.

Id resolution: a declared id is used as given, None falls back to the transport id, and blank, whitespace, number, boolean, list and object values raise ValidationError naming sessionId rather than being replaced. Tests: test_a_declared_id_is_used_as_given, test_a_missing_id_falls_back_to_the_transport_id, test_a_malformed_id_is_refused_rather_than_replaced.

Schema edit: `sessionId` is added as a described string, `required` and `additionalProperties` stand, a tool's own schema object is not changed, and a schema with no properties still gets it. Tests: the four with_session_id_argument tests in tests/test_session_activity.py.

Every tool the server lists advertises `sessionId` as an optional string and keeps its own arguments, through a real client. Tests: test_every_tool_advertises_an_optional_session_id, test_a_listed_tool_keeps_its_own_arguments.

overview.body: Covers the optional `sessionId` argument on every MCP tool, the fallback to the connection's transport id, and the in-memory cache of when each session last ran a tool, all in the MCP surface of src/server.py plus a new pure module, src/session_activity.py. It deliberately leaves out any reader of the record beyond a method on the cache, any persistence, and any attribution of page edits to sessions. A `sessionId` is a self-declared label, not an identity: nothing authenticates it or checks that it is unique.

body.text: The sessionId argument

Every tool the server lists advertises an optional string `sessionId`, and no tool function declares it. It is never in `required`. An agent sends the same value on every call. Two agents sending the same value count as one session.
Pure side: src/session_activity.py

A new module holding every rule. It imports only the standard library and `.errors`, reads no clock and does no I/O: the time is passed in. The cache keeps its map in memory, which is why it is a small class rather than free functions.

body.source:
SESSION_TTL = timedelta(minutes=15)
SESSION_ID_ARGUMENT = "sessionId"


class SessionActivity:
    def __init__(self) -> None: ...
    def record(self, session_id: str, now: datetime) -> None: ...
    def active(self, now: datetime) -> dict[str, datetime]: ...


def resolve_session_id(declared: object, transport_id: str) -> str: ...
def with_session_id_argument(parameters: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]: ...

body.text: `record` sets the session's timestamp to `now`, overwriting any earlier one, then evicts expired entries. `active` evicts expired entries and returns a copy of what remains, mapping session id to last-active time. An entry is expired once `now - last_active >= SESSION_TTL`, so an entry exactly one TTL old is gone. Eviction happens only inside these two methods; there is no timer. Both run on the server's one event loop with no `await` inside them, so no lock is needed, and with a handful of sessions the walk on each tool call is negligible next to the workspace file most tools read.

`resolve_session_id` returns `declared` when it is a non-blank string, returns `transport_id` when `declared` is None, and otherwise raises `ValidationError`, so a JSON null counts as leaving the argument out. `with_session_id_argument` returns a copy of a tool's JSON-schema `parameters` with `sessionId` added to `properties` as a string carrying the description 'The session you are working from. Send the same value on every call.' That text is repeated on all 25 tools, so it stays one line. The input is not mutated, and `required` is untouched.
Effect side: the middleware in src/server.py

`SESSION_ACTIVITY = SessionActivity()` sits beside `STORE`, resolved from the module at call time so tests can repoint it the same way. The middleware reads the clock and the request and holds no rules of its own.

body.source:
class _TrackSessionActivity(Middleware):
    @override
    async def on_list_tools(
        self,
        context: MiddlewareContext[mt.ListToolsRequest],
        call_next: CallNext[mt.ListToolsRequest, Sequence[Tool]],
    ) -> Sequence[Tool]:
        return [tool.model_copy(update={"parameters": with_session_id_argument(tool.parameters)})
                for tool in await call_next(context)]

    @override
    async def on_call_tool(
        self,
        context: MiddlewareContext[mt.CallToolRequestParams],
        call_next: CallNext[mt.CallToolRequestParams, ToolResult],
    ) -> ToolResult:
        assert context.fastmcp_context is not None  # set for every tool call
        arguments = dict(context.message.arguments or {})
        declared = arguments.pop(SESSION_ID_ARGUMENT, None)
        with _guard_tool():
            session_id = resolve_session_id(declared, context.fastmcp_context.session_id)
        SESSION_ACTIVITY.record(session_id, datetime.now(timezone.utc))
        message = context.message.model_copy(update={"arguments": arguments})
        return await call_next(context.copy(message=message))


mcp.add_middleware(_TrackSessionActivity())
mcp.add_middleware(_RefuseInvalidDeclarations())

body.text: Registered ahead of `_RefuseInvalidDeclarations` because the first middleware added runs outermost (probed), so a call refused for invalid declarations still counts as activity. `instructions()` is unchanged: its `mcp.list_tools()` runs middleware, so the schemas it projects already carry `sessionId`.
Telling agents: src/instructions.py

One new bullet in the opening list of `_PROSE`, after the Self-directing and Agency bullets: '**Say which session you are working from:** pass the same `sessionId` on every tool call - your harness's session id if it gives you one, otherwise an id you create once at the start of the session. It is optional; leave it out and the call is counted under your connection, whose id changes when you reconnect.'
States of an entry

Absent, then present on a session's first call, refreshed by each later call, and gone at the next `record` or `active` once a full TTL has passed. Everything is lost on a process restart and on any HMR reload that re-executes src/server.py, because `SESSION_ACTIVITY` is rebuilt with the module. That is accepted: the next call repopulates it.
Error paths

A `sessionId` that is present but is not a non-blank string raises `ValidationError` with the message '`sessionId` must be a non-blank string: the id of the session you are working from. Leave it out if you have none.', translated to `ToolError` by `_guard_tool`. Nothing is recorded and the tool does not run. A call whose tool then fails, or which `_RefuseInvalidDeclarations` refuses, stays recorded, because the session did act.

Decided: an agent-supplied `sessionId` tool argument, advertised on every tool by middleware. Rejected: the transport id alone, which needs no communicating, moves on every reconnect and cannot tell apart agents sharing a connection. Rejected: `_meta`, which arrived as None at the middleware and which an LLM agent cannot set. Rejected: a custom HTTP header, which is fixed in client config rather than per session and does not exist on `--stdio`. Rejected: declaring the parameter on all 25 tool functions, which repeats itself and misses any tool added later; `_RefuseInvalidDeclarations` set the precedent of hanging such behaviour on the call.

Decided: fall back to `Context.session_id`. Rejected: leaving the call untracked, which would miss sessions and make every client change before the record meant anything. Rejected: making `sessionId` required, which breaks every existing client and test. Cost accepted: a session mixing both styles appears twice until its entries expire.

Decided: every `tools/call`, recorded in `on_call_tool` before the tool runs, so refused and failing calls count. Rejected: only `mutatePageBatch`, which would show a session reading pages as idle. Rejected: hooking every request through `on_request`, which would count `initialize` and `tools/list`, so merely connecting would read as work.

Decided: `SessionActivity.active(now)` is the only reader, and nothing outside the tests calls it yet. Rejected: an `activeSessions` MCP tool and a web view: neither was asked for, each widens a public surface, and either can be added later without changing this design.

Decided: `SESSION_TTL = timedelta(minutes=15)`, a module constant. Rejected: an environment variable, which is configurability nobody asked for. Rejected: a maximum entry count, because eviction on every `record` keeps the map to sessions active within the TTL, on a server that is only hosted locally. Rejected: a timer task, which would need the start and stop handling src/cleanup.py carries for its sweep, when eviction inside `record` and `active` does the same job.

feature-brief:mw53bq7n-a128c5.title: Send stage guidance and full field instructions in mutatePageBatch `next` on a transition and again once stale

summary.body: An agent working on a page for a long time loses what it was told at the start of a stage (context compaction, a long-running stage), because mutatePageBatch now echoes stage guidance only on a transition and drops a populated field's instruction. The outcome wanted: one decision drives both. A write that moved the page to a new status, or that lands more than five minutes after the page's guidance was last delivered, gets the full `next` with the stage guidance and every field instruction; any other write gets the trimmed echo. The server keeps a small transient record of per-page events with a timestamp and a TTL so old entries expire, holding a single event for now and read with a simple comparison in mutatePageBatch. It is not persisted wiki state: losing it costs at most one extra full echo. It survives hot reloads by being a dependency-free module, not by joining the reloader's excludes.

items.name: src/server.py
items.text: Effects. The tool shell: mutatePageBatch (sets omit_stage_guidance from result.transitioned), nextActions and createPage are the three places guidance reaches a caller, so the comparison and the recording both belong here. STORE is built in the module body, so anything built beside it is rebuilt whenever this module re-executes. The only await in mutatePageBatch is ws_reloader.refresh() after the next payload is built.

items.name: src/store.py - next_actions, MutatePageResult
items.text: Effects (file storage), consumed unchanged. next_actions is the single place guidance keys are assembled and already takes omit_stage_guidance; MutatePageResult.transitioned already says whether the batch moved the page. Neither needs to change: only the value the tool passes for the flag does.

items.name: src/hmr_server.py and src/hmr_live_refresh.py
items.text: Effects. Reloader passes excludes=[_LIVE_REFRESH_FILE]; hmr_live_refresh holds the ws_reloader singleton and is the precedent for state that must outlast a reload. Read for the HMR trade-off. Neither needs changing unless the cache is added to the excludes.

items.name: src/pagetypes/_stage_guidance.py and specs.status_guidance
items.text: Pure, read only. Source of the text a re-emit repeats. Measured per status: 787 to 1897 characters. Only feature-brief, bug-report, simple-change, architecture and decision-record declare any; epic, agent-plan, feature-spec, implementation-plan, testing-plan, document and toc declare none, so a write on those pages re-emits nothing.

Both `mcp` fixtures rebind server.STORE per test and drive tools through a fastmcp Client. test_mutate_page_batch_omits_guidance_on_a_content_only_write pins the behaviour inside the window. Tests that call the tool on a page created through STORE directly would now see a first-write re-emit.
