requires-python = ">=3.14" (pyproject.toml). The cache needs no new dependency.
Project hints (CLAUDE.md): use the word "create" instead of "mint"; run pytest with --testmon.

Self-direction invariant, verbatim: "nextActions for a focused page and createPage's echo always carry the page's guidance keys". The cache may only ever add guidance to a mutatePageBatch echo, never remove it from these two.

Authoring invariant, verbatim: "next_actions is the single place any guidance key is assembled", and Self-direction: "All three instruction channels ride inside `next`". A re-emit goes through the existing flag and adds no new response key.

The stage guidance's pure/effectful split: the rules take the time as an argument and the shell reads the clock. Store.cleanup_workspace accepting an explicit `now` is the local precedent, and it is how tests cross an expiry without waiting.
Web UI invariant, verbatim: "hmr_live_refresh.py is the only module in the reloader's excludes". Holds unless deliberately changed and reconciled.

Concurrency: all MCP tools are `async def` on one event loop (Authoring & mutation, corrections at a35b133, confirmed in server.py), and mutatePageBatch has no await between building next and returning except the final refresh. A check-then-record with no await between them cannot interleave. Inferred from reading, not from a test.
User requirement: the whole feature can be disabled, and is disabled by default in test mode, so the cache stays empty in test mode unless a test is specifically exercising it.
User requirement: the cache module itself is responsible for test mode. Callers carry no enabled check and do not know the switch exists.

Authoring & mutation invariant "A write response carries guidance at most once, inside `next`, and only when its batch moved the page to a new status" and the matching Self-direction invariant are contradicted by design: a write that stays in its status can now carry it. The rule must be restated, and feature-brief:mw4znaz1-e5165a's accepted consequence (an agent losing context mid-stage must call nextActions) is deliberately reversed for the stale case.
The mutatePageBatch docstring (src/server.py:505) says stage guidance comes only with a transition. It reaches every agent as the tool description and has to change with the behaviour.

Store.set_page_status, the web admin FSM bypass (route_set_page_status, src/server.py:268), moves a page's status outside mutatePageBatch and touches no cache entry. A write inside the window after an override stays silent about the new status. Not a regression: today it stays silent indefinitely.

HMR placement: excluding the cache from reload, the obvious copy of hmr_live_refresh, breaks the only-one-excludes invariant and leaves edits to the cache's own code silently not taking until a restart. A probe against the real reactivity.hmr reloader showed a third way: a module with no in-package imports is untouched when its importer or the importer's other dependencies re-execute, and is rebuilt only when its own file changes. See the HMR question.

createPage's comment says guidance is not shown for auto-pinned child pages. They never get an entry, so a first write on one counts as stale. No production pinned child declares stage guidance, so nothing changes today, but a fixture or future type that does gets its text on the first write.

The record is per page, not per agent session: a second agent, or a session that compacts inside the window, gets nothing until the window lapses. Inherent in the ask, recorded so it is not mistaken for a bug.

feature-brief:mw0kfj8w-ab4d9b dropped a populated field's instruction from every write echo. A transition echo now brings those instructions back, and so does a stale write. tests/test_server.py::test_mutate_echo_omits_populated_instructions_but_next_actions_keeps_them must be read against this: it passes only if its write is not a transition and lands inside the window. Self-direction invariant "Only mutatePageBatch's echo omits a field edge's instruction" still holds but needs its condition restated.

The event cannot mean the last transition alone. Were it recorded only on a transition, every write after minute five would re-emit in full. It therefore means the last full delivery: refreshed by a transition, a stale re-emit, createPage and a focused nextActions.

The cache needs is_test_mode, and a module-level in-package import would end its survival across reloads. A function-local import does not: a probe against the real reactivity.hmr reloader showed that with the import inside a method, editing the imported module left the cache the same object with its entries, and the next call saw the new function. An empty cache also reads as lapsed, so the cache's question must answer no while off, rather than the caller seeing a miss.

architecture:mrtqsthj-dfd190 Self-direction - Data model: the closing sentence on when mutatePageBatch leaves out the guidance keys. Details: "The three instruction channels" and all of "Why a write's echo carries stage guidance only on a transition", including its accepted cost. Invariants: the last one. Code references: add the new module.

architecture:mrtqsspj-0a2ae4 Authoring & mutation - Data model: "with omit_stage_guidance unless the batch moved the page". Details: the tail of "Why guidance rides inside next" and the transition clause in "How workspace guidance is stored and surfaced". Invariants: "A write response carries guidance at most once".

architecture:mrw6s6q6-fb2ff5 Web UI, HMR & live reload - Data model: "The one piece of long-lived in-process state that must outlast a reload" is no longer the only one. Details: add how a dependency-free module outlives reloads without being excluded, if that placement is chosen.

Where should the cache live, given HMR? (a) a dependency-free reloadable module, which survives every reload except an edit to itself and changes no invariant; (b) built beside STORE in server.py, which resets on most source edits at the cost of one extra 1-2 KB guidance text per active page per reload; (c) added to the reloader's excludes, which survives everything but breaks the only-one-excludes invariant and means edits to it silently need a restart.
items.answer: User decided: a dependency-free reloadable module, src/event_cache.py. It keeps its entries through every reload except an edit to itself, changes no invariant, and only has to stay free of in-package imports.

items.text: Does this feature also re-emit a populated field's instruction after five minutes, or only stage guidance, leaving fields as a later event the cache can take?
items.answer: User decided: include field instructions, as ONE additional page-level event rather than an event per field. It tracks when all of a page's field instructions were emitted: all are emitted the first time, the populated-omit rule then applies for five minutes, then all are emitted again once.

items.text: Does a stale re-emit carry the guidance_<field> workspace keys as well as the stage text, or only the stage text?
items.answer: User decided: both. A stale write carries the stage text and every guidance_<field> key, through the existing omit_stage_guidance flag, exactly as a transition does.

items.text: Does a page with no live entry count as stale? Yes means the first write after a restart, or on a page never emitted in this process, carries guidance; no means the guidance can stay withheld until the next transition.
items.answer: Yes. A miss counts as stale, because the safe failure of a lost entry is one extra re-emit, whereas treating a miss as fresh could withhold guidance until the next transition. It is also what delivers the user's emit all the first time rule.

items.text: Is the window measured from the last delivery or from the last write? The ask says the last delivery, so a steady writer gets the text every five minutes rather than only after a quiet gap.
items.answer: From the last delivery, as the ask states. A steady writer gets the text about every five minutes, which is what makes the record a simple timestamp comparison with no per-write bookkeeping.

items.text: Does the field-instruction decision keep its own event, as first answered, or share the single stage guidance event?
items.answer: User decided, superseding the answer to the field-instruction question: a single event only. Both stage guidance and full field instructions are driven by one decision, the batch's `transitioned` or the event having lapsed.

items.text: How is the feature switched, and what does a write echo when it is off?
items.answer: User decided the feature can be disabled and is off by default in test mode, with the cache staying empty there unless a test is specifically exercising it. The environment variable PASTA_EVENT_CACHE decides: 0 is off, any other value is on, and unset is on except in test mode. Off, a write echoes exactly what it does without this feature.

items.text: Who owns the on/off switch, the cache module or its caller?
items.answer: User decided: the cache module itself, including its use of test mode. Callers carry no check. The cache answers is_due, which is False while off, so an empty disabled cache does not read as lapsed.

items.text: PR #49 review: does the switch stay an environment variable, and does the cache take a force argument?
items.answer: User decided in review on PR #49: a module-level variable and setter replace PASTA_EVENT_CACHE, and force is dropped in favour of `or result.transitioned` in mutatePageBatch. A transition is therefore full with the cache on or off. This supersedes the answer that off restores the pre-feature echo exactly.

items.text: PR #49 review: should the cache keep its own test-mode check, or should the test harness disable it?
items.answer: User decided in review on PR #49: the harness disables it. tests/conftest.py calls set_cache_disabled(True) beside set_test_mode(True), the cache drops its test-mode check, and its switch is a plain value, true for enabled and false for disabled. This supersedes the answer that the cache module reads test mode itself.

findings.issue: EventCache.record and is_due read the environment and the test-mode flag through _enabled, so the class is not strictly a function of its arguments, which the pure/effectful split would otherwise ask for. Accepted: the user requires the module to own the switch, and expiry itself stays clock-free, so tests still cross the TTL with an explicit now. No plan change.

items.message: Add a transient per-page event cache
Keep the event cache off in test mode unless a test asks for it
Record full guidance deliveries from createPage and nextActions
Send a full next on a transition and once guidance has lapsed
Drop force from is_due and let a transition go full on its own
Switch the event cache with a module variable instead of an env var
Check the transition before the event cache
Disable the event cache from the test harness with a plain switch
Send a full mutatePageBatch next on a transition and once guidance has lapsed (#49)

# src/event_cache.py
def _enabled() -> bool:
    """False when PASTA_EVENT_CACHE=0; any other value enables it. Unset, it is on everywhere but
    test mode, so a test opts in rather than inheriting echoes that depend on timing."""
    # Imported on call: a name read while this module executes would tie it to that module's reloads.
    from .pagetypes._registry import is_test_mode

    setting = os.environ.get("PASTA_EVENT_CACHE")
    return not is_test_mode() if setting is None else setting != "0"


# first lines of EventCache.record
if not _enabled():
    return

# first lines of EventCache.is_due
if not _enabled():
    return False

def _guidance_is_due(cache, wid, pid):

def _lapse_guidance(cache, wid, pid):

    ttl = server.GUIDANCE_TTL_SECONDS
    cache.record(wid, pid, server.GUIDANCE_EMITTED, time.monotonic() - ttl - 1, ttl)

import asyncio, os, sys
from importlib import import_module
from pathlib import Path
from reactivity import async_effect, derived
from reactivity.hmr.core import HMR_CONTEXT, AsyncReloader

src = Path("src").resolve()
os.environ["PASTA_DATA_DIR"] = sys.argv[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(src.parent))

class Reloader(AsyncReloader):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(str(src), includes=[str(src)], excludes=[str(src / "hmr_live_refresh.py")])

reloader = Reloader()

@derived(context=HMR_CONTEXT)
def server():
    return import_module("src.server")

async def main():
    seen = []
    @async_effect(context=HMR_CONTEXT, call_immediately=False)
    async def watch():
        module = server()
        seen.append((id(module.STORE), id(module.page_events)))
    await watch()
    server().page_events.record("ws", "page", "event", 0.0, 1e9)
    for path in (src / "server.py", src / "pagetypes" / "_registry.py"):
        before = seen[-1][0]
        reloader.on_changes({path}); await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
        cache = import_module("src.event_cache").page_events
        print(path.name, "STORE rebuilt:", seen[-1][0] != before, "cache kept:", id(cache) == seen[0][1],
              "entry kept:", not cache.is_due("ws", "page", "event", 1.0))
    reloader.on_changes({src / "event_cache.py"}); await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    print("event_cache.py cache recreated:", id(import_module("src.event_cache").page_events) != seen[0][1])

asyncio.run(main())

def is_due(self, workspace_id: str, page_id: str, event: str, now: float) -> bool:
    """Whether `event` should happen on a page: no live record of it. Never while the cache is
    off, because an empty cache would otherwise read as everything being due."""
    if not _enabled():
        return False
    entry = self._entries.get((workspace_id, page_id, event))
    return entry is None or not entry.is_live(now)

overview.body: Covers one subsystem, the self-direction roll-up as it reaches a write: mutatePageBatch decides between a full `next` and a trimmed one from a single boolean, the batch having transitioned or the page's guidance having lapsed from a new transient per-page event cache. The cache sits behind one on/off switch in the cache module, on by default, and callers carry no check. The test suite disables it for the whole run, so it stays empty there unless a test opts in. A transition goes full whether the cache is on or off. Deliberately left out: per-field events; persisting anything; any change to src/store.py, whose two existing flags are enough; any change to the reloader's excludes; configuration of the five minute window; src/instructions.py, which review on PR #46 said to leave alone; and the pasta architecture pages, which are reconciled after the implementation lands.

body.text: Behaviour

A mutatePageBatch write is full when the batch moved the page to a new status, or when the page has no live guidance event. A full write's `next` is exactly what nextActions returns for that page: the stage guidance, every `guidance_<field>` key and every field instruction. Any other write's `next` has no guidance keys and leaves the instruction off a field edge whose field is populated, as today. The four lists hold the same edges either way. A rejected batch returns an error and no `next`, and records nothing.

This changes two things a write does today. A transition echo now carries populated fields' instructions, where it used to drop them. A content-only write more than five minutes after the last full delivery now carries everything, once: its recording makes the next write trimmed again.

The event records a full delivery, not a transition. Every path that hands a caller the full payload for a focused page records it: createPage for the created page, nextActions when given a pageId, and a full mutatePageBatch write. A trimmed write records nothing, and neither does a whole-workspace nextActions, which has no focused page. Were only transitions recorded, every write after minute five would be full.
Event cache - src/event_cache.py (new)

This is a clock-free store: every operation takes `now`, so expiry is a function of its arguments and tests cross it without waiting. The event is a plain string so a later event needs no change here. The TTL sits on the entry rather than the cache because the comparison belongs to the event that recorded it. Expired entries are dropped on each `record`. A read leaves the dict alone, so there is no timer and nothing to start from a lifespan.

The switch lives in this module, so a caller never sees it: disabled, `record` stores nothing and `is_due` answers False. The module imports nothing from its package, which is what carries it across a reload.
Tool surface - src/server.py

The server owns the event name, the window and the clock. It reads `time.monotonic()`, because the window is an in-process duration and must not jump when the wall clock is corrected. The comparison stays in the mutatePageBatch body. Each tool's response shape is unchanged.

GUIDANCE_TTL_SECONDS = 300.0

                       GUIDANCE_TTL_SECONDS)


# mutatePageBatch

page = result.page

body.text: The mutatePageBatch docstring's last sentence, which every agent reads as the tool description, becomes: Echoes the new status, the current `statusRevisionToken`, and next actions. A transition, or a write more than five minutes after they were last sent, carries stage guidance and every field instruction; any other write leaves out stage guidance and the instruction of a field already populated on its page - nextActions carries them all.
Switching it off

`_enabled` in src/event_cache.py is the one switch, a plain module-level boolean that is true by default and set through `set_cache_disabled`, a name chosen to say the cache is on unless something turns it off. Nothing in production calls the setter, so turning the cache off on a running server means changing the variable's default, which a hot reload picks up. Callers carry no check and do not know the switch exists.

Disabled means the cache is absent rather than empty. An empty cache would read as lapsed, so `is_due` answers False before it looks at anything. Nothing is stored, so the cache stays empty, and a content-only write gets the trimmed echo. A transition is not the cache's to switch: mutatePageBatch checks `result.transitioned` first, which makes it full either way and skips the cache, so a transition carries populated fields' instructions while disabled, test runs included.

tests/conftest.py calls `set_cache_disabled(True)` beside `set_test_mode(True)`, so the cache is disabled for a whole test run and stays empty. A test exercising the cache opts in through a conftest fixture, which enables it, swaps in an empty cache for that test alone so entries cannot leak between tests, and disables it again afterwards. The cache's own tests go through the same fixture, and a test of the disabled state reads the real singleton, which nothing writes to in a test run.

body.text: Data shapes
Error paths and edge cases

A miss counts as lapsed, whether the page was never delivered in this process, its entry expired, or the cache module was edited. The first write after a restart is therefore full, and so is the first write on a pinned child, which createPage does not record. An entry exactly at its TTL is still live, because the ask is more than five minutes. A status declaring no guidance omits the key through the existing absent path, so a full write there adds only instructions. The web admin status override records nothing, so a write inside the window stays trimmed, as it is today. A full write on a parent page carries its pinned children's instructions too, because that is what nextActions returns for the subtree. Under stdio each server process has its own cache.

The check and the record run with no await between them on the one event loop every tool runs on, so they need no lock. Entries live for five minutes and are dropped on each record, so the dict holds at most one entry per page delivered in the last five minutes, and the sweep is linear in that small number.
A consequence to accept

The record is per page, not per agent session: a second agent, or a session compacted inside the window, gets nothing until the window lapses or it calls nextActions. A page written steadily gets a full echo about every five minutes, whether or not the agent lost anything, which is 1 to 2 KB of stage text plus the rollup's instructions. That is the price of a check needing no per-write bookkeeping.

The cache is a reloadable module that imports nothing from its package, src/event_cache.py, and a probe against the real reactivity.hmr reloader confirmed the behaviour: editing the importer or the importer's other dependency rebuilt the object beside STORE and left the leaf's singleton and its entries in place, and editing the leaf rebuilt it with the new code live. Rejected: building it beside STORE in server.py, which resets on most source edits for one extra 1 to 2 KB per active page per reload; and adding it to the reloader's excludes, which breaks the only-module-in-the-excludes invariant and means an edit to its code silently takes nothing until a restart.

Field instructions are in scope. The first answer of one additional page-level event is superseded by the single-event decision below. Rejected: an event per field, which the user ruled out, because it adds a populate record per (section, field) to the write path for a reminder that is fine as a set; and leaving fields out, which keeps a populated field's instruction unrecoverable from a write.

One event, and one boolean drives both `omit_populated_instructions` and `omit_stage_guidance`: `result.transitioned or not live`. A consequence is that a transition now carries every instruction, reversing that part of the populated-omit feature. Rejected: a separate field event, which the user dropped as more state for the same reminder, and which lets the two reminders drift apart by up to a window; and keeping transitions on the populated-omit rule, which needs a second comparison.

A full write carries the stage text and every `guidance_<field>` key through the existing omit_stage_guidance flag, exactly as a transition does. Rejected: stage text only, which needs a second flag on next_actions, the configurability the transition feature already rejected, and leaves an agent reminded of the stage but not of the house rules.

A missing entry counts as lapsed. A lost entry then costs one extra full echo, and the first-delivery case needs no separate path. Rejected: treating a miss as fresh, which could withhold guidance indefinitely on a page that never transitions again in this process, the failure this feature exists to fix.

The window runs from the last full delivery, as the ask states, with `is_live` true up to and including the TTL. Rejected: measuring from the last write, which would only fire after a quiet gap and so never remind a steady writer, and needs a record on every write; and measuring from the last transition alone, which would make every write after minute five full.

Decided in review on PR #49: `force` is dropped, mutatePageBatch uses `result.transitioned or is_due(...)`, checking the transition first so a transition skips the cache, and both omit flags are `not emit_in_full`. A transition is therefore full with the cache on or off, so off stops the five minute re-emit and the recording but does not restore the pre-feature transition echo, which an earlier version of this spec required. Rejected: `force` through is_due, which kept off exact at the cost of an argument on the cache and a second transitioned term in the caller.

One module-level boolean, `_enabled`, true by default and set through `set_cache_disabled`. Decided in review on PR #49, replacing first the PASTA_EVENT_CACHE environment variable as more machinery than the switch needs, and then a three-state value that followed test mode. Rejected: both of those; and leaving the cache empty in test mode and changing nothing else, because an empty cache reads as lapsed and every write would go full.

The switch lives in the cache module and callers of the cache carry no check. The caller asks `is_due` rather than for an entry, because only the cache can tell a disabled cache from a miss. The earlier answer that the module also reads test mode itself is superseded by the next decision. Rejected: a public `enabled` attribute, which leaves the check in the caller.

Decided in review on PR #49: tests/conftest.py calls `set_cache_disabled(True)` beside `set_test_mode(True)`, and the cache has no test-mode check. The switch is a plain on/off value, and the module imports nothing from its package at all, which makes its reload rule simple to state. The trade accepted is that the rule for test runs lives in the harness rather than the module. Because the run always disables the cache, a test runs the module fresh to pin that its default is on. Rejected: reading is_test_mode through a function-local import, which worked and kept the rule in the module, at the cost of a three-state value and an import that needed explaining.

feature-brief:mw5hlioy-20d166.title: Single balanced backticks in an inline text run are stored and shown verbatim

summary.body: Writing a text run that mentions something like `now` in backticks fails the whole write, and that is the only symbol slip seen in practice. The outcome wanted: an inline text run may contain single backticks as long as they are balanced (their count is divisible by 2). They are stored as part of the text run, unchanged, and shown verbatim in the rendered output rather than interpreted as Markdown. An unbalanced backtick keeps being rejected, and so do adjacent backticks, so a triple-backtick fence cannot pass on its even count. `**` and link syntax also keep being rejected: there is no need to loosen them. This differs from the abandoned brief feature-brief:mw0l93ml-a44e6b, which rewrote backtick spans into `{code}` runs: here nothing is rewritten and the text stays a text run.

items.text: Pure constant. `_MARKDOWN_TOKENS = ("**", "`", "](")` (L64) is the whole rejection list, and the comment above it (L61-63) describes it as emphasis/code/link tokens. Changes: the backtick leaves the tuple and the comment stops naming code. The run-grammar comment (L51) stays true.

items.text: Pure. `_reject_markdown` (L41) raises on any token and is the only reader of `_MARKDOWN_TOKENS`. `_validate_run` calls it on a bare-string run (L53) and on a text run's `text` (L77), and never on a `{code}` or `{ref}` run. Marked and linked text runs therefore share the same check. Everything reaches it through `validate_inline_content` -> `validate_arg_value` -> `validate_block`/`validate_blocks`, so every block path inherits one change. No other module calls it. Changes: this is where the balance check goes.

Confirmed by running it, not only by reading: a probe rendered `say `now`` in a paragraph, a bold run, a heading, a list, a quote and a table cell. Abandoned brief feature-brief:mw0l93ml-a44e6b and PR #48 solved the same failure the opposite way, rewriting a backtick span into a `{code}` run before validation and accepting a stray backtick. PR #48 closed unmerged, and nothing from it is on main, though its branch worktree-backtick-code-runs still exists. This ask gives way on neither point: text is stored as sent, and an odd count stays rejected. Nothing is taken from that work, including its run schema and feature-spec description changes, which this ask did not request.
`_MARKDOWN_TOKENS` is a presence check, and balance is a count, so the backtick cannot stay in that tuple. It needs its own check in `_reject_markdown`.

The current error for a backtick says 'express emphasis or a link with a structured run', which does not help with an unbalanced backtick. The new rejection needs its own message naming the imbalance and `{'code': ...}`.

The two render paths read the same stored text differently. The web view shows literal backticks. The MCP path returns the characters as typed inside Markdown, so a client that renders that Markdown would show inline code. Escaping there would break the never-escapes contract and put backslashes in the output, so the MCP output stays as it is. Prose and list element text already behave this way.

Text such as `**kwargs` written in backticks in a text run stays rejected for its `**`, because backticks here are plain text and not a code span. That matches the ask, which leaves `**` and link symbols alone, but it means the mention has to be written as a `{code}` run.

tests/test_commands.py L1315 and tests/test_pagetypes.py L502 assert the behaviour this feature removes. Each should keep its coverage (a table cell, and a token inside a `{text}` run) by switching to a `**` token, with the backtick rule covered by new tests.

architecture:mrtjuul6-5221b2 Page types & FSM implementation, Invariants: 'A blocks field carries structured inline runs, not raw markdown ... markdown emphasis or link tokens inside a plain-text run are rejected'. It gains that single balanced backticks are literal text in a run, and that an unbalanced backtick or adjacent backticks are rejected.
Does balanced mean only that the backtick count is even, so a doubled pair around a word is allowed, or should adjacent backticks stay rejected because the ask talks about single occurrences?
items.answer: Count only: a run is balanced when its backtick count is divisible by 2, which is the definition the ask gives. A doubled pair around a word has four backticks and is allowed, and a triple fence has three and is rejected. Decided by the agent, since a wrong guess costs little: such text is stored and shown verbatim either way. Flag it to the user at the gate.

items.text: Is balance judged per text run, or across all the runs of a block, so that a backtick opening in one run and closing in the next counts as balanced?
items.answer: Per text run. The ask says 'in a text run', and each run is already validated on its own. A backtick opening in one run and closing in the next leaves each run odd, so both are rejected.

items.text: Does displayed verbatim require a change to the MCP render path, which returns raw backticks inside Markdown that a client could render as inline code?
items.answer: No renderer changes. The probe in grounding shows the web view already displays literal backticks with no `<code>` element, and the MCP path already returns the characters exactly as typed. Escaping on the MCP path would add backslashes to the output and break its never-escapes contract. New tests pin both paths.

items.text: Correcting the first question, which the agent answered with a plain count: must each backtick stand alone, so that a triple fence opening and closing, six backticks and an even count, stays rejected?
items.answer: User decided: yes. Single occurrences are required, to avoid a triple-backtick open and close, which totals six and is even. Each backtick must stand alone and the count must be even, so adjacent backticks of any length stay rejected. This supersedes the agent's answer to the first question.

overview.body: This spec covers one rule in the inline-run grammar. A text run may hold single backticks when their count is divisible by 2: they are stored in the run exactly as sent and shown verbatim. An odd count and adjacent backticks are still rejected, each with an error of its own. It deliberately leaves out any rewriting of the text into `{code}` runs, any loosening of `**` or `](`, any change to either renderer or to search, and any change to describe or to field descriptions.

body.text: The behaviour

The rule applies to the text of every text run: a bare string and the `text` of a `{text}` run, marked or linked. That covers every run-bearing body arg of every field, because all of them go through one validator. There is no per-field setting. `{code}` and `{ref}` runs are not checked, as today. The check only accepts or rejects, so a value is stored exactly as sent.

body.source:
sent                                  result
"say `now` please"                    stored as sent
{text: "say `now`", bold: true}       stored as sent
"`a` and `b`"                         stored as sent
"``doubled``"                         rejected: adjacent backticks
"```"                                 rejected: adjacent backticks
"```\nfence\n```"                     rejected: adjacent backticks (6 in total, even)
"a stray ` here"                      rejected: unbalanced backticks
"`a` and ` b"                         rejected: unbalanced backticks
["say `", {text: "now`", bold: true}] rejected: each run is odd on its own
"`**kwargs`"                          rejected: Markdown syntax ('**')
"`[a](b)`"                            rejected: Markdown syntax ('](')
{code: "x`y"}                         stored as sent, code runs are not checked

body.text: Pure core: the rejected tokens (specs.py)
The backtick leaves the token list, because the list is a presence check and balance is a count.

body.source:
# Markdown emphasis/link tokens rejected inside a plain-text run. Kept deliberately narrow
# (bold/link markers) so ordinary prose containing a lone `*` or `_` or even a file with
# double '__' is not falsely rejected. Backticks are judged separately, since single balanced
# ones are literal text.
_MARKDOWN_TOKENS = ("**", "](")

body.text: Pure core: the backtick checks (validation.py)

Two checks go at the end of `_reject_markdown`, which both text-run paths in `_validate_run` already call. The token loop and its message are unchanged, and tokens are checked first, so a run with several problems reports the token. Adjacency comes before the count, because a fence is the likely cause and three backticks should be told so rather than told to close a pair. Each check has its own message, since the fixes differ: a fence belongs in a code block. A plain presence check in `"``" in text` also covers any longer run of backticks.
Effects

There are none to add. The change is a pure declaration and a pure check. Rendering and search already handle the stored text correctly, as recorded on the brief, so neither changes. No migration is needed: the grammar runs only on write, and stored runs hold no backticks today.
Error paths

Adjacent backticks and an odd backtick count each raise ValidationError with the message above. As with every run rejection, this aborts the whole batch and nothing is written. `**` and `](` raise the existing Markdown syntax error, including inside backticks. Malformed runs raise exactly what they raise today.

Balance is judged per text run. Rejected: judging across a block's runs, which would need the validator to see neighbouring runs and would accept a pair spanning differently marked text. An author splitting a mention across runs gets a clear error.

Neither renderer changes. The web path already escapes the backtick so it displays literally, and the MCP path already returns it as typed. Rejected: escaping on the MCP path, which would add backslashes and break the contract that the path never escapes; and rendering these runs as inline code, which is the Markdown interpretation the ask rules out. A client that renders the MCP Markdown will show inline code, as it already does for prose and list element text.
Superseded by the decision on the corrected question. The agent first chose a plain count, which the user overruled at the PR because a triple-backtick open and close totals six and would pass.

Each backtick must stand alone and the count must be even. Chosen by the user: single occurrences are required so a triple-backtick fence stays rejected. Adjacency gets its own check and message, because a fence needs pointing at a code block. Rejected: a plain count, which lets a fence through on its even total; adding the doubled backtick to `_MARKDOWN_TOKENS`, whose message talks about emphasis and links and never mentions code; and allowing a doubled pair while refusing only triples, which the user's single-occurrence rule excludes.

feature-brief:mw5hrywm-7ffca7.title: Retire the 'pasta' skill name in favour of 'cook'

summary.body: The repo ships one workflow skill under two names, `pasta` and `cook`. Remove the `pasta` alias so `cook` is the only name for that skill, and drop every mention of the `pasta` skill name from the README's install instructions, so a new user only ever learns and copies one name. The install command also has to work as printed on both macOS and Linux. The product, MCP server and workspace stay called pasta; only the skill name goes.

items.name: .claude/skills/pasta/SKILL.md
items.text: The alias being removed. Static markdown read by the agent harness, no logic and no effects. Differs from the cook skill only on line 2, `name: pasta` against `name: cook`; `diff` of the two files shows that single line. It is the only file in `.claude/skills/pasta/`, so removing it removes the directory and the `/pasta` command.

items.name: .claude/skills/cook/SKILL.md
items.text: The surviving skill. Static markdown, read but not changed: its body already says everything the alias said. Its `# Pasta usage` heading and its references to the pasta MCP name the product, not the skill.

items.name: README.md, Quick start > Give your agent the habit (lines 68, 71, 74)
items.text: The install instructions, and the only tracked file that names the skill: `git grep -i skill` outside `.claude/skills` and `graphify-out` hits these three lines and two unrelated uses of 'skilled' in src/pagetypes. Line 68 says 'bundled skills', line 71 copies `{pasta,cook}`, line 74 teaches `/pasta` with `/cook` as the alternative. Static prose, no effects.

The product name stays. Everything else called pasta is out of scope: the `pasta` key in the mcpServers example, the `/pasta/mcp` endpoint, `.pasta-data`, `PASTA_DATA_DIR`, the repo path `path/to/pasta` in the copy command, and the `# pasta` README title.

README rules from the GitHub README page, Decisions section: 'The skill-copy step is ONE command', 'with no global-install variant', it ends 'on a bold instruction to ask the agent to cook a feature, a simple change, a bug report or some documentation', 'Shell fences are tagged `text`, not `bash`', and 'No em dashes in the file.'

From CLAUDE.md: 'Use the word "create" instead of "mint" when creating something.' and 'Run pytest with --testmon to speed up red-green testing.' The justfile `testincr` recipe runs `uv run pytest --testmon`.

src/instructions.py:41 ends a Red Flags row with 'Invoke pasta.', which can be read as invoking a skill called pasta. In context the whole table is about using the pasta MCP ('Create a pasta page', 'Check for pasta pages') and the reader is already inside those instructions, so it still reads correctly once the skill is gone. Left as it is; no test pins the wording either way.

Removing the alias is a breaking change for `/pasta` in this repo and for anyone who copied the skills earlier: a checkout that already holds `.claude/skills/pasta/` keeps working locally, but `/pasta` stops working here and the README no longer mentions it. That is what was asked for, and no alias or deprecation note is being kept.

graphify-out/graph.json holds a 'Pasta Workflow Skill' node from the deleted file. graphify-out is gitignored and `.git/hooks` has no active hooks, so the node stays until the next graph rebuild. Harmless, but a query may name the skill until then. No in-flight branch touches the skill files: `git log --all` on both directories shows only history already on main.

GitHub README (user-facing), document:mtiodadq-2fb6a6, Decisions section: the bullet 'The skill-copy step is ONE command copying both skills at once' goes stale; it becomes one command copying the one skill. That bullet's note that the command uses `cp -t`, fails on BSD cp and was kept as written goes too: the command is now `cp -R` and works on macOS and Linux. Add a line under Shipped saying the alias was retired.
Does `/pasta` survive in any form, such as a deprecated alias or a migration note in the README?
items.answer: No. The ask is to remove the name, so the directory is deleted outright with no alias or note.

items.text: With `/pasta` gone, what happens to README line 74's 'Then start work with' sentence, given the bold line directly under it already says to `/cook`?
items.answer: Drop the sentence. The bold line directly below already tells the reader to `/cook`, so keeping it would say the same thing twice in a row. The two sentences about the skill itself stay.

items.text: Does 'Invoke pasta.' in src/instructions.py:41 change as part of this work?
items.answer: No. The table it sits in is about using the pasta MCP, and the reader is already inside the MCP's own instructions, so it reads correctly with the skill gone. Changing server instructions is outside an ask about the README and install steps.

items.text: Should the README's 'The skill is four lines.' be corrected as part of this work?
items.answer: Yes. Decided by the user at the ship gate: the README now says 'The skill is three lines.', matching the three non-blank lines of the cook skill without its frontmatter.

items.text: What form should the README's copy command take so it runs as printed on both macOS and Linux?
items.answer: `cp -R path/to/pasta/.claude/skills/cook .claude/skills/`, as the user asked at the ship gate. It stays one command after the `mkdir -p`, and it uses only the `cp -R source target` form that GNU and BSD cp share. `cp -t` is the GNU-only part being removed.

overview.body: Removes the `pasta` skill alias and the mention of it in the README's Quick start, leaving `cook` as the single name for the workflow skill. This changes one skill directory and one README subsection. It leaves alone the `cook` skill's content, the MCP server and its instructions, and everything else named pasta, because those name the product rather than the skill.

body.text: Skill files

Delete `.claude/skills/pasta/SKILL.md`, which is the only file in that directory, so the directory goes with it and git records a single deletion. `.claude/skills/cook/SKILL.md` is unchanged. After this `/cook` is the only way to start the workflow from a skill, and `/pasta` is an unknown command in a fresh checkout.
README

Three edits inside the 'Give your agent the habit' subsection of `README.md`. Line 68 changes 'the bundled skills' to 'the bundled skill'. Line 71's copy command names the one directory and swaps the GNU-only `cp -t` for `cp -R <source> <target>/`, which GNU and BSD cp both accept, and stays one command in a `text` fence. The source has no trailing slash, because BSD cp would then copy the directory's contents rather than the directory. Line 74 loses its first sentence, keeps the two about the skill, and says three lines rather than four. The subsection reads exactly as follows afterwards:

body.source:
### Give your agent the habit

An MCP server the agent *can* use isn't one it *will* use. Copy the bundled skill so the workflow starts in pasta rather than in an unplanned code edit:

```text
mkdir -p .claude/skills && cp -R path/to/pasta/.claude/skills/cook .claude/skills/
```

The skill is three lines. All it does is tell the agent to call the servers instructions tool.

**Now ask your agent to `/cook` a feature, a simple change, a bug report or some documentation.**

body.text: Pure logic and effects

There is no code in this change: it deletes one markdown file and edits another, so there is no logic to place on either side and no interface, state or error path to specify. A reader who follows the new copy command gets the `cook` directory alone, and if the source path is wrong `cp` fails as it did before.

Delete the alias outright. Rejected: keeping `.claude/skills/pasta/` as a deprecated alias, and adding a migration note to the README. Both would keep teaching the name this work exists to remove, and a checkout that already copied the skill keeps it locally anyway.

Drop the 'Then start work with' sentence. Rejected: rewriting it as 'Then start work with `/cook`', which would repeat the bold line directly below it. The README page's decision that the step ends on that bold instruction is what carries the call to action.

Leave 'Invoke pasta.' in src/instructions.py as it is. Rejected: rewording it to name the MCP. The row still reads correctly in a table about using the pasta MCP, and editing server instructions would widen a change that is otherwise confined to the skill and the README.

Say 'The skill is three lines.', as the user asked at the ship gate. It matches the three non-blank lines of the cook skill without its frontmatter. Rejected: leaving the old claim as a known leftover, which was the first position in this brief.

Use `cp -R path/to/pasta/.claude/skills/cook .claude/skills/`, as the user asked at the ship gate. It is the portable form the README page's earlier note already named for macOS. Rejected: keeping `cp -t` with a note for macOS readers, and printing a separate command per platform, because the README keeps the skill-copy step to one command.

summary.body: Bring every direct Python dependency up to its current release, headlined by FastMCP 3.4.4 -> 4.1.6 (which moves the MCP SDK from 1.28 to 2.3), so the server stays on a supported framework line. The outcome is the same server behaviour on newer libraries: every MCP tool, the web UI, and the HMR dev server's in-process reload all keep working, and the test suite stays green. Grounding showed that the public FastMCP API pasta uses carries over unchanged. The real work is the HMR module: its mount swap still holds on v4, but its trick for telling connected MCP clients that the tools changed after a reload is silently dead on SDK 2.x and has to be rebuilt on the SDK's new per-client `Connection` object. One camelCase field read in `instructions()` also moves to snake_case.

items.name: pyproject.toml
items.text: Declares the direct dependency floors. Config only, no logic. `uv tree --depth 1 --outdated` shows the latest releases: fastmcp 3.4.4 -> 4.1.6, fastapi 0.139.2 -> 0.162.0, wenmode 0.12.1 -> 0.15.3, python-statemachine 3.2.0 -> 3.2.2, sphinx 9.1.0 -> 9.2.0, sphinxcontrib-mermaid 2.1.0 -> 2.1.1; dev group: basedpyright 1.39.9 -> 1.40.2, pytest 9.1.1 -> 9.2.0, pytest-testmon 2.2.0 -> 2.3.0. hmr, jinja2, myst-parser, pydot, sphinx-autodoc2 and sphinx-autobuild are already at their latest.

items.name: uv.lock
items.text: The resolved environment, currently fastmcp 3.4.4 / mcp 1.28.1 / starlette 1.3.1 / pydantic 2.13.4 / uvicorn 0.51.0 / anyio 4.14.2 / httpx 0.28.1. Regenerated by `uv lock --upgrade`. fastmcp 4.1.6 brings in fastmcp-slim 4.1.6, mcp 2.3.0, mcp-types 2.3.0 and httpx2.

items.name: src/hmr_server.py (build_dev_app)
items.text: Effectful shell: uvicorn, the file watcher, the reactive reloader and the MCP mount swap. It touches four fastmcp/mcp internals, each checked against the fastmcp 4.1.6 / mcp 2.3.0 wheel source. (1) Mount/unmount via `base_app.mount(mcp)` then `base_app.providers[-1]` and `providers.remove(...)`: STILL VALID. In v4 `FastMCP` subclasses `AggregateProvider`, `providers` is a plain list, and `mount()` with no namespace calls `add_provider`, which appends exactly one `FastMCPProvider`. (2) Session capture by wrapping `base_app._mcp_server.run`: BROKEN. `_mcp_server` is still a LowLevelServer with `run()`, but `StreamableHTTPSessionManager` now drives each stateful session through `serve_loop(...)` (its own comment: 'Drive via serve_loop (not Server.run())'), so the wrap never fires over HTTP. (3) Patching `ServerSession.__init__`: WRONG OBJECT. In mcp 2.x `ServerSession` is a per-request proxy built once per inbound message; the per-client object is `mcp.server.connection.Connection`, which has `send_tool_list_changed` / `send_prompt_list_changed` / `send_resource_list_changed` on its standalone stream. They are best-effort and never raise. Every Connection is built through `Connection.__init__` (via `for_loop` for handshake sessions, `from_envelope` for modern requests). (4) `fastmcp.utilities.lifespan.combine_lifespans` and `http_app(path=...).lifespan`: unchanged.

items.name: src/server.py
items.text: Builds `mcp = FastMCP("pasta")` and `mcp.http_app(path="/mcp")`, combines lifespans, and registers `_RefuseInvalidDeclarations(Middleware).on_call_tool` with `MiddlewareContext` / `CallNext` / `ToolResult` (from `fastmcp.tools`) / `ToolError`. All of these exist unchanged in v4. Line 358 in `instructions()` reads `tool.to_mcp_tool().inputSchema`, a camelCase field that v4 bridges with a deprecation warning; the snake_case name is `input_schema`. No use of Context, ctx.sample/elicit/set_state, task=True or mount(prefix=). Tool definitions are pure wrappers over the store (effects live in src/store.py).

items.name: tests/test_server.py, tests/test_workspace_guidance.py
items.text: Drive the tools in-process with `async with Client(mcp)` and read `result.data`. In v4 a default Client negotiates the 2026-07-28 protocol (mode="auto"), but these tools use none of the APIs that era removes, so the suite is the regression check for the MCP surface.

items.name: tests/test_hmr_server.py
items.text: Covers only `_LoggingErrorFilter`. Its docstring says the reload machinery (mount swap, session notify) is exercised by hand against a running dev server, so nothing in the suite pins the fastmcp/mcp internals that hmr_server relies on.

items.name: src/render_html.py, tests/test_render.py (wenmode)
items.text: Only `Wenmode(github)` from `wenmode` / `wenmode.presets`; pure Markdown-to-HTML conversion. The 0.12.1 -> 0.15.3 bump is a 0.x minor jump and could change output; test_render.py exercises the same preset.

items.name: main.py, scripts/mcp_probe.py
items.text: main.py runs `run_dev_server(host, port)` (with `--port`) or `mcp.run(transport="stdio")`; the stdio call is unchanged in v4. scripts/mcp_probe.py (`just probe`) does a raw streamable-HTTP handshake offering protocol 2025-06-18 using `httpx` directly. It is the existing manual tool for checking a live dev server.
pyproject.toml: `requires-python = ">=3.14"`; the environment runs CPython 3.14.6.

fastmcp 4 floors, from the official upgrade guide (gofastmcp.com/getting-started/upgrading): 'pydantic >= 2.12 is now the floor'; 'The server extra floors Starlette >= 1.0.1'; 'FastAPI 0.133.0 is the first release that admits Starlette 1.x'. From the mcp 2.3.0 wheel METADATA: `starlette>=0.48.0; python_version >= '3.14'`, `uvicorn>=0.31.1`, `anyio>=4.10; python_version >= '3.14'`, `httpx2>=2.10.0`, `mcp-types==2.3.0`.

Floor convention (INFERRED by comparing pyproject.toml to `uv tree`, not written down anywhere): every direct dependency floor in pyproject.toml equals its currently locked version, e.g. `fastmcp>=3.4.4` with 3.4.4 locked.
CLAUDE.md: 'Run pytest with --testmon to speed up red-green testing.' and 'Use the word "create" instead of "mint" when creating something.'

HMR invariants from the 'Web UI, HMR & live reload' architecture page that the change must keep: src.server is imported only through the reloader's finder, never at hmr_server module top level; hmr_live_refresh.py is the only module in the reloader's excludes; the hot-reload machinery is dev-only and the stdio transport has no hot reload; reloads keep MCP sessions alive by swapping the mount and sending tools/list_changed.
pyproject.toml `[tool.pyright]`: `typeCheckingMode = "recommended"`, `include = ["src/**/*"]`, with reportPrivateUsage disabled. `just types` runs basedpyright over src.

src/hmr_server.py session capture (`_patch_session_init`, `_run_with_session_capture`, `notify_sessions`) does not work on mcp 2.x. The `_mcp_server.run` wrap never runs on the HTTP path (serve_loop is used instead), and `ServerSession` is now a per-request proxy, not a per-client session. After the upgrade, MCP clients would silently stop receiving tools/list_changed on reload unless this is rewritten. The per-client object to capture is `mcp.server.connection.Connection`.

The 2026-07-28 protocol era is sessionless: on streamable HTTP a modern request gets a Connection with no standalone channel, and `Connection.notify` drops list_changed with a debug log ('dropped ... no standalone channel'). A reload notification can only reach clients on a handshake-era protocol (2025-xx) with an open standalone stream, or modern clients over a duplex transport. This limits the 'sessions survive the reload and are told the tools changed' invariant, and no code change can lift it.
src/server.py:358 `tool.to_mcp_tool().inputSchema` is a camelCase read that fastmcp 4 bridges with a deprecation warning on every `instructions` call; it must become `input_schema`.

Comments in src/hmr_server.py name the old internals: the module docstring's brittleness note ('base_app._mcp_server.run for session capture') and the mount comment ('a fastmcp 3.4.x internal'). They become wrong once the capture is replaced.

pyproject.toml's `docs` dependency group (`sphinx>=8.1`, `myst-parser>=4.0`, `sphinxcontrib-mermaid>=1.0`) duplicates main dependencies with older floors. It looks redundant, but it is outside this change; raise it rather than delete it in passing.

scripts/mcp_probe.py and scripts/feature_brief_probe.py `import httpx`, which is not a declared dependency. fastmcp 4 / mcp 2 drop httpx for httpx2; httpx still resolves only through `fastapi[standard]` (fastapi itself and fastapi-cloud-cli), so the probes keep working, but only transitively.

Architecture 'Web UI, HMR & live reload' (architecture:mrw6s6q6-fb2ff5): the Data model sentence 'notifies live client sessions (tools/list_changed)'; the invariant 'Reloads preserve clients, not just modules ... sessions are sent tools/list_changed' (now limited to handshake-era / duplex connections); the invariant 'The hot-reload machinery ... reaches into a few private fastmcp/mcp internals (mount/unmount, session capture)', which should name the v4 internals (`providers` list, `Connection` capture); the Sync commit.

Feature brief 'Self-describing instructions & page-type introspection' (feature-brief:mumk21zg-588866) records 'fastmcp 3.4.4: mcp.list_tools() is synchronous'. It is a shipped historical record, so it stays as written and only needs noting, not editing.
Does 'update library versions' mean every direct dependency (main and dev groups) moved to its latest release with the floors raised to match, or only fastmcp plus what it forces?
items.answer: Every direct dependency in the main and dev groups goes to its latest release via `uv lock --upgrade` (transitives included), and each pyproject.toml floor is raised to the version that resolves, following the existing floor-equals-lock convention. This includes the 0.x jumps (fastapi 0.162, wenmode 0.15); the test suite decides whether any of them breaks something.

items.text: How should the HMR dev server tell connected MCP clients about a reload on SDK 2.x, now that `_mcp_server.run` is bypassed on HTTP and `ServerSession` is a per-request object?
items.answer: Capture every `mcp.server.connection.Connection` by wrapping `Connection.__init__` for the life of the dev server (installed in reloader_lifespan, restored on shutdown), and on reload call `send_tool_list_changed` / `send_resource_list_changed` / `send_prompt_list_changed` on each live one. This replaces the `_mcp_server.run` wrap and the `ServerSession.__init__` patch entirely.

items.text: Should the fastmcp/mcp internals that hmr_server depends on get automated contract tests, so the next upgrade fails in pytest rather than silently in the dev server?
items.answer: Yes. Three small tests in tests/test_hmr_server.py exercise the real helpers: the mount/unmount swap, connection capture, and the list_changed fan-out. The mount helper and the notify helper move to module level so the tests can call them without a live uvicorn process.

items.text: Should the redundant `docs` dependency group in pyproject.toml be removed as part of this change?
items.answer: No. It is unrelated to the upgrade; it stays as found and is raised in the hand-off instead.

items.text: Should the server override fastmcp 4's new default 30-minute idle timeout for stateful HTTP sessions (`http_session_idle_timeout="auto"`)?
items.answer: No. Keep the SDK default. An expired session is re-initialized by the client, and adding configuration nobody asked for is outside this change. It is recorded as a behaviour change of the upgrade.

items.text: wenmode 0.15 (part of this upgrade) emits 'DeprecationWarning: Passing github without calling it is deprecated and will be removed in 1.0; use github() instead.' at src/render_html.py:27 (`Wenmode(github)`), and tests/test_render.py:499 builds the same thing. Should the upgrade adapt the call?
items.answer: Yes. It is the same kind of adaptation as the inputSchema rename: a deprecation the upgrade itself introduced, on a path the library says it will remove. Change `Wenmode(github)` to `Wenmode(github())` in src/render_html.py and in tests/test_render.py (which deliberately mirrors the web routes' preset), and land it in the upgrade commit. tests/test_render.py is the check that the rendered output is unchanged. Added to the implementation plan as a step before the upgrade commit.

    # fastmcp 4 keeps camelCase reads on SDK models working through a warning bridge that is

def test_a_mounted_server_is_served_through_the_proxy_until_unmounted():
    # The reload swap leans on a fastmcp internal: mount() appends one provider to the proxy's
    # `providers`, and removing that provider unmounts it. An upgrade that moves this fails here
    # rather than leaving the dev server serving a stale or doubled tool set.
    proxy, child = FastMCP("proxy"), FastMCP("child")

    @child.tool
    def ping() -> str:
        return "pong"

    async def tool_names() -> set[str]:
        return {tool.name for tool in await proxy.list_tools()}

    unmount = _mount(proxy, child)
    assert "ping" in asyncio.run(tool_names())
    unmount()
    assert "ping" not in asyncio.run(tool_names())

class _RecordingOutbound:
    """Stands in for a client's standalone stream, recording each notification sent down it."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.sent: list[str] = []

    async def notify(self, method, params, opts=None):
        self.sent.append(method)

    async def send_raw_request(self, method, params, opts=None):
        raise AssertionError("a reload sends notifications, never requests")


class _BrokenOutbound(_RecordingOutbound):
    async def notify(self, method, params, opts=None):
        raise RuntimeError("stream gone")


@pytest.fixture
def capturing():
    restore = hmr_server._capture_connections()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        restore()
        hmr_server._live_connections.clear()


def test_a_connection_built_while_capturing_is_recorded(capturing):
    connection = Connection.for_loop(_RecordingOutbound())
    assert connection in hmr_server._live_connections


def test_a_connection_built_after_capture_stops_is_not_recorded():
    hmr_server._capture_connections()()
    connection = Connection.for_loop(_RecordingOutbound())
    assert connection not in hmr_server._live_connections


def test_a_reload_tells_each_live_connection_every_list_may_have_changed(capturing):
    outbound = _RecordingOutbound()
    connection = Connection.for_loop(outbound)  # held, so the weak set keeps it
    asyncio.run(hmr_server._notify_list_changed())
    assert connection in hmr_server._live_connections
    assert outbound.sent == ["notifications/tools/list_changed",
                             "notifications/resources/list_changed",
                             "notifications/prompts/list_changed"]


def test_one_broken_connection_does_not_stop_the_others_hearing_of_a_reload(capturing):
    # A client that vanished mid-reload must not cost every other client its refresh.
    broken, healthy = _BrokenOutbound(), _RecordingOutbound()
    connections = [Connection.for_loop(broken), Connection.for_loop(healthy)]
    asyncio.run(hmr_server._notify_list_changed())
    assert len(connections) == 2
    assert healthy.sent == ["notifications/tools/list_changed",
                            "notifications/resources/list_changed",
                            "notifications/prompts/list_changed"]

# --- MCP connection capture ------------------------------------------------------------
# So we can push tools/list_changed to live clients on reload, every Connection the SDK builds is
# recorded. A Connection is the per-client object that outlives its requests; one with no
# standalone stream has nowhere to deliver a notification, and the SDK drops it there.
_live_connections: WeakSet[Connection] = WeakSet()


def _capture_connections() -> Callable[[], None]:
    """Record every Connection the SDK builds from now on; return the function that stops it."""
    original_init = Connection.__init__

    def capture_init(self: Connection, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        original_init(self, *args, **kwargs)
        _live_connections.add(self)

    Connection.__init__ = capture_init

    def restore() -> None:
        Connection.__init__ = original_init

    return restore


async def _notify_list_changed() -> None:
    """Tell every live client connection its tool, resource and prompt lists may have changed."""
    for connection in list(_live_connections):
        for send in (
            connection.send_tool_list_changed,
            connection.send_resource_list_changed,
            connection.send_prompt_list_changed,
        ):
            with suppress(Exception):
                await send()

import asyncio
import pathlib
import sys

from fastmcp import Client
from fastmcp.client.messages import MessageHandler

URL, TOUCH = sys.argv[1], pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2])


class Listen(MessageHandler):
    def __init__(self):
        self.changed = asyncio.Event()

    async def on_tool_list_changed(self, message):
        self.changed.set()


async def main():
    handler = Listen()
    async with Client(URL, message_handler=handler, mode="legacy") as client:
        await client.call_tool("listWorkspaces", {})
        TOUCH.touch()
        await asyncio.wait_for(handler.changed.wait(), timeout=20)
        print("list_changed received")
        result = await client.call_tool("listWorkspaces", {})
        print("tool call after reload ok:", result.is_error is False)


asyncio.run(main())

overview.body: Moves every direct dependency to its current release, with FastMCP 3.4.4 -> 4.1.6 (MCP SDK 1.28 -> 2.3) as the headline, and adapts the one subsystem the move actually breaks: the HMR dev server's notification to connected MCP clients after a reload. It covers the pyproject.toml floors and uv.lock, one snake_case field rename in src/server.py, the rewrite of src/hmr_server.py's session capture onto the SDK 2.x `Connection`, and contract tests that pin the internals hmr_server relies on. It deliberately leaves out adopting any new v4 feature (the sessionless protocol era, background tasks, caching, request state), the redundant `docs` dependency group, and any change to session timeouts or transport settings.

body.text: HMR dev server (src/hmr_server.py)

This is all effectful shell; there is no new rule to separate onto a pure side. The mount swap keeps its mechanism, which still holds on v4: `FastMCP` subclasses `AggregateProvider`, `providers` is a plain list, and a namespace-less `mount()` appends exactly one `FastMCPProvider`. It moves from a closure inside `build_dev_app` to a module-level helper so the tests can call it directly.

Handshake sessions build it through `Connection.for_loop` and modern requests through `Connection.from_envelope`; both run `Connection.__init__`. Its `send_*_list_changed` methods notify on the connection's standalone stream.

body.text: Removed: `_active_sessions`, `_pending_session_patches`, `_patch_session_init`, the `_original_run` / `_run_with_session_capture` wrap of `base_app._mcp_server.run`, the `from mcp.server.session import ServerSession` import, and the `mount_mcp` and `notify_sessions` closures. `serve_mcp` calls `_mount(base_app, mcp)` and `_notify_list_changed()` in their place, with unchanged order and locking.

Lifecycle: `reloader_lifespan` calls `restore_connection_init = _capture_connections()` as its first statement, before the first mount. Its `finally` calls `restore_connection_init()` after the existing teardown, so `Connection.__init__` is the SDK's own again once the dev server stops. Only the dev server installs the capture; the stdio path and the test suites that import src.server never touch `Connection`.

Error paths. A connection without a standalone channel (a 2026-07-28 request over HTTP, or a stateless one) drops the notification inside the SDK with a debug log, so sending to it is a harmless no-op. A closed stream is swallowed by `Connection.notify`. Any other exception from one connection is suppressed, so the remaining connections are still notified, as today. A connection whose session has ended is collected and leaves the WeakSet on its own.

Comments: the module docstring's brittleness note names the v4 internals: `base_app.providers` for mount/unmount and `Connection.__init__` for connection capture. The 'a fastmcp 3.4.x internal' wording on the mount comment goes, since the comment now sits on `_mount`.
Behaviour that changes with the upgrade

These are not code changes, and they are stated so nobody mistakes them for regressions. (1) A reload notification reaches clients speaking a handshake-era protocol (2025-xx) with an open standalone stream. A client on the sessionless 2026-07-28 era over HTTP has no channel to receive it, and picks up the new tools on its next tools/list. (2) A stateful HTTP session idle for 30 minutes (the SDK default) expires, and the client re-initializes.
Tests (tests/test_hmr_server.py)

Three contract tests exercise the real helpers without uvicorn, so the next framework upgrade that moves these internals fails in pytest. A fixture restores `Connection.__init__` and clears `_live_connections` around each test. (1) `_mount`: a child FastMCP with one tool is listed by `await base.list_tools()` after `_mount(base, child)`, and is no longer listed after the returned unmount is called. (2) `_capture_connections`: a `Connection.for_loop(outbound)` built while capture is active is in `_live_connections`; one built after `restore()` is not. (3) `_notify_list_changed`: a captured connection whose outbound records `notify(method, params, opts)` calls receives exactly `notifications/tools/list_changed`, `notifications/resources/list_changed` and `notifications/prompts/list_changed`. The module docstring changes from 'only the reporting is covered' to name these contract tests too.

All direct dependencies (main and dev) go to latest via `uv lock --upgrade`, with floors raised to match. Rejected: only fastmcp plus what it forces. The ask says 'library versions, including FastMCP', which reads as all of them, and one re-lock is cheaper than a second upgrade pass later. Rejected: leaving floors at the old values. That breaks the floor-equals-lock convention the file already follows, and would let a fresh resolve land on fastmcp 3.

Wrap `Connection.__init__` for the dev server's lifetime and notify through `Connection.send_*_list_changed`. Rejected: keep wrapping `_mcp_server.run`. On SDK 2.x the HTTP session manager calls `serve_loop`, not `Server.run()`, so the wrap is dead code. Rejected: a fastmcp middleware on the proxy reading `ctx.request_context.session._connection`. That is just as private, and only sees a connection after its first routed request. Rejected: dropping the notification. Handshake-era clients would keep a stale tool list after every reload, breaking the architecture invariant that sessions survive reloads and are told about them.

Add three contract tests that call the real helpers, and lift `_mount` and `_notify_list_changed` to module level so they can. Rejected: keep testing the reload machinery only by hand. That is how the SDK 2.x breakage would have shipped unnoticed: nothing errors, the notification just stops. Rejected: a full dev-server integration test. It needs uvicorn, a file watcher and a real edit, which is the cost the existing suite deliberately avoided.
Leave the `docs` dependency group as found. Rejected: deleting it in passing. It is unrelated to the upgrade, and build guidance says to raise such things rather than fix them along the way.

Keep fastmcp 4's default idle timeout (`"auto"`, 1800 s in the SDK). Rejected: passing `session_idle_timeout=None` to `http_app`. It is configuration nobody asked for, and an expired session is transparently re-initialized by a conforming client. It is recorded under 'Behaviour that changes with the upgrade' instead.

simple-change:mw6yyp6d-b9b66e.title: Single backticks for inline code in Python docstrings and comments, and backticked symbol names back in hmr_server.py

change.component: Inline-code markup in Python docstrings and comments (text only, across the tracked .py files; no executable code changes)

summary.body: Today, at main 271866c, 113 inline-code spans in the docstrings and comments of 11 tracked Python files use RST-style double backticks (``x``) while the other 782 use single backticks, and the module and `_LoggingErrorFilter` docstrings of src/hmr_server.py name symbols with no backticks at all, because #52 (6906114) stripped the double backticks there instead of converting them. After the change every one of those spans uses single backticks (`x`), and the names in that hmr_server.py text that resolve to Python symbols are wrapped in single backticks again.

motivation.body:
The user asked: "Fix all double backticks to single backticks and add back hmr_server.py backticks around resolvable symbol names." It follows an overview of the codebase showing that double backticks are a minority style, 113 of 895 inline-code spans (about 13%), concentrated in a few RST-style module docstrings led by src/testtypes.py, src/docsgen.py and scripts/validate_workspace.py. sphinx-autodoc2 renders these docstrings as MyST, where both forms become the same code span, so the doubles only cost consistency with the single-backtick house style. #52 was the only commit that removed backticks this way, and it left hmr_server.py naming symbols as bare words, unlike the rest of the codebase.

One risk is worth stating while nothing is built: a docstring read at runtime (a FastMCP tool description taken from __doc__, for example) would change text a client sees, so the change must confirm none of the affected docstrings are read that way. Backticks inside ordinary string literals, such as Markdown that docsgen emits, are program output and out of scope.

criteria.text: A scan of every git-tracked .py file finds 0 double-backtick inline-code spans (``x``, not part of a ``` fence) in docstrings and comments. At 271866c the same scan finds 113 (112 in docstrings, 1 in a comment) across 11 files.

Apart from the src/render.py docstring in the criterion below, the change only adds or removes backtick characters: every other changed file, with all backtick characters deleted, is byte-identical before and after.

Backticks outside docstrings and comments are untouched, so program output such as the Markdown src/docsgen.py emits is unchanged: in every file, the number of backtick characters outside docstrings and comments is the same before and after.

In the src/hmr_server.py module docstring and the `_LoggingErrorFilter` docstring, these names are wrapped in single backticks: src.server, base_app, src.server.mcp, src.server.app, ws_reloader.refresh, reactivity.hmr, base_app.providers, FastMCPProvider, mcp.server.connection.Connection, src.cleanup and sys.excepthook. Text that does not resolve to a Python symbol stays bare: tools/list_changed, /ws/reloader, uvicorn-hmr, mcp-hmr, hmr (a distribution name; `import hmr` fails) and main.py.

The `_checkbox` docstring in src/render.py writes its literal checkbox markers as single-quoted strings, '[x] ', '[ ] ' and '', instead of backtick spans, because they are text values rather than symbols or names (the user asked for this when the empty `` marker turned up). The function's code is unchanged.
`uv run pytest --testmon` passes, and a full docsite build (scripts/gen_page_type_docs.py, then `sphinx-build -a docsite -b html`) finishes with 0 warnings.
