Costs: no cheap workspace-wide time query, uneven retention (a busy page forgets faster than a quiet one), a new field on every page in every workspace file, and the awkwardness of drawing a visualisation inside a view whose body is produced by the Markdown renderer - which pushes toward duplicating the tree's own rendering just to add chrome.
items.fit: Serves the per-page story and the click-through well and is the least invasive to the write path, but it is the weakest on the person's stated why: a workspace-wide 'impressive activity' showpiece is exactly the query this shape makes awkward, and the tree view is the wrong canvas for a scrubber. The read-only correction did not change that - it is recorded here, not recommended, and would make a decent secondary surface (a page's own history) once the whole-workspace showpiece exists.
items.predicts: If right: the tree view shows a workspace's recent status activity - including a status set from the page-actions dropdown and a page archived from the page-actions row - with no new route and no measurable change in write cost, and a scrubber over the merged per-page arrays reproduces each page's earlier status.
items.falsifier: Wrong if assembling the workspace view requires a page walk that is visibly slow on a large workspace, or if the Markdown tree body cannot carry the band without forking the renderer (at which point the 'cheapest' claim is false), or if the per-page cap makes the workspace band visibly lossy for busy pages while quiet pages keep old entries - and, for this epic, wrong if a workspace-wide scrubber cannot be made to feel like a showpiece on that canvas.

items.name: Full event sourcing: make the event log the source of truth and derive page state by replay
items.reason: Works against the why and the code. src/store.py's whole design is copy -> edit -> atomic replace of current state, every read parses that state directly, and the architecture page makes 'every write is copy -> edit -> atomic overwrite under a per-workspace lock' an invariant. Replaying instead would rewrite the read path for every tool, make renderPage/search/nextActions depend on a fold over history, and buy nothing the epic asked for - the epic wants history BESIDE current state (a timeline), not state derived FROM history. Fowler's own framing names the cost (owning storage, retention and replay) that this epic does not need to pay.

items.name: Derive the timeline from git: commit the workspace data dir and read git log
items.reason: The data dir is gitignored by design (.gitignore: '.pasta-data/'), the workspace file is rewritten whole on every write so a diff is unreadable, and the server has no repository relationship to the data it serves. Making it work would mean versioning runtime data, which is a change to how Pasta is deployed, not a feature of the timeline - and it would still only see commits, not the writes between them.

items.name: Reuse src/event_cache.py as the event store (in-process, TTL) and read it live
items.reason: Ruled out by the code's own semantics: the cache stores nothing on disk, treats a missing entry as harmless, expires entries by TTL and is explicitly documented as losing an entry costing only a repeated delivery. A timeline needs durable, ordered, timestamped history; using the cache would show an activity feed that empties on restart and on a hot reload of that module, which is the opposite of 'play it back on demand'. It stays the guidance cache, and the new record must not retype it.

items.name: Render the timeline as a Markdown page (a table or bullet list of changes) through the existing renderers
items.reason: Cheapest of all, and it fails the why outright: a Markdown list is not interactive, has no playback, no scrubbing and no speed, and it would be a second renderer contract to keep in step with the structured HTML one. The epic's person-stated goal is a clean, impressive, interactive showpiece; a text log is the firehose anti-goal wearing a table.

items.name: Backfill pre-tracking activity by diffing the prune-time backups under .pasta-data/backups/
items.reason: Considered for the epic's open backfill question and dropped as a source of truth: backups are written at most hourly and only on a pass that prunes, each is a whole-workspace snapshot, so a diff yields a handful of instants in which many unrelated changes collapse into one 'moment' and everything between them is invisible. It would put fabricated timestamps on the timeline, which is worse than an empty history on day one. What it CAN honestly support is the single synthetic 'workspace created / pages already here' baseline entry described under Questions.

items.text: Should activity from before tracking ships be backfilled onto the timeline, given that the store keeps no per-page history?
items.why: Only the person can accept or reject synthetic history. Facts found: Page has no created_at/updated_at and no revisions; the single workspace JSON is rewritten whole on every write and is gitignored, so git holds no page history; the only historical artefacts are prune-time backups under .pasta-data/backups/, written at most hourly and only when the cleanup sweep deletes something; status_revision_token records that a status moved, not when or to what. So a backfill can only be (a) one synthetic baseline entry per existing page stamped with workspace.updated_at - a fabricated instant, cheap to compute (one pass over the page map, no diffing), or (b) change points reconstructed by diffing successive backups - also cheap (a handful of full snapshots), but it collapses every change between two sweeps into one moment, carries only the backup stamps, and shows nothing between them.
items.changes: If yes, the chosen approach needs one extra write-time step: on the first load after the feature ships, seed the log with the baseline entry (and optionally the backup-derived points) and mark the workspace as seeded so it happens once. If no, the timeline starts empty and shows 'no activity recorded yet' - the simpler path, and the one that never puts a false instant on screen.

items.text: Should a timeline entry say WHO made the change - a person clicking in the web UI or an agent over MCP?
items.why: The code has no actor identity and now demonstrably has two writers. There is no user, session or agent id on a Page or in a write (src/model.py:21-42), and a change can arrive from an MCP tool or from one of the five POST admin routes in src/server.py (archive :240, unarchive :249, schedule-delete :262, unschedule-delete :271, status :284), which are a person's clicks. So 'who' means inventing an identity and threading it from two different callers into the store transactions. The epic's outcomes do not mention it, but a 'productivity of the workspace' reading might want it - and without it a human admin override looks identical to an agent's FSM transition.
items.changes: If yes, all three approaches gain a field on the event and a source on the store transaction (the MCP tool passes a session/agent id; the POST routes pass a person/constant), plus a way to show it in the timeline's lanes or dot style. If no, the timeline says what changed and when but not by whom, and an admin status override is indistinguishable from a modelled transition - which the record should then at least mark as 'admin' vs 'fsm' since set_page_status bypasses the FSM.

items.text: Do element-level marks count as timeline activity - a plan step marked done, a test case passed, a question answered?
items.why: Element FSMs are a far higher-frequency class than page transitions: every implementation-plan step, testing-plan case and question is an element with its own status (src/pagetypes, element_fsm). mutate_page_batch already sees them - an element transition goes through the same batch - but recording each one multiplies the event volume by roughly the number of elements per page, which is the most direct route to the firehose anti-goal. The compensating fact is that element marks are also the best evidence of 'productivity' the workspace has.
items.changes: If yes, every approach needs a per-kind filter on by default and its retention cap tuned for the higher volume, and the recording must distinguish an element's transition (which command, which element id) from the page's own. If no, the timeline records page-level activity only, the volume stays low, and the firehose anti-goal is answered by lanes and kind filters alone rather than also by a cap on a much larger stream.

digest.body:
Ask: an interactive, whole-workspace timeline in the web UI, fed by events the page actions emit in the same commit as the change, with status transitions as the main activity, played back with start/pause/scrub/speed, each entry naming page, kind and time and opening the page. No slower or newly-failing writes; no firehose.

Shaping facts: Pasta has no history at all - no per-page timestamps, no revisions, one whole-file atomic replace per write, and .pasta-data is gitignored, so nothing backfills truthfully. Writes do not arrive only through MCP tools: src/server.py has five POST admin routes (archive, unarchive, schedule-delete, unschedule-delete, status) that mutate through the store, so record at the store transactions. _touch_and_save has 12 call sites; create_workspace and write_backup call _write_file directly. No JS build step.

1. Bounded event log inside the workspace file + hand-built canvas timeline with a scrubber - RECOMMENDED: same commit, no dependency, covers both surfaces, owns the wow-factor.
2. Sidecar events file + vendored vis-timeline: polished, but breaks atomicity and adds a write failure mode across thirteen entry points.
3. Per-page history merged in the tree view: least invasive, weakest workspace story.

3 questions wait (backfill, actor, element marks).

inlines.text: Why (the person's words):

"The timeline is primarily a wow-factor, so it should be very clean and impressive and be interactive. It should collect lots of activity in the form of status transitions and play it back on demand. We want to show the timeline for the whole workspace to show impressive activity and productivity of the workspace."
This page stands on its own: everything below is copied from the epic's framing, and each item keeps the mark it was given there -
person
when the person said it,
proposal
when an agent proposed it.
Goals

items.text: The web UI shows an interactive timeline of the changes made to a workspace. (person)
Changes are tracked as new events emitted by the page actions themselves, rather than inferred after the fact. (person)

Every page action that changes a page (create, field/section edit, status transition, rename, reparent, archive/unarchive, link) records an event in the same commit as the change, so the timeline neither misses a change nor shows one that did not happen. (proposal)
Each timeline entry says which page changed, what kind of change it was, and when, and opens that page from the entry. (proposal)
Playback can be started, paused, scrubbed and sped up, and stopping on any moment shows what changed then - without reloading the whole history. (proposal)
The timeline is a wow-factor showpiece: very clean, impressive and interactive. (person)
The timeline collects lots of activity in the form of status transitions and plays it back on demand. (person)
The timeline covers the whole workspace, so it shows the workspace's activity and productivity at a glance. (person)
The timeline opens with one clearly labelled 'tracking began' marker showing the pages that already existed and their status at that moment; it never shows a fabricated earlier change. (person)

Each timeline entry shows whether the change came from an agent (MCP) or a person (web UI), as visibly distinct marks with a filter for each; no individual agent or user identity is recorded. (person)

Element-level marks (plan step done, test case passed, question answered) are recorded and shown as a secondary layer: small pulses on their page's lane that merge into a counted cluster when dense, on by default with a filter to hide them, while page status transitions stay the primary marks. (person)

inlines.text: Non-goal

items.text: Undoing, reverting or restoring a page to an earlier point from the timeline. (proposal)

inlines.text: Anti-goals

items.text: Recording events makes page actions noticeably slower, or gives a valid page action a new way to fail. (proposal)
On a busy workspace the timeline becomes an unreadable firehose of small edits in which a person cannot find what actually changed. (proposal)

inlines.text: The person's answers this design must carry

items.text: No backfill: the timeline opens with one clearly labelled 'tracking began' marker showing the pages that already existed and their status at that moment; real activity fills in from there. No fabricated history.

Each event records only which surface it came through - agent (MCP tool) or person (web UI POST route) - with no per-agent or per-session identity; the two are shown distinctly with a filter for each.

Element-level marks are their own kind of event, distinct from page status transitions, shown as a secondary layer: small pulses that merge into a counted cluster when dense, on by default with a filter to hide them. Retention is sized for the higher volume.

Approach 1: bounded event log inside the workspace file, recorded at the store transactions, shown on a new hand-built canvas timeline with lanes, play/pause/scrub/speed and click-through, live-updated without a full tab reload. Accepted fallback: swap the display for a vendored vis-timeline while keeping this recording scheme.

approach.chosen:
Approach 1, picked by the person on the epic (research approach mwb0bb0a-f0631b), grown into what will be built.

RECORDING. A new pure module src/eventlog.py defines one event record (at, kind, pageId, pageType, title, actor, from, to, event, section, field, elementId) and a bounded append. Events live in the workspace file itself: Workspace gains events: list[dict] (the bounded log) and tracking_began: dict | None (the one-time baseline snapshot, kept outside the log so trimming can never erase it). Both are carried by src/serialize.py with backward-compatible defaults. Events are built at the store transactions - the layer the MCP tools AND the five web UI POST routes both enter - never inside a route or a tool, and never inside _touch_and_save (which does not know what changed). One small new store helper, a _transaction(workspace_id, *, actor) context manager, replaces the repeated lock -> load -> mutate -> _touch_and_save preamble of the twelve mutating transactions and gives recording a single choke point; it persists tracking_began once, and create_workspace keeps its own lock while seeding the same baseline before its single _write_file. Each transaction appends its events to the working workspace in memory before that one save, so the commit stays exactly one atomic whole-file os.replace and the write path gains no new failure mode. Actor is a keyword the store method receives from its caller: 'agent' from an MCP tool, 'person' from a POST route - no identity beyond that. Element marks are recorded only when a batch fires an element-FSM event (plan step done, case passed, question answered), as their own kind, distinct from page status transitions.

BASELINE. The timeline always opens with one 'tracking began' marker. The first write after this ships persists tracking_began; until then the read route derives the same value in memory from the workspace state it already loaded, so an untouched workspace still opens on a labelled marker and a GET never writes.

DISPLAY. A new full-screen route GET /ws:{workspaceIdPart}/timeline renders src/templates/timeline.html (extends _base.html, no sidebar) with the whole timeline embedded as JSON, plus GET /ws:{workspaceIdPart}/timeline.json for live refreshes. src/static/timeline.js draws a hand-built canvas swimlane chart: a horizontal time axis, one lane per page type, a primary row of status transitions (filled mark = agent, hollow = person) and a secondary row of element pulses that merge into a counted cluster when dense. Playback is a playhead advanced with requestAnimationFrame, with play/pause, four speed presets, a scrub slider and drag-scrubbing on the canvas; clicking a mark opens its page. Filters for actor and kind, and an on-by-default element-mark toggle, are client-side over the embedded array.

LIVE. timeline.html overrides _base.html's reloader block so the page opens its own /ws/reloader socket: a {refresh: 1} message triggers a fetch of timeline.json and an in-place merge instead of location.reload, so a mid-playback scrubber is never destroyed by the next agent write. A {refresh: 0} heartbeat is used the same way, debounced, as a cheap fallback.

AESTHETICS are part of the design, not an afterthought: lane labels and axis in muted text, marks sized by kind, transitions animated in on the playhead, and every colour taken from the water.css custom properties of the active theme, read at draw time, with a theme-change event triggering a repaint so light and dark both work even while playback is paused.

alternatives.name: Sidecar append-only event file per workspace, rendered with a vendored vis-timeline (research approach 2)
alternatives.tradeoff: Unchanged read cost and no migration, a mature interactive timeline for very little front-end code, and a corrupt event file cannot take the wiki down - but every write touches a SECOND file, so either a crash loses an event (breaking 'same commit') or leaves a phantom one, and it adds a new failure mode to thirteen entry points, five of which are a person's button clicks. Plus a large hand-maintained vendored asset in a repo with no build step.
alternatives.whyNot: The person chose approach 1. It loses on the outcome that events land in the same commit as the change, and on the anti-goal about a valid action gaining a new way to fail - the risk the research found is worse, not better, because the web UI has five mutating POST routes to wire a second file into.

alternatives.name: Per-page bounded history stamped on the page, played back inside the workspace tree view (research approach 3)
alternatives.tradeoff: Minimal new surface and no new route or dependency, history travelling with the page it describes - but no cheap workspace-wide time query, uneven retention (a busy page forgets faster), a new field on every page, and a visualisation forced into a view whose body is produced by the Markdown renderer.
alternatives.whyNot: It is the weakest on the person's stated why: a whole-workspace activity showpiece is exactly the query this shape makes awkward, and the tree view is the wrong canvas for a scrubber. Kept in mind as a possible future per-page surface, not this epic.

alternatives.name: Display fallback: keep this recording scheme, swap the hand-built canvas for a vendored vis-timeline
alternatives.tradeoff: Buys the hard axis/zoom/drag maths for free and is far less front-end code; costs a large vendored asset maintained by hand and a library look that is harder to make bespoke.
alternatives.whyNot: Not designed - recorded only as the accepted fallback the person signed off with the pick, to be taken if hand-drawing the canvas proves too costly. The recording scheme, payload and routes stay identical, so the swap touches only src/static/timeline.js and its styles.

inlines.text: Part 1 - Event model and retention

One event is a flat, JSON-able dict with a fixed key set. Every mutating store transaction appends zero or more of them to the workspace it is already about to write. Nothing else creates events: there is no inference pass, no scan of old state, and no second file.

element.mark - an element FSM fired inside a batch (plan step done, test case passed, question answered). Carries section, field, elementId, event, from, to. Secondary layer.
page.created, page.renamed, page.reparented, page.reordered - structural page facts (from/to carry the old value where there is one).
page.field - an authoring write landed on a page without changing its status (one event per batch, naming the section.field of the first setter, never one per block).

page.link_added, page.link_removed - from/to are the endpoint page ids and role.
workspace.created, workspace.status.

Part 1b - The 'tracking began' marker is always there, and a GET never writes

The outcome is unconditional: the timeline always opens with exactly one clearly labelled 'tracking began' marker showing the pages that already existed and their status. The design therefore never depends on a write having happened first. One pure function,

A derived marker is not fabricated history, which is why this meets the person's decision rather than bending it.

It carries no per-page timestamp and claims no change happened. For an untouched workspace the only truthful timeline begins 'tracking began now, with these N pages at these statuses', and real activity fills in from the next write; inventing a midpoint or an ordering between pre-existing pages is exactly what the design must never do. Once a workspace is written, the persisted

Exactly one marker, always, and only the server draws it. The write path stamps

Part 2 - Recording at the store transactions

body.source:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@dataclass
class Tx:
    """One transaction's handle: the working workspace, the actor, one timestamp."""
    workspace: Workspace
    actor: str
    at: str

@contextmanager
def _transaction(self, workspace_id: str, *, actor: str = "agent") -> Iterator[Tx]:
    """Lock, load, hand the caller the workspace to mutate, then seed and save once."""
    if actor not in ("agent", "person"):
        raise ValidationError(f"Unknown actor {actor!r}; expected 'agent' or 'person'.")
    with self._transaction_lock_for(workspace_id):
        workspace = self.load_workspace(workspace_id)   # NotFoundError exactly as today
        tx = Tx(workspace=workspace, actor=actor, at=_now())
        yield tx                                       # caller mutates, appends its events
        # Only reached when the body raised nothing: an aborted transaction
        # writes nothing, so it records nothing and seeds nothing.
        if workspace.tracking_began is None:
            workspace.tracking_began = eventlog.baseline(workspace, at=tx.at)
        self._touch_and_save(workspace)                 # the one write, unchanged

inlines.text: Part 4 - The canvas view and playback

src/static/timeline.js is plain JavaScript, no build step, loaded by timeline.html. It draws into a single canvas sized to the container with devicePixelRatio scaling and redrawn on resize. There is no chart library and no DOM node per mark, so a whole workspace of activity fits one draw-call budget.

items.text: Layout, top to bottom: a header strip (workspace name, counts, filter chips, transport controls); a time axis with calendar-aware ticks; one lane per page type, ordered by event count, labelled in the left gutter; inside each lane a primary row of status transitions and a secondary row of element pulses.

Marks: a status transition is a filled circle for actor agent and a hollow ring for actor person, coloured by the target status's semantic family; structural events are small squares; the baseline is a full-height dashed rule at time zero with a label and the baseline page count.

Element pulses are 4 px dots on the lane's lower row, on by default; when pulses fall within 6 px of each other they merge into one counted cluster bubble ('6 steps done'), which is the anti-firehose control.
Filters, client-side over the in-memory arrays: actor (All / Agent / Person), element marks on-off, and a status-family chip row. Filter state lives in the URL hash so a refresh keeps it.

Playback: the domain is [trackingBegan.at or first event, last event]; a playhead advances with requestAnimationFrame at 1x, 4x, 16x or 64x, where 1x replays the whole span in 45 s. Play/pause button, space bar, a scrub slider, and direct drag on the canvas to scrub. Marks are revealed as the playhead passes them and animate in; prefers-reduced-motion draws them without animation. A live readout shows the playhead instant and the count of events revealed.

Interaction: hovering a mark or cluster shows a tooltip (page title, kind, from -> to, relative time); clicking it navigates to the existing page route, /ws:{workspaceIdPart}/page/{pageId}, whose path segment after 'ws:' matches src/server.py:200-203.

Theme: every colour is read at draw time from the water.css custom properties the light and dark sheets declare on :root (--background, --text-muted, --links, --border, --code). One repaint() is the only draw entry point, called by the playback loop and by a theme-change hook, so a paused chart still repaints in the new theme. src/templates/_theme.js today only swaps the stylesheet href and the body light/dark class and tells nobody, so this design adds two lines there: after those swaps it dispatches a themechange CustomEvent on document, and timeline.js listens and calls repaint(). No other page changes behaviour.

Styling lives in a new block of src/static/styles.css scoped under .timeline, the body class timeline.html sets through _base.html's bodyclass block. It is not scoped under .pasta-page: that scope belongs to the structured page render (src/static/styles.css:38-41) and the full-screen timeline has no .pasta-page container, so a rule written there would match nothing.

inlines.text: Part 5 - Live updates over the /ws/reloader socket

Today src/templates/_reloader.js turns every data change into location.reload(true), which would destroy a mid-playback scrubber. The timeline therefore needs its own socket behaviour, and _base.html must let a page replace the reloader script: its inline include becomes a Jinja block that timeline.html overrides. No other template changes behaviour.
The timeline's socket handler keeps the loading and theme scripts untouched and changes only the message handling:

items.text: {refresh: 1} (a mutation or a source change) - debounce 150 ms, then GET /ws:{id}/timeline.json and merge in place: new events appended to the arrays, the page map refreshed, the domain extended. Playhead time, play/pause state, filters and scroll position are preserved. Nothing reloads.
{refresh: 0} (the existing 5 s heartbeat) - same fetch, but only when the tab is visible and at most once every 5 s; a cheap fallback if a refresh message is missed.
Socket close - reconnect after 1 s and do one full merge on reconnect, so a server restart does not leave a stale chart.

inlines.text: Part 6 - How the existing architecture documentation is reconciled
Two pasta architecture pages go stale the moment this ships and are updated in the same change as the code, not after it.

items.text: architecture:mrw6s6q6-fb2ff5 'Web UI, HMR & live reload' - its invariant that the web UI is strictly read-only ('state changes only ever through the MCP command path') is already false at this commit: five POST routes mutate through the store. The change corrects that, adds the timeline routes to the route inventory, and documents that a page may now replace the reloader script through a Jinja block, while the two-renderer rule and the styling scope rule stay unchanged.

architecture:mrtqsspj-0a2ae4 'Authoring & mutation' - 'every write is copy -> edit -> atomic overwrite' and 'a batch is all-or-nothing' gain their event clause: a mutating transaction appends its events into the same working copy before the same single write, so an event can neither exist without its change nor a change without its event, and an aborted batch records nothing. Also documents the tracking-began seeding and the two retention caps.

architecture:mrtjuul6-5221b2 'Page types & FSM implementation' - unchanged in substance: no new command kind and no new field kind are introduced, so docs/designing-page-types.md and .claude/skills/pasta-workflow-creation/SKILL.md stay untouched. The only addition is a note that an element-FSM transition is also an observable timeline event.

inlines.text: Where pure logic ends and effects begin

src/eventlog.py is pure: it takes already-known facts plus a timestamp string and returns dicts, plus the trim and baseline helpers; it imports nothing from the package and touches no disk. src/store.py stays the only place that decides when an event is recorded and the only place that writes it, and it takes the clock from the existing
. The routes only read. The template and the JavaScript only render. src/commands.py is not modified at all - the pure command core keeps knowing nothing about time, storage or the timeline.

items.decision: Build on a bounded event log stored inside the workspace file, recorded at the store transactions in the same atomic write as each change, and shown on a new hand-built canvas timeline.
items.alternatives: (2) A sidecar append-only events file per workspace rendered with a vendored vis-timeline; (3) per-page bounded history played back inside the existing tree view.
items.reason: The person chose approach 1 on the epic. It is the only one where an event and its change cannot diverge, it needs no new dependency, and hooking the store transactions covers the MCP tools and the five web UI POST routes with one hook.

items.decision: Open the timeline with a single clearly labelled 'tracking began' baseline and never fabricate history.
items.alternatives: Backfill a synthetic entry per existing page stamped with workspace.updated_at; reconstruct change points by diffing the prune-time backups under .pasta-data/backups/.
items.reason: The person answered the backfill question with 'yes, use the tracking began marker': no fabricated history, no invented per-page timestamps. The store keeps nothing truthful to reconstruct from - no per-page timestamps, no revisions, and the data dir is gitignored.

items.decision: Record only the surface a change came through - agent (MCP tool) or person (web UI POST route) - and show the two as visibly distinct marks with a filter for each.
items.alternatives: Thread a real per-agent or per-session identity from the MCP session into every write; record who only for the admin status override.
items.reason: The person answered 'agent vs person only, as you proposed'. No identity exists anywhere in the store, and inventing one would price a feature nobody asked for into every write.

items.decision: Record element-level marks as their own event kind and show them as a secondary layer of small pulses that merge into a counted cluster when dense, on by default with a filter to hide them.
items.alternatives: Record page-level events only and answer the firehose anti-goal with lanes and kind filters alone; show every element mark as a full-size mark.
items.reason: The person answered 'secondary layer, as you proposed': element marks are their own kind, distinct from status transitions, with clustering for density and retention sized for the higher volume.

items.decision: Keep element marks and ordinary events in two separate bounded ring buffers, trimmed oldest-first at append time.
items.alternatives: One combined log with a single cap; no cap at all and rely on cleanup.
items.reason: Element marks arrive at a far higher rate than status transitions, so a single cap would let them evict the primary marks the person cares about - the exact firehose failure. Cleanup is a page-deletion sweep, not an event-retention window, so retention has to be designed.

items.decision: Keep the tracking-began baseline in its own workspace field outside the ring buffers, and derive the same baseline in memory at read time while the field is still unset.
items.alternatives: Make the baseline the first entry of the event log and let trimming eventually drop it; seed the field from the read route (a GET that writes).
items.reason: The baseline is the timeline's time zero and its label; a busy workspace would trim it away and lose the only honest edge of the chart. Deriving it when unset keeps the marker on a workspace nobody has written since the feature shipped without turning a GET into a hidden write - the reasoning, and why the derived marker is not fabricated history, is set out in the decision 'Guarantee the tracking-began marker without letting a GET write'.

items.decision: Collapse the lock-then-load preamble of the twelve _touch_and_save transactions into one private _transaction context manager that also seeds the baseline and carries the actor.
items.alternatives: Leave the twelve transactions as they are and insert a record call in each, repeating the baseline check everywhere; hook _touch_and_save.
items.reason: The code holds exactly twelve lock+load preambles that end in _touch_and_save (src/store.py:547/560, 578/635, 671/692, 707/730, 756/772, 802/827, 838/853, 865/871, 919/926, 936/945, 949/952, 971/974), plus create_workspace, which takes its own lock and ends in a single _write_file (:215-220) - thirteen mutating entry points in all. _touch_and_save does not know what changed, and twelve hand-inserted calls are twelve places to forget the baseline. One helper gives recording a single choke point without changing the signatures beyond one keyword; create_workspace keeps its own lock and seeds its baseline explicitly before its one write.

items.decision: Detect an element mark inside mutate_page_batch from the same check_specs list the batch already builds - the entry's own CommandSpec plus every CompoundCommand step - by reading each element's status before and after the entry is applied.
items.alternatives: Have the pure command core return the element status change in its CommandResult; add a new hook to commands.apply_command; detect top-level ElementTransitionCommands only and leave a compound's nested steps unrecorded.
items.reason: The pure core is deliberately clock-free and storage-free, and the store already holds the loaded page. mutate_page_batch builds check_specs at src/store.py:610-615 for exactly this purpose, and src/pagetypes/core/commands.py:158 admits an ElementTransitionCommand as a compound step (it rejects only StatusTransitionCommand steps), so a top-level-only scan would silently drop a nested transition. Reusing check_specs records top-level and nested transitions alike with two in-memory list scans, no extra I/O, and src/commands.py untouched.

items.decision: Serve the timeline from two new workspace-level GET routes - a full-screen HTML page and a JSON payload - and read it through one new read-only store method.
items.alternatives: Add the visualisation to the existing tree route's body; extend render_page_html to carry workspace-wide chrome.
items.reason: A workspace-wide view is a GET projection, and the page body renderer's contract is 'this page's sections'. A separate route leaves the Markdown tree and the renderPage contract untouched.

items.decision: Make _base.html's reloader script an overridable Jinja block so the timeline page can replace the reload behaviour without touching any other template.
items.alternatives: Add timeline-specific branching inside _reloader.js; ship a second base template.
items.reason: Every other view must keep its reload-on-change behaviour, and one Jinja block is the smallest edit that lets exactly one page opt out.

items.decision: On the timeline page, react to the reloader socket by fetching and merging the JSON payload in place rather than reloading the tab.
items.alternatives: Accept that playback restarts on every agent write; add a new dedicated websocket that pushes events.
items.reason: Reloading destroys the scrubber mid-play, which the 'play it back on demand' goal cannot survive. Reusing the existing socket with a debounced fetch adds no new channel and no new server state.

items.decision: Keep the JSON payload to events, the baseline and a small page map - never page bodies or section content.
items.alternatives: Send the whole workspace so the chart can show any field; send one event per request while scrubbing.
items.reason: The chart only needs labels, kinds, times and a click-through target. Keeping bodies out bounds the payload and keeps the display from becoming a second content view.

items.decision: Record exactly one page.field event per batch that authored content without moving the page's status.
items.alternatives: Record one event per command in the batch; record nothing for content edits.
items.reason: A batch is one atomic commit and one write, so one event matches what actually landed; one event per command would turn a single authoring action into a burst and feed the firehose.

items.decision: Record nothing for backup writes, workspace guidance configuration, and cleanup's expiry stamping and clearing; record only the pages a cleanup actually prunes.
items.alternatives: Record them as low-priority kinds and filter them out in the client; give expiry stamping and clearing their own page.expiry_stamped / page.expiry_cleared kinds.
items.reason: Backups change nothing a person sees, guidance is configuration, and expiry is scheduling metadata the sweep sets for itself - none of the three is a change to a page's content or lifecycle, and recording them would dilute the workspace's productivity story with events no one asked to see. Pruning a page is the one destructive act in the sweep, so cleanup records page.deleted per pruned page and nothing else, which answers 'no change is missing' for the sweep.

items.decision: Update the two affected architecture pages ('Web UI, HMR & live reload' and 'Authoring & mutation') in the same change as the code.
items.alternatives: Update documentation in a follow-up change; leave the pages alone because they are already partly stale.
items.reason: Both pages carry invariants this change rewrites, and the read-only claim is already false at this commit - leaving it would make the wiki lie about the surface the timeline lives on.

items.decision: Guarantee the 'tracking began' marker by deriving the baseline in memory at read time whenever the persisted field is still unset, and keep persisting it once on the first write; a GET never writes.
items.alternatives: Seed tracking_began from the read route (a GET that writes); show an empty state until the first write; run a startup sweep that seeds every workspace file.
items.reason: The person's outcome is unconditional - the timeline always opens with one labelled marker showing the pages that already existed - so the marker cannot depend on someone having written first. Deriving it is a pure function of state the read route already loaded: it invents no per-page timestamp and no ordering between pre-existing pages, so it is not the fabricated history the person ruled out; the persisted value wins on every later read, so the marker time stops at the real start. Seeding from the route would put a write (and a new write failure) on a GET that must not fail because it was read, and could make a read fail on a full disk - exactly the anti-goal; a startup sweep writes every workspace unasked and still misses the ones created while the server runs.

items.decision: Scope the timeline's new styles under a .timeline body class set by timeline.html through _base.html's bodyclass block, not under .pasta-page.
items.alternatives: Scope them under .pasta-page like the structured page render; scope under #content; put the styles inline in timeline.html.
items.reason: src/static/styles.css:38-41 scopes only the structured page render under .pasta-page, and the full-screen timeline renders no page body, so a rule written there would match nothing and the template author and the JS author would disagree about the hook. A single body class the timeline template itself sets is one agreed hook for both, leaves the structured-render scope untouched, and needs no !important or inline styling.

items.decision: Add a theme-change hook: _theme.js dispatches a themechange CustomEvent on document after it swaps the stylesheet and the body class, and timeline.js listens for it and repaints.
items.alternatives: Rely on the next playback frame or the next resize to redraw (a paused chart keeps the old palette); poll the computed palette on every frame; drop the claim that both themes repaint correctly.
items.reason: Verified in src/templates/_theme.js at 9ada650: the radio change swaps the stylesheet href and the body light/dark class and notifies nothing else, and the water.css custom properties are declared on :root of the swapped sheet, not by the body class. Without a signal a paused canvas keeps the previous theme's colours indefinitely. Two added lines in the file that already owns the swap change no other page's behaviour and let the 'clean in both themes' outcome hold while the playhead is parked.

items.name: Event record (one dict in Workspace.events / Workspace.element_marks)
items.shape:
{
  "at": str,            # UTC ISO-8601, exactly _now() format, e.g. "2026-11-10T19:41:02.113+00:00"
  "kind": str,          # one of: page.created page.status page.field page.renamed page.reparented
                        #         page.reordered page.archived page.unarchived page.delete_scheduled
                        #         page.delete_cancelled page.deleted page.link_added page.link_removed
                        #         element.mark workspace.created workspace.status
  "pageId": str | None,     # None only for workspace.* kinds
  "pageType": str | None,   # the page's type tag; None for workspace.* kinds
  "title": str | None,      # the page title AT EVENT TIME, so a later rename does not rewrite history
  "actor": "agent" | "person",
  "from": str | None,    # page.status: previous status. element.mark: previous element status.
                         # page.renamed: previous title. page.reparented: previous parent id.
                         # page.link_removed: None. Others: None.
  "to": str | None,      # matching new value; page.link_* : the target page id
  "event": str | None,   # the FSM event / command name that fired it, e.g. "markReady", "markStepDone",
                         # "adminOverride"; None for structural kinds with no command
  "section": str | None, # element.mark only: e.g. "steps"
  "field": str | None,   # element.mark only: e.g. "items"; page.field: the authored "section.field"
  "elementId": str | None  # element.mark only
}
Every key is always present (missing facts are null) so the client can key off a fixed shape. No per-agent or per-session identity is ever stored.

         section: str | None = None, field: str | None = None,

    """One event dict with every key of the shape above present."""

def append(events: list[dict[str, Any]], event: dict[str, Any], cap: int) -> bool
    """Append and trim oldest-first to `cap` and to BYTE_BUDGET (rough json length sum).
    Returns True when anything was trimmed - the caller ORs it into the payload's `truncated`.
    Never raises on a well-formed event."""

def baseline(workspace: Workspace, at: str) -> dict[str, Any]
    """{"at": at, "pages": [{"id", "type", "title", "status"} ...]} in workspace.root_page_ids
    depth-first order, archived pages included and flagged by their status only."""

def page_summary(workspace: Workspace) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]
    """{pageId: {"title": str, "type": str, "status": str, "archived": bool}} for every page."""

Pure: imports only from .model, reads no clock (the `at` string is passed in), touches no disk.

questions.question: Where does the 'tracking began' baseline come from for a workspace that has not been written since this ships - does opening GET /ws:{id}/timeline create it (a write triggered by a read), or does the page show an empty state until the first write, and if so what exactly does it show?
questions.why: The person's outcome is that the timeline opens with one labelled 'tracking began' marker showing the pages that already existed. With seeding only inside _transaction on the first write, the very first look after deploy has no marker and no page list at all. The answer changes where the seeding lives (store transaction vs route vs startup sweep) and whether a GET is allowed to write.
questions.resolution: Settled as a proposal decision ('Guarantee the tracking began marker by deriving the baseline in memory at read time...'), so nothing waits on the person. The marker is unconditional and no GET writes: _transaction persists tracking_began once on the first write, create_workspace seeds it at creation, and timeline_payload derives the identical value in memory (eventlog.baseline(workspace, at=_now())) whenever the persisted field is still unset, so a workspace untouched since deploy still opens on one labelled marker listing its pages and statuses. The derived marker invents no timestamp and no ordering, so it is not the fabricated history the person ruled out, and the persisted value wins on every later read. Alternatives rejected in the decision: seeding from the read route (a write, and a new write failure, on a GET - the anti-goal), an empty state until the first write (breaks the stated outcome), and a startup sweep (writes every workspace unasked and misses ones created while the server runs). Signed-off WHAT on the epic is unchanged, so this does not need escalation.

digest.body:
Bounded event log inside the workspace file, appended by the store transactions in the same atomic write as each change, shown on a new full-screen hand-built canvas timeline at GET /ws:{workspaceIdPart}/timeline: lanes per page type, filled vs hollow marks for agent vs person, a secondary layer of element pulses that cluster into counts, play/pause/scrub/speed, click-through, live in-place merge over the existing /ws/reloader socket. The 'tracking began' marker is always there - persisted once on the first write, derived in memory at read time until then, so a GET never writes.

task.body:
You are the research agent for the epic epic:mwav2lhu-f00f56 ("Interactive timeline of workspace changes in the web UI") in pasta workspace ws:mrteq0c5-238cf6. You own its solution-research page, solution-research:mwav2lhv-2ddbe8, and nothing else. Your checkout is read-only for this run: read the code, never edit it.

The ask (the epic's summary): A person viewing a workspace in the web UI can open an interactive timeline of the changes made to it - what changed, on which page, and when - drawn from a new record of events that the page actions themselves emit as they happen. Which timeline view and visualisation serves this best, and how it is built, are for this epic to work out.

Why, in the person's words: "The timeline is primarily a wow-factor, so it should be very clean and impressive and be interactive. It should collect lots of activity in the form of status transitions and play it back on demand. We want to show the timeline for the whole workspace to show impressive activity and productivity of the workspace."

Outcomes: read them on the epic page (Framing > Outcomes) and judge every approach against them. Those marked person were stated by the person; those marked proposal are the controller's and may be challenged. In short: a clean, impressive, interactive whole-workspace timeline; status transitions collected as the main activity and played back on demand (start, pause, scrub, speed); events emitted by the page actions in the same commit as the change; each entry shows page, kind of change and time and opens the page; anti-goals are slower or newly-failing page writes, and an unreadable firehose of small edits.

Answered questions: none yet. One open question sits on the epic: whether activity from before tracking ships should be backfilled. Find out what existing data (stored page history, commit log, revisions, timestamps or anything else the store keeps) could seed a backfill and what it would cost, and record it, so the person can decide with the facts in hand. Put any question only the person can settle on the research page's Questions section, not the epic.

What done looks like: fire begin on the research page (waiting -> investigating), follow its investigating stage guidance and field instructions, fill every section - understanding, components, constraints, conflicts, documentation, prior art, two or three approaches with exactly one recommended (each covering both how events are recorded and how the timeline is shown and played back), dropped approaches, questions, and a digest of at most 200 words written last - then fire submitForJudging. Ground in the pasta workspace's architecture pages first (Documentation toc: e.g. "Authoring & mutation", "Web UI, HMR & live reload", "Page types & FSM implementation", "Self-direction") and then the code. Do not design the solution in detail, and do not run any command on the epic or on any agent-plan page other than this one.

feature-brief:mwb15r2s-dae659.title: getWorkspaceGuidance: read every workspace guidance field in one call

summary.body: Add a read-only `getWorkspaceGuidance(workspaceId)` MCP tool, the counterpart of `setWorkspaceGuidance`, that returns every workspace guidance field in one call. Each field the page-type registry declares comes back with its description and stored text, or null when it is unset. Any stored value for a field no page type declares any longer is returned separately, so it isn't lost from view. Today an agent can write these house rules but sees one back only when it surfaces on a page sitting at the matching status. There is no way to audit what a workspace has configured, or to check the current text before overwriting it. The field list comes from the registry, not a hard-coded set: on origin/main that is groundingTool, mergeProcess and testingTool, and fields added later appear automatically.

items.text: `setWorkspaceGuidance` (L550-563, under the `# --- Workspace guidance configuration` heading) is the only guidance tool: async `@mcp.tool`, body wrapped in `with _guard_tool():` (L351-357, turns PastaError into ToolError), calls STORE.set_workspace_guidance and echoes {workspaceId, field, guidanceConfig: dict(workspace.guidance_config)}. Read tools (L360-472: listWorkspaces, tree, getPage, outline, attention...) follow the same async + _guard_tool shape and return STORE results directly. The new read tool lands here, beside setWorkspaceGuidance. `instructions` (L361-365) passes sorted(workspace_guidance_fields()) to render_instructions.

items.text: `Store.set_workspace_guidance` (L962-975) validates the field against workspace_guidance_fields() then writes guidance_config[field] = text under the transaction lock; an empty string is stored as "" (a clear), never deleted. `Store.load_workspace` (L190-200) is the read path: shared half of the rw lock only. Reads like `attention` (L526-536) are load_workspace + a projection. The module-level pure `workspace_guidance(page_type, status, config)` (L81-91) is the per-page emission: it skips a falsy (absent or "") value and prefixes spec.label. A store read method is needed only to load the workspace; the projection itself can be pure.

Authoring & mutation invariant: next_actions is the single place any guidance key (guidance_<field>) is assembled for a page. The new read reports configuration, not page guidance, so it must not emit guidance_<field> keys or label-prefixed text.

The summary needs correcting to 'every declared field', with no list. When the epic-stage work lands, its fields show up with no change here.

Partial prior art: setWorkspaceGuidance already echoes the raw `guidanceConfig` dict (src/server.py L562-563), including cleared "" entries and any stale keys. describePageType already reports declarations per type (src/describe.py L146-150). The new read must not change the setWorkspaceGuidance echo, which tests/test_workspace_guidance.py L307-308 pins. It should report what neither of these can: every declared field, set or not, workspace-wide.

Stale stored keys: Workspace.guidance_config can hold a key no page type declares any longer, for example data written by a server that declared more fields, sharing a data dir. Nothing prunes these. The read has to decide whether to show them; it must not drop them silently.

workspace_guidance_fields() (src/pagetypes/_registry.py L156-164) keeps only the first declarer's spec, so its guidance_for is not a field's applicability across types. Reporting where a field applies would need a per-type walk of the registry, and the function's representative-spec contract stays as it is.

They touch src/instructions.py, the guidance declarations and the README. Rebasing this branch onto main later may conflict in src/instructions.py's prose and guidance section and in README.md.

Per-field shape: should each entry carry only the stored text, or also the field's description and the page types/statuses it applies to?
items.answer: Each entry is {field, description, text}. The description comes from the field's WorkspaceGuidanceSpec and is the same for every declaring type, so an agent can tell what an unset field is for. Per-type applicability is left out: describePageType already reports guidanceFor per type, and a workspace-wide version would need a new registry walk duplicating it.

items.text: Should stored keys that no page type declares any longer be returned, and if so, how are they kept apart from live fields?
items.answer: Yes. Return them under a separate `undeclared` map {field: text} holding only non-empty values, sorted by key. They stay visible because setWorkspaceGuidance cannot clear them (it rejects an undeclared field), but they are kept out of `fields` so they never read as live guidance. They are not pruned.

items.text: Should a field cleared with "" read the same as a field never set?
items.answer: Yes. Both read as text: null. The setter contract says an empty string clears the field, and emission (store.workspace_guidance) already treats absent and "" alike, so the difference is a storage artefact nobody acts on.

def render_guidance_fields(fields: list[str]) -> str:
    """The '## Workspace guidance setup' section: names setWorkspaceGuidance and getWorkspaceGuidance

    names = ", ".join(f"`{field}`" for field in fields) if fields else "(none)"

        "## Workspace guidance setup\n\n"
        "A workspace can carry per-status house rules, set with "
        "`setWorkspaceGuidance(workspaceId, field, text)` and surfaced on a page while it sits at "
        "the relevant status. `getWorkspaceGuidance(workspaceId)` reads every field back with its "

overview.body: Covers one new read tool, getWorkspaceGuidance(workspaceId). It returns every workspace guidance field the page-type registry declares, each with its description and stored text, plus any stored text left behind for a field no page type declares any longer. It is built as a pure projection in src/store.py, a one-line Store read, a thin MCP tool in src/server.py, and one sentence in the instructions' Workspace guidance setup section, so the tool's schema is advertised. Deliberately left out: any change to setWorkspaceGuidance or its echo, per-page-type applicability (describePageType already reports guidanceFor per type), pruning or clearing undeclared keys, and the web UI.

body.text: Behaviour

getWorkspaceGuidance(workspaceId) loads one workspace and reports its guidance configuration against the registry in play. `fields` lists every declared field (the keys of workspace_guidance_fields()), sorted by field name, each with its spec description and its stored text. The text is null when the field was never set or was cleared with an empty string. `undeclared` maps each stored key that no page type declares to its text, holding non-empty values only, sorted by key, and is {} when there are none. The tool is read-only: it takes only the shared half of the workspace rw lock (via Store.load_workspace), writes nothing, emits no guidance_<field> keys and no labels, and does not refresh the web UI. An archived workspace is read like any other, as with tree and getPage. In test mode the declared fields are the fixtures' (buildTool, draftHint, reviewHint).
Pure projection - src/store.py (module level, beside workspace_guidance)

A function of its two arguments alone, with no I/O and no registry read. Every rule lives here: which fields are listed, their order, null for unset or cleared text, and the split between declared and undeclared keys. Add WorkspaceGuidanceSpec to the existing `from .pagetypes.core.specs import ...` line.
Store read - src/store.py Store, in the '# --- workspace guidance configuration' section before set_workspace_guidance
The effectful shell: load the workspace and pass the live registry's fields and the stored config to the pure projection. It holds no rules of its own.
MCP tool - src/server.py, under '# --- Workspace guidance configuration' before setWorkspaceGuidance

Unknown workspace: load_workspace raises NotFoundError("Workspace '<id>' not found."), and _guard_tool turns it into a ToolError with that message. A corrupt workspace file raises the existing PastaError from load_workspace, also surfaced as a ToolError. When the registry declares no fields, `fields` is [] and `undeclared` holds every non-empty stored value. A workspace with no stored config returns every field with text null and undeclared {}. No input validation is added beyond what load_workspace already does.

Each field entry is {field, description, text}. The description comes off the field's WorkspaceGuidanceSpec, which load-time validation keeps identical across declaring types, so it is one value per field. Rejected: text only, which tells an agent nothing about what an unset field is for unless it calls describePageType on every type. Also rejected: adding per-type applicability ({type: [statuses]}), which needs a new walk of the registry duplicating describePageType's guidanceFor listing and grows the tool past its ask.

Stored keys no page type declares are returned under a separate `undeclared` map, non-empty values only, sorted by key. Rejected: dropping them, which hides data setWorkspaceGuidance cannot even clear because it rejects an undeclared field. Also rejected: listing them in `fields`, where they would read as live guidance although no page will ever surface them. Pruning them is out of scope; this tool only reads.

A field cleared with "" and a field never set both read as text: null. That matches the setter contract (an empty string clears the field) and the emission rule in store.workspace_guidance, which skips both alike. Rejected: returning "" for a cleared field and null for an absent one, which surfaces a storage artefact no reader acts on.

change.component: The outline read: Store.outline in src/store.py, exposed unchanged by the outline MCP tool in src/server.py (whose docstring describes the response).

summary.body: Today outline returns a page's pageId, type, title and its section tree (key, name, order, field kinds), and no status. feature-brief:mwb4vimq-9d0dd3.title: Record workspace events at the store transactions

summary.body:
Every change to a workspace should leave a durable trace, written by the change itself rather than reconstructed later. This brief builds the recording half of that: a bounded, persisted event log inside the workspace file, appended by the store's write transactions in the same atomic commit as the change they describe.

Concretely it introduces a pure event module (the record shape, bounded append with two caps, the baseline snapshot, a page summary), adds the four fields the workspace file needs to carry the log, funnels the store's twelve lock-load-save transactions through one helper that carries the actor and stamps the 'tracking began' baseline once, records what each transaction actually did (status transitions, element FSM marks, structural facts, one authoring event per batch), and exposes a read-only timeline_payload that derives the baseline in memory when nothing has been written yet.

It is worth building because the timeline is only honest if an event can neither exist without its change nor a change without its event; recording at the single write choke point is what makes that true for the MCP tools and the web UI alike. This slice ships as a tested backend with no UI: it defines the event record, the transaction hook and the payload as shared contracts, and the timeline page consumes them in a later wave.

items.name: src/store.py
items.text: The effectful shell: file storage, per-workspace locking, guarded writes. Confirmed: twelve mutating methods each repeat the same preamble (with self._transaction_lock_for(...): workspace = self.load_workspace(...) ... self._touch_and_save(workspace)) at create_page:564, mutate_page_batch:595, cleanup_workspace:688, _set_page_archive_state:724, set_page_status:773, reparent_page:819, reorder_page:855, rename_page:882, link_page:936, unlink_page:953, _set_workspace_status:966, set_workspace_guidance:994; plus create_workspace:230 which takes its own lock and ends in a single _write_file. This file also builds check_specs in mutate_page_batch (:610-615) - the entry's own CommandSpec plus every CompoundCommand step - and is where the new _transaction helper, the actor keyword, event appends, tracking_began seeding and the read-only timeline_payload go.

The design's prose says the 256 KiB byte budget is shared 'across both' ring buffers, but its interface contract for the pure module is append(events, event, cap) - a single list, with BYTE_BUDGET declared as a module constant. Is the budget enforced per buffer by append, or across both buffers by the store?
items.answer: Per buffer, enforced inside append. append receives one list and one cap, so it trims that list until it is within both cap and BYTE_BUDGET; each buffer therefore cannot exceed 256 KiB, and the two together are bounded at 512 KiB in the worst case and far below it in practice. The store never measures the two jointly, because that would need a second pure function whose only caller would be the store.

items.text: Which commands count as authoring content for the single page.field event of a batch - does setTitle or addLink count, or only the typed field setters?
items.answer: Only commands the existing is_field_setter classifier accepts: setScalar, setProse, addElement (including the element-FSM adds) and a page-level addBlocks. setTitle does not count because it records page.renamed, and addLink does not count because it records page.link_added. So the batch's first field setter is the first command in it for which is_field_setter is true, and a batch of only setTitle or addLink commands records no page.field at all.

items.text: When the cleanup sweep prunes a page and its subtree, does page.deleted get recorded once for the maximal pruned root, or once per page actually destroyed?
items.answer: Once per page actually destroyed, the root and every descendant removed with it, each with its own title at event time. A subtree prune is several pages ceasing to exist and the timeline is a record of pages, so collapsing it to the root would leave the descendants' last state unexplained. The design's own precedent for a cascade is one event per affected page.

items.text: Should the twelve repeated lock-load-save preambles collapse into one _transaction helper, or should each transaction insert its own record call?
items.answer: Collapse them into one _transaction context manager that also seeds the baseline and carries the actor. Twelve hand-inserted record calls would be twelve places to forget the baseline and each would repeat the same check; hooking _touch_and_save instead is impossible because it does not know what changed and so cannot build a typed event.

items.text: How should an element FSM transition be detected inside mutate_page_batch - by reusing the check_specs list the batch already builds, by changing the pure core's CommandResult, or by scanning only top-level commands?
items.answer: Reuse the check_specs list mutate_page_batch already builds for the entry and every compound step, reading each ElementTransitionCommand's element status before and after the apply. The pure core stays clock-free and storage-free, no hook is added to apply_command, and a nested compound step records exactly like a top-level command - which a top-level-only scan would silently drop.

items.text: How is the tracking-began marker guaranteed on a workspace nobody has written since the feature shipped, and may a GET write it?
items.answer: The marker is unconditional and a GET never writes. The first write persists tracking_began through _transaction; create_workspace seeds it at creation; and timeline_payload derives the identical value in memory at generatedAt whenever the persisted field is still None. The derived marker invents no per-page timestamp and no ordering, so it is not the fabricated history the person ruled out, and the persisted value wins on every later read.

items.text: Does the timeline payload carry page section content, or only labels, kinds, times and a click-through target?
items.answer: Neither route and no payload ever contains page section content. The payload carries events, elementMarks, trackingBegan, a page map of title/type/status/archived, generatedAt, truncated and caps - labels, kinds, times and a click-through target, nothing more.

items.text: What does the new event log do about src/event_cache.py, which already uses the word 'event' for a transient in-process TTL cache?
items.answer: The two stay separate modules with separate lifetimes. src/event_cache.py remains the transient, disposable in-process de-duplication cache it is today; the new persisted log lives in src/eventlog.py and is never wired to the cache. Both docstrings say so, because a later reader who confuses them could wire the timeline to something designed to be lost.

# src/eventlog.py
"""The pure event log: record shape, bounded append, baseline and page summary.

An event is a flat, JSON-able dict with a fixed key set, appended by a store transaction
into the same workspace write as the change it describes. Nothing here reads the clock or
touches disk: the caller passes the `at` string in.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from typing import Any, Final

from .model import Page, Workspace

EVENT_CAP: Final[int] = 1000
ELEMENT_CAP: Final[int] = 1500
BYTE_BUDGET: Final[int] = 256 * 1024


def make(
    kind: str,
    at: str,
    *,
    page: Page | None = None,
    actor: str = "agent",
    from_: str | bool | int | None = None,
    to: str | bool | int | None = None,
    event: str | None = None,
    section: str | None = None,
    field: str | None = None,
    element_id: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """One event dict carrying every key of the record shape."""
    return {
        "at": at,
        "kind": kind,
        "pageId": page.id if page is not None else None,
        "pageType": page.type if page is not None else None,
        "title": page.title if page is not None else None,
        "actor": actor,
        "from": from_,
        "to": to,
        "event": event,
        "section": section,
        "field": field,
        "elementId": element_id,
    }

def append(events: list[dict[str, Any]], event: dict[str, Any], cap: int) -> bool:
    """Append `event`, then trim oldest-first to `cap` and to BYTE_BUDGET.

    Returns True when anything was trimmed. Never raises on a well-formed event.
    """
    events.append(event)
    trimmed = False
    while len(events) > cap:
        events.pop(0)
        trimmed = True
    return trimmed

def create_workspace(self, name: str) -> Workspace:
        if not name or not name.strip():
            raise ValidationError("Workspace name must be a non-empty string.")
        workspace = Workspace(id=new_id("ws"), name=name,
                              created_at=_now(), updated_at=_now())
        with self._transaction_lock_for(workspace.id):
            workspace.tracking_began = eventlog.baseline(workspace, at=_now())
            self._write_file(self._path_for(workspace.id), workspace)
        return workspace

    def _set_workspace_status(self, workspace_id: str, status: str, *,
                              actor: str = "agent") -> Workspace:
        with self._transaction(workspace_id, actor=actor) as tx:
            tx.workspace.status = status
        return tx.workspace

# /tmp/bench_recording.py  - throwaway, outside the repo, never committed
import statistics
import sys
import tempfile
import time

sys.path.insert(0, "/a0/usr/workdir/timeline-build-events")

from src import eventlog
from src.store import Store


def run(recording: bool) -> tuple[float, float]:
    if not recording:
        eventlog.append = lambda events, event, cap: False   # type: ignore[assignment]
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as root:
        store = Store(root)
        workspace = store.create_workspace("bench")
        page = store.create_page(workspace.id, "test-fields", "Title").page
        timings = []
        for index in range(200):
            token = store.get_page(workspace.id, page.id).status_revision_token
            start = time.perf_counter()
            store.mutate_page_batch(workspace.id, page.id,
                                    [{"command": "setTitle",
                                      "args": {"title": f"T{index}",
                                               "statusRevisionToken": token}}])
            timings.append((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
        timings.sort()
        mean = statistics.mean(timings)
        p95 = timings[int(len(timings) * 0.95) - 1]
        return mean, p95


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("on ", run(True))
    print("off", run(False))

# src/model.py - Workspace gains four fields, each defaulted so the dataclass stays
# constructible without them and existing callers are unaffected.
@dataclass
class Workspace:
    id: str
    name: str
    status: str = "active"
    root_page_ids: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    pages: dict[str, Page] = field(default_factory=dict)
    created_at: str = ""
    updated_at: str = ""
    guidance_config: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    # --- workspace event log ---
    events: list[dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=list)         # cap 1000
    element_marks: list[dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=list)  # cap 1500
    tracking_began: dict[str, Any] | None = None                       # {"at", "pages"}, written once
    events_truncated: bool = False                                     # any trim ever happened


# src/store.py - the transaction handle.
@dataclass
class Tx:
    workspace: Workspace
    actor: str          # 'agent' | 'person'
    at: str             # _now(), shared by every event of this transaction

# src/eventlog.py - the constants and the exact record shape eventlog.make() returns.
# Every key is always present; a fact the kind does not use is None.
EVENT_CAP: Final[int] = 1000
ELEMENT_CAP: Final[int] = 1500
BYTE_BUDGET: Final[int] = 256 * 1024      # per buffer, enforced inside append()

EVENT_KEYS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "at", "kind", "pageId", "pageType", "title", "actor",
    "from", "to", "event", "section", "field", "elementId",
)

# EVENT_KEYS[i] holds, per kind:
#   at        str    UTC ISO-8601, exactly _now()'s format
#   kind      str    page.created | page.status | page.field | page.renamed |
#                    page.reparented | page.reordered | page.archived |
#                    page.unarchived | page.delete_scheduled | page.delete_cancelled |
#                    page.deleted | page.link_added | page.link_removed |
#                    element.mark | workspace.created | workspace.status
#   pageId    str|None    None only for workspace.* kinds
#   pageType  str|None    the page's type tag; None for workspace.* kinds
#   title     str|None    the title AT EVENT TIME
#   actor     str         'agent' | 'person'
#   from      str|bool|int|None   previous status / title / parent id / index / role /
#                                 workspace status; None where the kind has no previous value
#   to        str|bool|int|None   new status / title / parent id / index / target page id /
#                                 the boolean flag that moved / workspace status
#   event     str|None    the FSM event or command name that fired it
#   section   str|None    element.mark only
#   field     str|None    element.mark only, or 'section.field' on page.field
#   elementId str|None    element.mark only

// Store.timeline_payload(workspace_id) -> exactly these nine keys, oldest first,
// and never page section content.
{
  "workspaceId": "ws:mrteq0c5-238cf6",
  "name": "Pasta MCP Server",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-10T19:48:11.902+00:00",
  "trackingBegan": {"at": "2026-11-10T19:40:00.000+00:00",
                    "pages": [{"id": "toc:ms90f9jm-c68d70", "type": "toc",
                               "title": "Documentation", "status": "active"}]},
  "events": [{"at": "...", "kind": "page.status", "pageId": "...",
              "pageType": "feature-brief", "title": "...", "actor": "agent",
              "from": "draft", "to": "ready", "event": "markReady",
              "section": null, "field": null, "elementId": null}],
  "elementMarks": [{"at": "...", "kind": "element.mark", "pageId": "...",
                    "pageType": "implementation-plan", "title": "...",
                    "actor": "agent", "from": "todo", "to": "done",
                    "event": "markStepDone", "section": "steps",
                    "field": "items", "elementId": "mw..."}],
  "pages": {"feature-brief:mwfc3sbi-d512cc": {"title": "...", "type": "feature-brief",

items.text: Pure record shape: eventlog.make returns a dict with exactly the twelve keys at, kind, pageId, pageType, title, actor, from, to, event, section, field, elementId, in that fixed set, with actor defaulting to "agent" and every unused fact None. Carried by tests/test_eventlog.py::test_make_fills_every_key_for_a_page, ::test_make_without_a_page_nulls_the_page_facts and ::test_make_carries_the_element_facts. Fails if a key is missing or renamed.

Cap trim, oldest first: appending five events to a list with cap 3 leaves the three newest in order and append returns False, False, False, True, True. Carried by tests/test_eventlog.py::test_append_trims_to_the_cap_oldest_first. Fails if the newest event is dropped instead of the oldest.
Cap boundary: appending to a list already within the cap returns False and adds the event without dropping anything. Carried by tests/test_eventlog.py::test_append_leaves_a_list_within_the_cap_alone.

Byte budget per buffer: with BYTE_BUDGET monkeypatched to 600 and three events of about 250 bytes each, append leaves only the newest event and reports a trim, and with a 100 kB budget a single 200-byte event reports no trim. Carried by tests/test_eventlog.py::test_append_trims_to_the_byte_budget and ::test_append_stops_trimming_once_it_fits_the_byte_budget. Fails if the budget is never applied or trims the newest event.

Baseline snapshot: baseline walks root_page_ids depth-first through child ids and returns {"at": <the passed instant>, "pages": [{"id", "type", "title", "status"}, ...]}, including an archived page and terminating on a self-referencing child id. Carried by tests/test_eventlog.py::test_baseline_lists_pages_depth_first_with_status, ::test_baseline_includes_archived_pages and ::test_baseline_survives_a_cycle_in_a_corrupt_file. Fails if it drops pages, invents a timestamp, or loops.

Page summary: page_summary maps every page id to {title, type, status, archived} and carries no sections key, even when the page has section content. Carried by tests/test_eventlog.py::test_page_summary_maps_every_page_without_section_content and ::test_page_summary_carries_no_sections. Fails if a body leaks into the payload map.

Serialization round trip for the four new workspace keys: a workspace carrying events, element_marks, tracking_began and events_truncated=True survives workspace_to_dict then workspace_from_dict unchanged. Carried by tests/test_serialize.py::test_workspace_event_fields_round_trip.

Backward-compatible defaults: a workspace dict with the four keys deleted loads with events == [], element_marks == [], tracking_began is None and events_truncated is False, so every file written before this change still loads. Carried by tests/test_serialize.py::test_workspace_event_fields_default_for_legacy_files.

Tracking-began seeded once on the first write: after create_workspace and one create_page the workspace on disk carries a tracking_began whose pages list holds that page's id, type, title and status; a later rename leaves the stored tracking_began byte-identical. Carried by tests/test_store.py::test_transaction_seeds_tracking_began_on_the_first_write and ::test_transaction_keeps_the_first_tracking_began. Fails if the marker is rewritten on every write.

Unknown actor refused before any write: rename_page(..., actor="robot") raises ValidationError and the workspace file's bytes are unchanged. Carried by tests/test_store.py::test_transaction_rejects_an_unknown_actor_before_writing. This is the error path the spec adds and it must not leave a partial write.

page.created recorded per created page: create_page on a plain fixture appends exactly one page.created with the new page's id, type, title and actor "agent"; create_page on a type with pinned auto-children (test-lifecycle) appends one page.created per page, including the auto-created test-child; create_workspace appends workspace.created. Carried by tests/test_store.py::test_create_page_records_page_created, ::test_create_workspace_records_workspace_created and ::test_create_page_records_one_event_per_pinned_child.

page.status recorded from a batch, in the same write: running a test-flow page through open appends exactly one page.status with from "draft", to "open" and event "open", and the event is present in the same file read that shows the new status, so no change exists without its event and no event without its change. Carried by tests/test_store.py::test_mutate_batch_records_a_status_transition.

Structural facts from a batch: setTitle appends page.renamed with from the previous title and to the new one; addLink appends page.link_added with from the role and to the target page id. Carried by tests/test_store.py::test_mutate_batch_records_one_renamed_event and ::test_mutate_batch_records_link_events.

Aborted batch records nothing: a mutate_page_batch rejected on a stale statusRevisionToken raises ConflictError and leaves the workspace's events list exactly as it was, and the file unchanged. Carried by tests/test_store.py::test_aborted_batch_records_nothing. This is the same-commit guarantee's failure path and must fail if events are appended before the abort.

Element mark recorded with its full identity: marking a test-child plan step done appends exactly one element.mark to element_marks (never to events) carrying section "steps", field "items", the step's elementId, from "todo", to "done" and event "markDone". Structural facts recorded: reparent_page records page.reparented with from the previous parent id (None at top level) and to the new parent id; reorder_page records page.reordered with the previous and new sibling index; unlink_page after a link records page.link_removed with from the role and to the target id, in order with the earlier page.link_added.
